Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:41:23 GMT

The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

"This is simply unacceptable."

Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.

"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.

"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."

Kate Parker, criminal barrister and founder of the Schools Consent Project, said legally, a third party or a partner cannot consent on a person's behalf.

"The law makes that very clear. A person consents if he or she agrees by choice and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice," she added.

"In a case like this where someone has been made unconscious, there is no possible way that that person is able to consent because of course they have no capacity."

She added that the defendants' claims that they thought Joanne Young had consented through her husband "doesn't make sense legally, and that's not a legal position that can be supported in court".

Parker said the defence used by the four men in the trial is not a correct application of the law but might be something defence lawyers would try and rely on as their client's genuine belief in their victim's consent, or in mitigation to try and get a lower sentence.

Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.

"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.

"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."

Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.

"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.

"So why are they still accessible?" she said.

Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.

"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.

"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."

Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.

"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.

"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help others when this has happened to them."

Zoe Watts is the founder of a global campaign called End Eye Check that works to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse.

Like Joanne Young and Bishop, Watts waived her right to anonymity after she was drugged and raped by her husband.

Watts hopes that Joanne Young's case "sets a precedent", but told Woman's Hour that the crime is more widespread than many realise.

"I have had women contact me from 25 different countries," she said.

"It's a daily process of women either contacting me because they've woken up to find their husband having sex with them while they're asleep and have done on numerous occasions.

"Or perhaps they're not sure if they've been drugged or maybe they are genuinely asleep and wake up and find him that way, or women that have found videos or recordings on their phone of things they haven't consented to," Watts added.

Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC that more needs to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.

"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.

"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.

"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."

Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told Radio 4's Woman's Hour that current laws do not do enough to protect women.

"The law says that somebody can seek a defence to defend themselves against a rape claim if they reasonably believe that they had consent," said Phillips.

"These people went on to argue that they reasonably believed that Joanne's husband had sought her consent and got it.

"They were found guilty, but it's whether the law needs to explicitly say, 'you cannot reasonably believe someone's given consent unless they have given it'.

"If there was clarity in the law, Joanne wouldn't have been put through the court case," Phillips added.

She also believes that more needs to be done to hold the websites hosting adverts and similar content to account.

"Can every pornographic site in our country categorically say that not one of these snuff videos or sedated videos is on their site?

"Unless they can guarantee it with a signed piece of paper from the person that they know is in that video [they should not be published]," Phillips said.

Sarah Hammond, the chief crown prosecutor at the CPS who oversees many complex sexual offence cases involving drugs, said Joanne's "incredibly powerful" statement after the convictions "laid bare the devastating impact of the horrific abuse she had suffered over so many years".

"A lot of people may not know exactly what consent means in law, but the principle is simple. Consent must be a free choice made by someone who has the freedom and capacity to make it, and nobody else can give consent on their behalf," she said.

"In this case, the evidence proved that not only did Joanne not consent to the sexual activity, but that the perpetrators could not reasonably believe that she was consenting.

"This meant asking what steps the perpetrators had taken to establish consent for themselves, rather than relying on assumptions or what somebody else had told them.

"The convictions of Philip Young, Dean Hamilton, Norman Macksoni, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins and Mohammed Hassan send a clear message: consent is something you establish with the person themselves, and where someone is drugged or otherwise incapacitated, they cannot make that choice."

Wiltshire Police Supt Int Geoff Smith, the lead investigating officer in the case, said he hoped the guilty verdicts made women feel "safer".

"I hope that men take note about seeking consent and what's required from them, and I hope that women feel more able and confident to come forward and speak out," he said.

"I really hope it makes a difference."

Man jailed for murder of woman drowned in Thames

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:59:20 GMT

A man has been jailed for life with a minimum of 22 years and six months after he murdered a woman, who was found drowned in the River Thames, while serving a suspended prison sentence.

The body of Jennifer Symonds, 44, was recovered from the river at Phyllis Court Club in Henley-on-Thames on the morning of 6 March 2026.

Last month, Nelio Gouveia, 45, of Phyllis Court Drive, Henley-on-Thames, pleaded guilty to her murder during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court.

During a hearing at the same court on Friday, Gouveia was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder and ordered to serve at least 22 years and six months behind bars.

It can now also be reported that Gouveia had been serving a two-year suspended prison sentence for a violent attack on a woman at the time of the murder.

Jailing him on Friday, Judge Jay said Gouveia's actions "stemmed from your propensity in certain circumstances to violence against women".

Reacting to the sentence, Gouveia, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey tracksuit and clutching white rosary beads, looked down at the floor.

His defence had earlier told the hearing that "he doesn't feel he is worthy of forgiveness and is deeply remorseful of what he has done".

Friday's hearing was told that Gouveia and Symonds had likely met on Red Lion Lawn in Henley and had been exchanging infrequent text messages.

On 5 March, the pair agreed to meet up at the theatre in the town, before spending the night together.

Gouveia then left Symonds at a pavilion by the water at Phyllis Court in the early hours, before he returned with a metal weight lifting dumbbell and attacked her.

CCTV of the attack was not played in court, with the judge describing it as "deeply disturbing and upsetting".

Thames Valley Police launched a murder investigation after being called to Phyllis Court Drive at about 07:50 GMT on 6 March.

Gouveia was arrested the same day, and charged on 8 March. A post-mortem examination showed Symonds had died from drowning.

Portugal-born Gouveia worked and lived as a kitchen porter at the Phyllis Court private members' club on the banks of the River Thames.

The court heard a fellow employee at the members' club had reported that Gouveia said: "If girls are annoying and aren't behaving, you just hit them."

The 45-year-old was sentenced in 2024 to a two year suspended prison sentence for assault occasioning actual bodily harm after he punched a woman in the face in 2022.

Gouveia also poured red wine over the victim, before hitting her over the head with a bottle.

"I genuinely believed that he was going to kill me or cause me some serious harm," the victim said afterwards.

Symonds was born in Zambia and moved to the UK aged three. She had worked for Microsoft until being made redundant in 2025.

Before her death, the court was told she had been seeking to rejoin the army cadets as a volunteer.

At Friday's hearing, Symonds' older brother Andrew emotionally described her as "vivacious" and "outgoing" with a "quiet sense of rebellion wrapped in imagination and warmth".

In a statement read out by the prosecution, her parents said she had been "loving kind, generous and caring" and "touched so many lives in a really positive way".

"She was an integral part of our lives. The grief and trauma is devastating," they added.

The court was also told that Symonds had pursued many outdoor activities and enjoyed being out in nature and by the river in Henley.

Her friend, Gary Hamilton, told the BBC ahead of the hearing that she loved spending time on his boat, and would "try any new adventure".

"Her laugh was very infectious", he said. "She was really, very, very bubbly."

"She'd always be looking out for people. So if anybody was wanting a conversation or down or anything, I know she'd go to them."

"The whole community has been mourning for her."

Symonds' friend Cameron Finlay-Cooper, 32, described the moment he found out about her death as a "sucker punch".

"It's just abhorrently awful, there's no other word to describe it. It really is just a wound that a lot of people are trying to recover from," he told the BBC.

"She really was loved by everyone in this town," he said, adding that his friend would be remembered for being a "really incredible person".

Jonathan Barter wants to install a memorial to his friend near to her favourite spot along the River Thames.

"It just occurred to me that perhaps the town council would consider allowing us to put a plaque in her memory."

Suggesting the Red Lion Lawn in Henley as its location, he said: "She lived just up the road here.. and I think was really her quiet place."

"I thought we mustn't let Jen be forgotten."

Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:55:11 GMT

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) with director of football Jason Wilcox

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.

Andrey Santos has started four Premier League games for Manchester United since his £50m summer move from Chelsea

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.

Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."

This video can not be played

Pochettino on his arrival at Man Utd

Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.

He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."

Two men dead after glider crashes into Loch Leven

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:54:52 GMT

Two men have died after a glider crashed into Loch Leven.

Police, ambulance, fire service and the coastguard were called to the scene near Kinross at about 11:00.

The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield near the loch, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight" but it was not clear what had caused the crash.

Police Scotland said the deaths were not being treated as suspicious and inquiries were ongoing to establish the full circumstances.

Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:54:29 GMT

Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Stacked England aim to pile on style and add to All Black misery

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:51:17 GMT

England thumped Japan 78-15 last weekend

There is a string of symbols tattooed on to Will Stuart's left foot.

A circle, two triangles, an up arrow, another circle, R1, L2, an up arrow, a triangle, and, finally L1 three times.

If you know, in this week of all weeks, you know.

England and British and Irish Lions star Stuart is indelibly, if jokingly, stamped with a Grand Theft Auto cheat code,, external which gives your character maximum in-game sex appeal.

In the absence of the injured Stuart and his cheat code at the start of this year, England certainly lost their mojo.

They had a terrible Six Nations. They were comfortably held at bay by South Africa. Five straight defeats ramped up pressure on the squad and their staff.

Stuart has now returned from a ruptured Achilles tendon and, with him, so has England's swagger.

Against Australia and Japan, England scored 20 tries.

They are ranked top of the Nations Championship for points scored and entries into the opposition 22m. Their attack has shown dexterity of a card sharp, with the sophistication of a socialite.

Those are the sort of intricacies needed to befuddle the best defences.

"We want England to support us. We want to bring joy to them," said head coach Steve Borthwick this week.

So far, this autumn, that objective has been achieved. Twickenham has been seduced by two charismatic displays which have been high on entertainment, if low on jeopardy.

Saturday will undoubtedly be different.

New Zealand are sore. Last weekend's defeat by Wales - their first in 73 years - stung. Coach Dave Rennie's public accusation that the players had "let the country down" will have salted wounds.

He may well have said the same of the insipid performance the team put up in a 33-19 defeat by England last year, under his predecessor Scott Robertson.

The Rennie-ssance overseen by their new boss, with wins over France, Ireland and South Africa in his first few months in charge, has given way to talk of looming crisis.

New Zealand have lost four of their past seven matches after going down 3-1 in the 'Greatest Rivalry' series against South Africa and losing to Wales last weekend

All Black backs are up hard against a brick wall. And big names - Will Jordan, Jordie Barrett, Cam Roigard and Damian McKenzie - are back to blast their way out of a hole.

England have had their fun over the past couple of weeks.

One of the benefits of being in the northern half of the Nations Championship is a steadier supply of fodder.

Fiji and Japan - the two teams invited to fill out the southern half of the new competition - have won only one of 10 games between them and have a combined points difference of minus 257.

Despite last week's reverse, New Zealand - along with world champions South Africa - are where southern-hemisphere quality is concentrated. And where England's revival will be truly stress-tested.

The comeback of Stuart, and others, has been key for England.

England made a clean sweep of their last autumn campaign, with a high-calibre set of replacements key.

Any lingering final-quarter hopes for the visitors were flushed out by England's depth on the bench.

Stuart is playing the front-row super-sub once again. Fin Baxter - another long-time injury absentee - starts at loosehead, to allow England to rotate between two top-class front rows.

George Martin - an old-school second row enforcer who is recently back from his own 14-month lay-off - is on a bench, also including Henry Pollock and Marcus Smith, loaded with stardust and points to prove.

George Furbank, whose running threat and playmaking ability from deep adds an extra dimension to attack, starts at full-back after a rotten run of knocks and set-backs.

Captain Maro Itoje seems rejuvenated by a summer off. Ollie Chessum is perhaps in the best form of his life. Seb Atkinson - still only eight caps into his Test career - has brought a mix of hard running and soft skills to 12.

Will Joseph's pace, power, good form and ability to play in midfield, as well as on the wing, has thrust him right into Rugby World Cup reckoning.

England aren't at full strength. Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tom Curry and Alex Mitchell are big misses. Sam Underhill and Guy Pepper too.

But injuries are inevitable. And England, at the moment, are relatively fully loaded.

"The last time we had this depth was a year ago," Borthwick said, drawing an implicit link back to England's purple patch of 12 straight wins through 2025 and the very start of 2026.

The mood music, like the performances, has been good.

Itoje suggested there was a renewed sense of purpose and ownership in camp. Borthwick credited the players with leading a successful drive to improve discipline.

Attack coach Lee Blackett's fingerprints are all over some of the attacking shapes thrown over the past fortnight.

The momentum is real.

Victory over New Zealand, of any kind, would stomp the accelerator to the floor.

If it comes with eye candy, all the better.

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:41:52 GMT

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

Daniel Thomas jailed for 15 months for slashing dinghy

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:39:49 GMT

Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said it was "more a matter of luck than judgement that serious consequences did not arise".

The dinghy was later destroyed by French authorities, meaning the value of the damage could not be proven.

Judge James Newton-Price KC said it was "not for me to make any judgement of the political cause," but that the attack was "intended to have an impact on a live audience".

Commenting on the Border Force, coastguard and RNLI crews, he said: "They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover."

Simon Pentol KC, defending, said the dinghy did not sink and made its way back to France without help.

The judge accepted that prison had caused hardship for Thomas's family, including his four children. He said the sentence would have been 20 months had he gone to trial, and his time on remand would count towards it.

A separate charge of failing to give police the PIN to his phone, which Thomas denied, was ordered to lie on his file.

He is due to stand trial at Westminster Magistrates' Court in June over separate alleged offences in Dover, which he denies.

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:19:08 GMT

Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".

In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.

That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.

That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government.

And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it.

This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government.

And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.

Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.

Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway.

At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.

Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go.

But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.

There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.

First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election.

In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union.

That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.

Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU.

That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives.

Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too.

That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.

And what of the domestic politics of this?

Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.

Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different.

He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation.

Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too.

Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.

This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble.

Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business.

Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?

On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years.

He was talking principally about economic transformation.

But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:07:55 GMT

The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."

One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.

A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.

If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.

British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.

The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.

The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.

The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.

The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme.

In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".

Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why... are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?

"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"

Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.

The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.

Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.

He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

'Dishonest' police officers sacked for lying over fatal crash searches

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:56:06 GMT

Two officers who lied about carrying out missing person searches linked to a crash in which three people died have been sacked after being found guilty at a police misconduct hearing.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

Members of Smith's family described the verdict as "an important step towards accountability".

Following the proceedings, Smith's mother Emma Borg said the family had to repeatedly revisit the "most painful period" of their lives.

She said her family felt their honesty and credibility was being "questioned" at a time when they "trusted the police to do their jobs".

"Instead, the dishonesty established during these proceedings undermined the missing persons' investigation and the trust our families desperately needed to have in those responsible for helping us," she added.

Lauren Doyle, Smith's sister, said they "never wanted to spend years scrutinising police decisions" and called the outcome of the proceedings an "important step".

She added: "Our search for answers continues. We will never lose sight of why we started."

The police watchdog call the officers' actions "inexcusable with both failing in the fundamental basics of policing".

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said a final written warning was not an option because the level of harm and culpability was too high. He also said there was a lack of mitigating factors.

Hardwick and Livingstone had deliberately misled a missing persons investigation, he added, which may have compromised the investigation, and had undermined public trust in the police in a high-profile case.

Hardwick faced six allegations, including that he lied about searching the homes of crash victims Smith and Russon, and that he also lied to his supervising officer and the police watchdog.

Livingstone faced four allegations, including that she lied about searching the two houses, as well as making a dishonest entry on the log and lying to her supervising officer.

The police disciplinary hearing at Rodney Parade, which lasted four days, was told that both officers were part of the team assigned to look into reports that Eve Smith, Darcy Ross and Sophie Russon had gone missing after a night out on Friday 3 March 2023.

The three women were reported missing to Gwent Police on 4 March, but were not found until 30 hours after the initial contact by the families.

Five people were found in a car in a wooded area off the A48, 46 hours after the vehicle had crashed.

Three of the cars occupants, Eve Smith, Rafel Jeanne, and Darcy Ross had died, and two, Sophie Russon and Shane Loughlin, were seriously injured.

Hardwick and Livingstone went to Russon's home and then on to Smith's house, and as part of Gwent Police's missing person policy were supposed to search the address to look for clues for what might have happened to them.

Hardwick wrote in the official log afterwards "premise search conducted" and told the police sergeant overseeing the case that the search at Russon's house had been carried out. He also said searches had happened when he spoke to the police watchdog, the IOPC, who later investigated.

This was in contrast to what Russon's father, Nathan, told the hearing, that the officers were at the house for a very short period and did not ask to search the bedroom.

Livingstone said she could not remember whether searches had taken place, but wrote what she agreed was a "poorly written" report in the official log, which the panel head heard was "deliberately vague" but suggested a search had taken place.

The panel found Hardwick and Livingstone had failed to conduct a search at Smith and Russon's homes.

Hardwick was found to have provided a false entry into the police log and had provided a dishonest statement when interviewed by the IOPC.

He had been found, in part, to have given a dishonest account of the search to his supervisor and found in part to have provided a dishonest account in a signed statement to the IOPC.

Livingstone was found to also have provided a false entry into the police log and to have had given a dishonest account of the search to her supervisor.

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said their behaviour had caused harm because of the impact on the family and had undermined public trust in the police in a case which resulted in significant levels of concern from the public.

Derrick Campbell, from the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said the officers failed to "act honestly and with integrity", saying property searches were a "basic but essential part in the early stages of a missing person investigation".

"PC Hardwick deliberately lied during the course of the missing person investigation, claiming on police records and to his supervisor that searches had been completed.

"PC Livingstone had ample opportunity to tell the IOPC the required searches had not been conducted.

"Instead, she did not give an account and stated she could not remember the specifics of her visits to the homes of two of the young women who had been reported missing," Campbell said.

Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:42:37 GMT

A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.

Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

Percy Jackson returns as teen stars adapt to life in the limelight

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:43:35 GMT

Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.

As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.

The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.

Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.

"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."

But it's not the only part.

Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.

His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.

Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".

"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."

The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.

An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.

So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.

"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.

"So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."

Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.

"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.

"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."

It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".

The first series was hugely successful with the opening episode of it reaching 13.3 million viewers, according to entertainment data company Luminate.

That dipped to just over 11 million for the second series and the cast is hoping a fresh take on the story will keep fans interested.

"I personally really like seeing people theorise about what's going to make it," says Simhadri.

"People who have read the books like talking about how they think we're going to adapt it, I love reading those."

It's been a big year for Greek mythology adaptations, with Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey getting huge box office numbers and critical acclaim.

Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Athena's daughter Annabeth Chase, says its popularity could be down to how people connect the ancient stories to their own lives.

"There's stories for everyone," she says.

"You can have a family where the dad is obsessed with The Odyssey but the children are too young, so they can just watch Percy Jackson.

"I feel like there's probably a cooking show about Greek mythology at that point, I mean like there's so many connections no matter what you like."

Percy Jackson is released on Disney+ and Hulu on Friday 20 November.

UK braces for coldest night of autumn so far with temperature of -10C forecast

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 08:12:15 GMT

The UK will experience the coldest night of autumn so far overnight on Friday, with a widespread frost developing as temperatures plummet below zero.

It will be particularly cold in northern areas, where temperatures of minus 1 (30F) to minus 5C (23F) are widely expected from the Midlands northward.

However, in rural areas of Scotland where there is some lying snow, it could get as low as minus 10C (14F).

It will stay cold with more overnight frost over the weekend, with cold health alerts from the UK's Health Security Agency remaining in force across northern England until Monday morning.

Frost is expected in many areas of the UK from the Midlands northward overnight on Friday into Saturday. This map shows temperatures expected at 06:00 GMT on Saturday.

The coldest night of the autumn so far was on Thursday night when the temperature got down to minus 8.4C (18F) at Tulloch Bridge, Highland.

Temperatures for many of us have been up and down recently due to cold Arctic air temporarily sweeping southward across the UK.

Southern areas of the UK have mostly held onto milder air from the Atlantic.

During Friday though a northerly wind will once again bring some of the colder air from the Arctic, and bring a colder day for most of the UK.

Any early cloud and rain in southern England will clear and for most of the UK it will be a bright day with some sunshine. A few wintry showers are possible across Scotland.

By night, temperatures will drop with frost expected widely, mostly across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Although it is likely to be the coldest night of the autumn so far, with minus 10C predicted in rural Scotland, we are a long way off the coldest November night on record, when a temperature of minus 16.1C was recorded in Cumbria in 1912.

We came closer to that record low temperature in 2025, when the UK experienced the coldest November night in 12 years with minus 12.6C in Moray.

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

How to look after dogs, cats and other pets in cold weather

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

After a cold start on Saturday morning, there will be a lot of dry and mostly sunny weather across the UK.

But milder air will start to move into the south-west of England again along with areas of cloud and rain by the end of the day.

Saturday night will not be as cold for most but frost is still likely to cover large areas of north-east England and much of Scotland with temperatures widely dropping to between zero and minus 5C.

Rain will continue on Sunday in south-west England, south Wales and even into parts of Northern Ireland.

Elsewhere should be mostly dry and while fairly cloudy, there should be some brighter interludes.

Maximum temperatures over the weekend will be on the colder side of average with 4 to 8C expected.

The polar vortex is the strong wind that circles high above the Arctic.

Very unusually the winds of the polar vortex weakened last week - the earliest time this has happened on record.

In some situations, the weakening of the polar vortex can lead to colder weather and even snow some weeks later.

But it is too soon for this weakening of the polar vortex to be having an influence on our weather.

Instead this colder snap is just part of the variability of weather in the UK.

The polar vortex has started to strengthen again and should get back to its normal strength in the coming weeks.

Scientists are still unsure how or if the weakening last week will have any influence on our weather in weeks to come.

Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:00:33 GMT

"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.

According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.

But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.

It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."

While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.

The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.

"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.

Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.

He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.

Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.

Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.

Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".

He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.

Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.

Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".

It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.

Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".

In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.

Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.

Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".

"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.

The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.

None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.

Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.

"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."

Additional reporting by Lorna Acquah and Abi Smitton
