Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 05:59:56 GMT

After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.

Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.

These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."

The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.

With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.

This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.

The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.

Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.

Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.

But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.

Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.

And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.

The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.

As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.

There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.

Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.

BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.

Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.

"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.

"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."

Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.

Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.

A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.

An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.

A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.

Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.

The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.

"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."

With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.

Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers.

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

Advertisement

Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.

OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.

What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.

In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.

How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses

I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “AI as Normal Technology” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.

The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “impossible” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.

Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.

In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”

Huge extinct orca may have eaten other whales

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Orcas may have been top predators in the ocean for longer than we had thought.

Long ago in the North Sea, massive ancestors of modern orcas may have terrorised other whales. Though the fossil remains are too fragmented to conclusively categorise the orca as a new species, the findings are transforming researchers’ understanding of the animals’ evolution.

“At least 2.5 million years ago, orcas were already very large and capable of hunting large game,” says Hidde Bakker at the Natural History Museum Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

Orcas filmed making sunfish explode by ramming them at high speed

In 1994, fishing vessels trawling the bottom of the southern North Sea between the UK and the coast of the Netherlands pulled up truckloads of fossils and mammoth tusks. Dozens of these fossils, now housed at the museum in Rotterdam, appeared to belong to some large but unknown species of orca (Orcinus) that lived 2.1 million to 2.6 million years ago. But no one had systematically studied them.

Bakker and his colleagues took the five most information-rich specimens – two skull chunks, a jawbone and some vertebrae – and compared them with living and extinct members of the dolphin family, of which orcas are the largest living members.

The only other fossil orca species known, says Bakker, is a 3.5-metre-long species that swam in the Mediterranean Sea around Italy at around the same time as the North Sea orcas were around. Analysis of its fossils suggests that the Mediterranean orca probably predominantly ate fish. But based on certain skeletal and dental clues, the North Sea orca seemed equipped to hunt larger fare.

Free newsletter

For one thing, the orca was enormous. Bakker and his colleagues think it could have been 7.7 metres long, which puts it on par with some of the largest male orcas today. It also had features commonly seen in the modern orca populations – called “ecotypes” – that specialise in hunting marine mammals. In particular, its teeth were set in very deep sockets that were reinforced with bone.

“In most dolphins, that’s not the case,” Bakker says. “It’s just more like a groove with teeth placed in it.”

The orca – which still hasn’t been given a formal new species name – also had a relatively mobile head, which would have allowed it to grip and tear large prey. These traits all hint that this predator could attack other big, powerful animals such as other dolphins or baleen whales.

A group of orcas in Monterey Bay, California, use a submarine canyon to isolate whale calves, and launch coordinated attacks on prey in the open ocean

It is possible that these orcas evolved in the ecological vacuum left behind by the extinction of rapacious, whale-eating sperm whales.

“We have some evidence now that [dolphins] took over their top predator niche,” Bakker says.

Figuring out more precisely when those sperm whales went extinct could help researchers better test that hypothesis, says Olivier Lambert at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. He’s also curious to know whether chemical signatures in the North Sea orcas’ teeth and bones could further confirm their diet and their place in the marine food web.

“Did they already feed on large marine mammals, fish, or a combination?” Lambert says. “This [research] may provide some insights about the emergence of some social skills [in orcas], like the highly coordinated hunting of giant whales.”

Woman entered hibernation-like state during winter for more than 30 years

New Scientist November 19, 2026

A woman experienced episodes of a “hibernation-like” state – when her body temperature dropped as low as 31°C (88°F) – during the winter for more than three decades. A post-mortem analysis suggests this might have been caused by a reduced number of connections between neurons in a brain region called the hypothalamus.

Some warm-blooded animals – such as dormice and ground squirrels – can enter a state called torpor, in which they become less active, reduce their body temperature and slow their metabolism to save energy. Prolonged torpor, known as hibernation, usually occurs during the winter, when food is scarce and temperatures drop.

Low on energy? A new understanding of rest could help revitalise you

While humans don’t have this ability, some researchers think we may have the genetic hardware to enter a reduced energy state, and discovering how to trigger this could have health benefits.

Advertisement

Chun-Xia Yi at the Amsterdam University Medical Centre and her colleagues were studying post-mortem brains, focusing on the hypothalamus – a brain region that controls body temperature, metabolism and the body clock. They came across the brain of a woman from the Netherlands whose medical records said she experienced a “hibernation-like syndrome”.

“When I learned about this particular brain donor, I discovered something quite extraordinary: she had experienced recurrent episodes of hypothermia and reduced activity during winter for more than 30 years, with a documented body temperature as low as 31°C,” says Yi. Most people would develop organ failure at such a low body temperature, but the woman recovered from torpor-like episodes for decades without organ damage, says Yi.

Free newsletter

The woman first developed the syndrome, which caused her to become sluggish, in her early 20s. Her medical records didn’t state how long each episode of torpor-like symptoms lasted, but they didn’t occur in the summer.

MRI scans taken when she was 55 revealed that her brain structure had no unusual features. She donated her brain to the Netherlands Brain Bank before she died at age 57 following unsuccessful surgical treatment for pneumonia, which was seemingly unrelated to her syndrome, says Yi.

There are seven known prior cases of humans seasonally entering a torpor-like state, says Matteo Cerri at the University of Bologna in Italy, who wasn’t involved in the study. But this woman seems to have experienced this for longer than others, and previous case reports didn’t examine people’s brains after they died for any changes that may underlie the torpor-like state, says Cerri.

To explore this, the researchers analysed slices of the woman’s hypothalamus. They found it contained about one-tenth of the amount of a protein called synaptophysin compared with three women of the same age who had no torpor-like symptoms.

Synaptophysin is found in synapses, the connections between neurons, so this suggests the woman’s brain contained fewer connections between neurons involved in regulating body temperature and the body clock. “Levels of synaptophysin in the hypothalamus decrease during hibernation in ground squirrels, suggesting a possible parallel between the woman’s condition and changes seen in hibernating mammals,” says Yi.

Radical new insights from the science of interoception – how the body senses its internal state – explain the real reasons we feel tired all the time, and how to re-energise

Further analysis revealed that neurons involved in controlling the body clock in the woman’s hypothalamus had almost completely lost a hormone called arginine vasopressin, while levels of another hormone called vasoactive intestinal peptide were also substantially reduced, compared with control brains.

All the neuronal changes may have enabled the woman to enter a torpor-like state in response to reduced exposure to sunlight or colder temperatures in the winter, without experiencing organ damage, says Yi. But it’s possible the brain changes resulted from, rather than caused, the woman’s syndrome, she says.

In ongoing work, the team is sequencing the woman’s genome, which could reveal any genetic mutations contributing to her syndrome. This could help pinpoint pathways that could be targeted with drugs to induce hibernation in people, for instance, to extend their survival while waiting for an organ transplant, or to reduce the need for food during space travel, says Cerri.

US bill aiming to boost clean energy could backfire

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Among the grass, sagebrush and tumbleweeds on a cattle ranch in Rawlins, Wyoming, workers have been building roads and pads for 600 wind turbines. Meanwhile, emission lines are being strung from the site to a hub in Nevada, where the electricity generated can help power Las Vegas and Los Angeles.

It will be one of the biggest wind farms in the US, a win for the economy and the climate. But it took 18 years to get the approvals to start building. Even less complex projects now typically wait five years to connect to the grid.

These delays are the target of a 400-page permitting reform bill backed by Republicans and US President Donald Trump as well as many Democrats. It has just passed the Senate and will now be taken up by the House of Representatives.

Advertisement

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it far easier to build renewable energy projects and transmission lines. One of its authors, long-time climate champion Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, says it would be the country’s “biggest implemented climate bill”.

But BAAJA would also speed up permitting for natural gas plants and pipelines, coal mines and data centres, while weakening environmental regulations. The American Petroleum Institute has even sent a BAAJA-branded food truck to hand out free tacos on Capitol Hill. The climate movement is split. Some experts fear the bill would increase greenhouse gas emissions, and former Vice President Al Gore called it a “serious mistake”.

Both sides say BAAJA is a gamble, but supporters say it’s one worth taking. Jigar Shah, who formerly oversaw infrastructure loans at the US Department of Energy, says it would set up a race between clean energy and fossil fuels. “The world’s best energy developers right now are in the clean energy space,” he says. “Why wouldn’t I bet on the world’s best energy developers?”

Free newsletter

Climate policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.6°C of warming by 2100, and greenhouse gas emissions are not yet falling, partly because additional renewable energy supply has been outpaced by additional demand from data centres. Data centre energy demand will double by 2030, and in the US, 60 per cent of that demand will be met by natural gas, according to the International Energy Agency.

The US grid, which is fractured into three separate grid regions and seven electricity markets, needs to speed up the build-out of renewables and transmission lines from the sunny, windy areas in the central US to the population centres near the coasts. But grid operators and regulators are overwhelmed, developers disagree on who should pay for transmission lines and court battles can last years. As a result, more than 2000 gigawatts of electricity generation and storage projects are awaiting grid connection, most of them renewable.

BAAJA would allow the federal government to override states’ objections and force grid regions to plan transmission lines together. But it would also narrow the timelines and reasons for challenging projects under environmental laws like the Clean Water Act, and, in some instances, cut lower district courts out of these cases. It essentially gives up tools to stop fossil fuel projects in exchange for tools to accelerate clean energy ones.

Environmentalists like Bill McKibben have warned that accelerated pipeline construction could lock in fossil fuel demand, and weaker protections would disempower concerned residents.

“Why would we choose now to give the fossil fuel industry what it’s wanted forever?” says David Watkins at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Compromise will be required; I just think the balance here is off.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Following this month’s election sweep, Democrats will take control of Congress in January and could potentially renegotiate the bill. But Trump would probably veto it, and even when the party controlled both Congress and the White House in 2022, it failed to pass a proposed permitting reform bill.

“You have a lot of newly elected oil-and-gas-state Democrats,” cautions Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh at Columbia University in New York.

Think tanks have projected that although the bill would increase liquefied natural gas exports, it would boost the build-out of renewables more than coal and gas plants. This would eventually reduce electricity prices by 3 to 5 per cent and US annual emissions by 0 to 4 per cent, depending on the future costs of clean tech and fossil fuels, according to Rhodium Group.

But modelling by Kevin Kircher at Purdue University in Indiana found that BAAJA would raise US annual emissions by 2 per cent. While energy demand will increase in any case, he argues the bill would increase demand still further, due in part to the Jevons paradox. This is when a decline in the cost of a resource leads buyers to consume more of it. For instance, if electricity prices did go down under BAAJA, cryptocurrency mining operations might run for longer periods or install more hardware.

“Unless all of that additional new electricity demand is met by clean energy, if even 10 per cent of it is met by fossil fuels, then emissions increase overall,” says Kircher. “People are severely underestimating the amount of new fossil fuel combustion that we will also see as a result of BAAJA.”

Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

US, Russia and China look set to block ban on autonomous weapons

New Scientist November 20, 2026

The US, China and Russia are expected to undermine attempts to enact a global ban on autonomous weapons at a conference this week. Such weapons are becoming an increasingly common feature of modern conflict, but are criticised as presenting an unacceptable risk to civilians and muddying the waters of accountability in war.

The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) is a United Nations treaty binding together 128 states to regulate excessively harmful or indiscriminate weapons. The treaty’s five existing protocols ban incendiary weapons, bombs that create shrapnel that can’t be detected by X-rays and lasers designed to blind soldiers – weapons that the global community has decided are beyond the pale.

For more than 10 years, states have debated adding autonomous weapons to the list. Members meet every five years to discuss what changes may be needed to the treaty, and this week the seventh such Review Conference is being held in Geneva. But there have been few signs of progress and efforts to bind parties to promises of action look set to fail.

Advertisement

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

The use of AI is common in militaries around the world, helping to pick targets among overwhelming piles of intelligence data and automating certain functions of weapons, including steering missiles and drones.

Humans are usually in the loop at some point, but on at least one occasion to date, fully autonomous drones have been used without human oversight to kill enemy soldiers. A senior figure in the Ukrainian defence industry told New Scientist earlier this year that a test took place two years ago that lead to two deaths.

It is that sort of weapon, where human input is minimal or non-existent, that most worries campaigners like Elizabeth Minor at pressure group Stop Killer Robots. “Machines shouldn’t make life and death decisions. Tasking weapons systems or algorithms to identify targets and kill people is just a moral red line we shouldn’t be crossing,” she says.

Free newsletter

Over the past three years, work has gone on behind the scenes in the CCW to lay out the groundwork for a ban. Peru, as chair of the conference, has proposed that negotiations should start on a protocol and that work to create that ban should finish within two years.

Minor says 130 countries support a ban or restrictions on autonomous weapons, and more than 70 are ready to begin negotiations. But she warns that the US, Russia and China, as well as other nations including the UK, Japan and South Korea, are likely to block such efforts. “What we’ll obviously see as the week goes on, unfortunately, is the weakening of this text [from Peru] at the behest of larger militarised states who want to continue to see these weapons unregulated,” she says.

Discussions are likely to run late into the night on 20 November and deliberations aren’t open to the public, with an announcement expected on 21 November. The CCW operates on unanimity, meaning that just one state can stymie action.

The US has already proposed at the meeting that further work should be carried out to investigate how existing international law applies to autonomous weapons, arguing that an update to the CCW is unnecessary, and essentially kicking the can down the road on a potential ban until the next meeting in 2031.

AIs can’t stop recommending nuclear strikes in war game simulations

Aurel Sari at the University of Exeter, UK, says autonomous weapons already fall under existing law around armed conflict, meaning those who use them must avoid attacks that would cause excessive collateral damage and take all feasible precautions to spare civilians. An autonomous weapon that can’t be used in line with these rules is already unlawful. But none of these existing laws ban their use, and Sari sees hurdles in the way of greater regulation.

“Supporters of a ban want to stop weapons that select and attack targets in ways their operators cannot predict or control. Meanwhile, states that operate defensive systems that react faster than any human can, such as systems protecting warships against incoming missiles automatically, do not want to see these prohibited,” says Sari. “A ban wide enough to meet the first concern risks also capturing these defensive systems, while a ban narrow enough to win the support of the major military powers might prohibit little that anyone intends to field.”

Because of this, the leading states that are developing these systems, among them the US, Russia and China, have different strategic priorities from others, says Sari.

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

“None of the major powers wants an agreement that would hand its rivals an advantage on the battlefield. A wide-ranging ban would appeal to them only if all their rivals observed it as well. That would require states to agree on exactly what the ban covers, to close the loopholes and to establish a reliable way of checking compliance,” says Sari. “None of these seems achievable at present.”

Countries are already using these weapons, but there is still time to act, says Minor. “I wouldn’t say that we’re too late to make rules. You can do this at any point. And there is still time to have a meaningful response to this that can prevent things going down an even worse path, but that depends on the international community really acting now.”

That could mean side-stepping the CCW entirely and taking the issue to the UN General Assembly, where you only need a majority to start negotiations on a treaty. “But they need to do it now otherwise we’ll just keep seeing this dynamic of a race to the bottom for these capabilities,” says Minor.

Unexpected stone tools from Israel raise questions about cultural evolution

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Half a million years ago, prehistoric hominins in the eastern Mediterranean produced some of the earliest known stone blades, 100,000 years before the technology became established in the region. This discovery adds to growing evidence that early humans repeatedly invented new tools without necessarily adopting them, raising questions about what really drove technological evolution in prehistory.

Blades are thin fragments of stone that are at least twice as long as they are wide. In the region of the eastern Mediterranean known as the Levant, a blade technology tradition called the Amudian techno-complex became widespread around 400,000 years ago. This replaced earlier “Acheulean” tools, which included classic teardrop-shaped handaxes, as well as flakes – sharp pieces of stone that are removed from a larger rock and are cruder and more irregularly shaped than blades.

Yet after analysing hundreds of stone artefacts at the archaeological site of Jaljulia in Israel, researchers found traces of serial blade production 500,000 years ago that used a specific technique resembling that used in the Amudian system.

Advertisement

Monsoon-driven wildfires may have shaped human evolution

“We identify an earlier, small-scale manifestation of this method, which we term Amudian–like,” says team member Vlad Litov at Tel Aviv University in Israel. He say the ancient tool-makers were “culturally conservative”, and their initial flirtation with blade tools never flourished into an established practice.

“Despite reaching the techno-cognitive capability to make some blades, these hominins still adhered to their traditional Acheulean technology,” he says.

Yet the Jaljulia hominins weren’t the only ones to experiment with blade technology long before accepting it into their toolkit. At both Kathu Pan in South Africa and the Kapthurin Formation in Kenya, archaic humans began making small numbers of blades around 500,000 years ago, only to abandon the tools for hundreds of millennia.

“At Kathu Pan, we see a really remarkable [blade] technology, but then we don’t find it anymore, and the next blade production is about 70,000 years ago,” says Michael Chazan at the University of Toronto.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The identities of the various tool-makers remain unclear, and the blades at Jaljulia, Kathu Pan and the Kapthurin Formation were all created using different methods. This suggests that unconnected hominin populations simultaneously invented the technology required to produce blades, representing a case of convergent cultural evolution.

Litov suspects the blades didn’t initially catch on because the Jaljulia hominins preferred their Acheulean tools when butchering large prey like elephants. He thinks that when proboscideans began to die out in the eastern Mediterranean around 400,000 years ago, Levantine hominins were forced to change their hunting strategies, providing an incentive to switch to the smaller Amudian blades.

“We think the widespread adoption of blades was tied to a shift toward hunting smaller prey, which required more precise, meticulous butchery to maximise caloric yield, alongside delicate tasks like skinning,” says Litov.

Combining archaeological evidence with ancient DNA and data on past climates shows us how long and winding the story of human evolution is, stretching back millions of years to when the first primates arose

Yet Chazan questions how much of an advantage these early blades provided. “Why would something that seems so highly adaptive [like the Amudian-like blades] not be sustained?” he says. “I think part of the answer is that they’re not superior. There’s nothing inherently better about a blade than a flake.”

Likewise, Steven Kuhn at the University of Arizona suggests that blades may have become truly useful only once humans learned to combine them with more advanced technologies to produce tools assembled from several parts, including those with a handle or “haft”.

“My opinion is that certain forms of blade production were advantageous in contexts where many tools were hafted,” he says. “Until hafted tools became important parts of toolkits, blades were just another source of sharp edges.”

The secret maths problems hidden throughout Japan

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Mathematics is rarely done in public. I’m not talking about arithmetic – of course, simple sums are common when shopping, though perhaps less so in an increasingly cashless age – but actual mathematics involving reasoning, logic, proof and even beauty. While statues, paintings and other artworks are sprinkled throughout the public realm, I can’t recall ever encountering mathematics in the wild.

Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?

Because of this, I was delighted to recently discover the Japanese practice of sangaku. Translated variously as “framed calculations” or “mathematical tablets”, these were painted wooden artefacts hung in temples and shrines across Japan depicting mathematical problems. Thousands of them were created during the Edo period of around 1603 to 1868, but only 900 survive today.

Now, thanks to a team led by Antonia Karaisl at Waseda University in Tokyo, many of these have been digitally preserved in an online catalogue called the Sangaku Archive.

Advertisement

“Sangaku have sort of fallen off the radar of public knowledge in Japan. They are positively obscure outside the country, so I thought that documenting them in a bilingual, centralised archive might help,” says Karaisl.

Here is a relatively easy example to understand (the diagram on the left):

This problem consists of a number of circles. The yellow one has a diameter of 5 units and the three red ones all have a diameter of 4. They sit snugly inside and around a white circle that has a chunk of another circle taken out of it. At the bottom of the picture is a black line. The tablet asks how long this line is and gives an answer – 16 units – along with a method for calculating it.

Crucially, the tablet doesn’t provide a proof for why this method works (it involves some elementary geometry). That was often the point of sangaku, to offer a challenge to the viewer.

“Sangaku serve to signal knowledge without actually transmitting it. They contain enough information for you to understand the problem and that the author has solved it,” says Karaisl. This is because mathematical knowledge at the time was closely guarded by private schools, so the sangaku were a way to advertise what students might learn.

This wasn’t their only purpose, however. “People had other motives to dedicate a sangaku: commemorate a personal feat or an event, or just doing it for the joy of it – much like social media, I guess,” says Karaisl.

Looking at the sangaku, I can’t help but be reminded of video games in which you wander through a world encountering puzzles along the way. Take The Witness, for example, which takes place on an island filled with puzzles that all involve drawing lines on a grid. That description sounds boring, but the sense of discovery and communication between the player and the game developer is incredible, as you explore both a visual landscape and a conceptual one to learn a strange new logical language.

Building the Sangaku Archive was its own journey of discovery, says Karaisl. A book published in 1998 lists the known locations of the extant sangaku, but actually getting in touch with local caretakers so she could access and photograph them all was much harder work. “Email is rare – it’s mostly phones, faxes and letters,” she says. “In the hopeless cases, the best you can do is physically go to the location and hope you’ll find a human being nearby who can tell you more – and if you’re lucky, someone will know someone who knows someone whose cousin’s wife’s brother holds the key or something.”

For the 70th anniversary of New Scientist, explore our immersive timeline of the biggest moments in science since 1956, from Sputnik 1 to the proliferation of AI chatbots

Karaisl says she has visited around 400 sangaku locations, most in small, rural shrines as the less remote ones have been destroyed by war or earthquakes. In one case, she cycled to a small temple in a mountainous area, only to find herself within 50 metres, but on the wrong side of a river, she says. “Since I was late already, I had to leave the bike in the bushes, clamber down the slope and across the river to then climb up through the thicket and come breaking out of the forest like some stray ogre with sticks and leaves on my clothes and in my hair, rather than coming up the road to meet the priest and the caretaker in a civilised fashion.”

Another fascinating aspect of sangaku is that that they record a particular way of doing mathematics that is unfamiliar to Western-trained eyes. During the Edo period, Japan had an isolationist outlook to Europe, and this included mathematics – for example, the development of calculus by the Europeans Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz in the 17th century didn’t reach Japan until much later. Many results were developed by Japanese mathematicians independently, and sometimes before, their Western counterparts.

Part of this Japanese approach to mathematics was a focus on experimental calculations, rather than deduction, according to Tsukane Ogawa at Yokkaichi University, Japan. When Euclid’s Elements, perhaps the foundational text of mathematical proof, arrived in Japan via a Chinese translation in the Edo period, Japanese mathematicians seemed uninterested. Rather than starting from a series of axioms and deriving logical proofs, Japanese mathematicians preferred to perform calculations, such as finding many digits of pi, and infer logical conclusions – the exact method demonstrated by sangaku.

Karaisl and her team continue to work on the archive, and she says she hopes that it will reach a broader audience beyond the research community. Personally, I’m fascinated by the idea of a culture that saw mathematics as something worthy of putting on public display, and the remaining sangaku are absolutely beautiful to look at. I would love for someone to take inspiration from The Witness and create a game with finding and solving sangaku at its heart.

The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury

New Scientist November 20, 2026

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

Advertisement

Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.

Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.

Free newsletter

Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.

Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.

CCTV witness catches Kisione Niutupuivaha indecently assaulting sleeping girl

New Zealand Herald November 20, 2026

Kisione Niutupuivaha during sentencing in the Nelson District Court. He has been jailed for indecently assaulting a young girl as she slept. Photo / Tracy Neal

Warning: This story includes details of child sex offending and may upset some readers.

A man who thought he was asleep when he indecently touched a young girl multiple times was caught in the act by an adult in the house who saw him on CCTV.

The girl, who was staying at a friend’s house, heard someone breathing over her and felt scared as Kisione Niutupuivaha shone a torch on her, then touched her.

Now, her mother is afraid the full impact of what happened might not yet be fully apparent.

Niutupuivaha was caught in the act by a person who saw what he was doing in the lounge via the live CCTV feed on her phone.

The 28-year-old was sentenced on Wednesday in the Nelson District Court to prison on three charges of indecently assaulting a female aged under 12.

His lawyer John Sandston said Niutupuivaha had taken a sleeping pill and believed he was asleep at the time of the offending.

“He doesn’t recall the offending because he took a sleeping pill, but admits there are photos of him committing the offences,” Sandston said.

Crown prosecutor Daniel Baxter described it as “brief, entitled, selfish offending” which had had a huge impact on the victim and her mother, and on the family where the offending occurred.

The victim’s mother said her daughter had been forced to deal with something no child should ever have to face.

For a long time after, her daughter would not leave her side, and was unable to go to school as she struggled to figure out what had happened.

“She has lost her sense of safety,” the girl’s mother said.

According to the police summary of facts, the victim was asleep on a couch in the lounge when Niutupuivaha approached her at least five times.

Each time he used his mobile phone torch to illuminate the victim as he stood over her.

Police said he pulled a blanket off the young victim, exposing her body.

As he stood over her, he indecently touched her a number of times.

The witness was in a different room and saw what he was doing via the feed on her phone, police said.

Niutupuivaha told police he “thought he was asleep at the time”.

Sandston sought to have the sentencing adjourned because no pre-sentence report had been prepared, but Judge Tony Snell said Corrections had been unable to get Niutupuivaha to comply with designated appointments to prepare the report.

He declined to grant the adjournment as Niutupuivaha had been given every opportunity to get a full report done, but this had not happened.

Judge Snell said any delay now was not desirable for the victims.

Contact the Open Justice team

Baxter said an aggravating feature of the offending was the large age gap between the victim and the offender, the “significant element of pre-meditation” and the harm caused to a vulnerable victim asleep in an unfamiliar setting.

Sandston said the offending was more spontaneous than it was planned over any long period of time.

He said Niutupuivaha had been in New Zealand for a number of years, had now lost his employment and accommodation, and was sorry for what had happened.

Judge Snell said, in sentencing him to 15 months in prison, that it was clear the physical touching of the victim was only the beginning of the harm caused.

“It’s quite clear there is significant harm at an ongoing level.”

From a starting point of 20 months in prison, Niutupuivaha was given a full 25% credit for his early guilty pleas, resulting in a 15-month prison term.

Judge Snell said in the absence of any suitable address, the only option was prison. Niutupuivaha was granted leave to apply for home detention if his situation changed.

He was now subject to the Three Strikes sentencing law, and was given his first warning.

Niutupuivaha is now a registered child sex offender, which could be reconsidered if his sentence was commuted to home detention.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

Apec summit: New Zealand cannot afford to be squeezed between Washington and Beijing – Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald November 20, 2026

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at Apec in Shenzhen, China, this week. Photo / Getty Images

There was a delicious irony in Chinese President Xi Jinping’s pitch to Apec business leaders gathered in Shenzhen for the CEOs Summit: China, he argued, is a champion of open trade, globalisation and a rules-based international economic system.

This is the same China that joined the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in December 2001, just weeks after hosting its first Apec leaders’ summit in Shanghai.

Washington’s complaints are substantial. Successive US administrations have argued that China’s state-directed model – with extensive subsidies, preferential treatment for state-owned enterprises and pressure on foreign firms to transfer technology – distorts competition and sits uneasily with WTO principles.

But 25 years on from that first China-hosted Apec, Xi is now using the platform to promote China’s credentials as a champion of international economic co-operation.

The timing is hardly accidental. Donald Trump’s America has turned increasingly towards tariffs, protectionism and economic nationalism.

Beijing sees an opportunity to position itself as a more reliable partner for countries dependent on open markets and predictable trading relationships.

Xi’s message was carefully calibrated. He called for an Asia-Pacific community built around openness, integration, innovation and inclusive development.

He backed the pitch with US$20 million for Apec practical co-operation, a new Centre for Asia-Pacific Community Studies in Shenzhen and co-operation institutions covering digital technology, cross-border data flows, clean energy and small business development.

He also reiterated China’s support for a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) which he first promoted when he hosted the 2014 Apec in Beijing.

But the real story emerging from Shenzhen goes well beyond trade. It is about who gets to shape the next economic order – and where New Zealand positions itself.

In the business discussions at the accompanying Apec CEOs’ Summit, the dominance of artificial intelligence and the green transition was unmistakable.

Chinese companies and American multinationals are looking at the commercial opportunities created by the next technological revolution, even as their governments grapple with strategic rivalry, technology controls and national security concerns.

AI infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, electric vehicles and the supply chains underpinning them are now central to the economic contest.

There is a paradox here. Washington and Beijing are competing fiercely for technological leadership while businesses on both sides recognise that the commercial opportunities are too large to ignore.

This competition will influence the cost of technology, energy security, the competitiveness of our exporters and the direction of future investment.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon used his presence in Shenzhen to meet New Zealand businesses operating in China and hear their assessment of commercial conditions and opportunities.

The New Zealand business delegation also provided a valuable ground-level perspective. Visits to technology companies including EV manufacturer BYD, and Oppo, an artificial intelligence application pilot base in Dongguan and meetings with Chinese businesses offered a glimpse of the scale and speed of China’s innovation ecosystem.

The takeout is sobering. We cannot assume our traditional strengths in agriculture, food production and services will be sufficient to maintain our competitive position.

One of the more important diplomatic developments in Shenzhen was Luxon’s engagement with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Wong has become an increasingly influential regional voice arguing that the Asia-Pacific must not fracture into competing economic blocs as globalisation becomes more fragmented and contested.

His message was pragmatic. Build on existing agreements such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, keep pursuing Apec’s longer-term free-trade ambition, and let willing countries make progress together when consensus among all economies proves impossible.

He also made an important point about artificial intelligence.

Co-operation should not be confined to the contest over which country produces the best chips or models.

There is considerable scope for collaboration on AI safety, responsible use, infrastructure and productivity.

Wong subsequently hosted Luxon, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese for lunch.

The four politicians lead countries with strong economic and security ties to the United States but also substantial interests in maintaining constructive engagement with China.

Carney – who also addressed the CEO Summit – has embarked on a pragmatic reset with Beijing, securing improved market access and tariff relief for Canadian exporters after years of strained relations.

Australia, too, has worked to stabilise its relationship with China following a period of serious trade tensions.

Neither country is abandoning its security concerns or strategic relationships with Washington. They are demonstrating that commercial engagement and strategic independence need not be mutually exclusive.

The CPTPP, representing 580 million consumers and 15.6% of global GDP, provides a valuable platform for this sort of co-operation.

It gives smaller economies collective leverage in defending predictable trading rules and building relationships beyond their immediate neighbourhood.

The challenge for New Zealand is how to make these relationships work harder for us.

The geopolitical theatre in Shenzhen was extraordinary.

On Wednesday, Xi met Russian President Vladimir Putin and called for China and Russia to deepen all-round co-operation and take the lead in advancing a multipolar world.

The following day, US President Donald Trump joined Xi and Putin for an unprecedented trilateral meeting involving the leaders of the world’s three major nuclear powers.

The discussions covered nuclear arms control and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Trump presented the gathering as an opportunity to make history.

The optics were remarkable: Washington, Beijing and Moscow sitting together to discuss the future of international security, when two of those players are engaged in war.

The meeting produced no major breakthrough. But the willingness of the three leaders to engage in this format is significant.

New Zealand should be particularly alert to the implications of Xi’s multipolarity agenda. Beijing and Moscow are explicitly advocating a different distribution of global power. That is not necessarily the same thing as defending the rules-based international system that New Zealand depends on.

There is another opportunity New Zealand should be considering with Luxon (assuming he retains the prime ministership) intent on making 2027 a year of renewed strategic focus on China.

Xi’s proposal to establish a World Association for Bay Areas Economic Co-operation is worth examining. The Chinese President wants to deepen connections between the world’s major bay areas (China’s Greater Bay and Silicon Valley) drawing on their concentration of technology, manufacturing, finance, innovation and international trade.

Auckland has a useful history to build on. In 2014, the city joined Los Angeles and Guangzhou in a Tripartite Economic Alliance designed to deepen trade and investment connections between the three sister cities.

Could Auckland leverage this to establish stronger connections with the Greater Bay Area, linking New Zealand businesses and institutions with technology, investment, education, advanced manufacturing and green-economy opportunities?

Shenzhen itself is a compelling illustration of what can happen when infrastructure investment, technology, openness and commercial ambition come together. Once a relatively small fishing settlement, it has become one of China’s most important technology and manufacturing centres.

Our China strategy should be about more than protecting existing trade in dairy, meat, forestry and tourism. It should encompass digital services, AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, education and new forms of investment.

The lesson from Shenzhen is that the old boundaries between trade, technology, energy and national security are disappearing.

Xi is offering a vision of an integrated Asia-Pacific with China at its centre. Trump is pursuing an America First economic agenda while engaging directly with Beijing and Moscow. Regional leaders such as Wong are warning against a fractured world of competing economic blocs.

We have a substantial economic relationship with China, a deep security relationship with traditional partners and a vital interest in the rules governing international trade and investment.

These relationships cannot simply be managed on autopilot.

Rotorua Hospital: Daughter seeks answers about father’s care and death

New Zealand Herald November 20, 2026

Vanessa Hakaraia with her father, Stacey Hakaraia, who died in Rotorua Hospital on August 28.

Stacey Hakaraia, 76, was admitted to Taupō Hospital after collapsing in pain. He never came home. His daughter is seeking answers about her father’s care, which she believes led to his untimely death at Rotorua Hospital.

Stacey Hakaraia could still walk, drive and spend time with his grandchildren before he collapsed at home in severe pain.

His daughter, Vanessa Hakaraia, believes his “horrific” treatment led to his death at Rotorua Hospital in August.

“He never got to go home.”

Hakaraia has filed two complaints and asked Health New Zealand for an independent investigation into her father’s care and death.

Health NZ has acknowledged the family’s distress and concerns raised about his care. The agency is reviewing the care provided and working to respond to the whānau.

Hakaraia, who lived with her father in Tihoi near Taupō, said he was admitted to Taupō Hospital after his fall on August 3.

Three days later, she claimed doctors told him cancer on his spine caused the fall.

He was transferred to Rotorua Hospital on August 7 for an MRI scan, she said.

After two unsuccessful MRI attempts due to back pain, his MRI was done on August 11.

The whānau were told after the scan he did not have cancer, prompting questions about why they were initially told he did have it.

Hakaraia said the conflicting information had caused the whānau significant distress.

On August 13, they were told he had a spinal/vertebral fracture, which would be treated with a brace.

By August 19, he still had no spinal brace and was still experiencing pain. He could not get out of bed and needed help with cleaning and using the bathroom, Hakaraia said.

Hakaraia said she told staff he was losing feeling in his feet. She claimed staff told him to keep moving his toes.

Hakaraia filed a formal complaint to Health NZ on August 19 and asked for a review of his legs and feet, confirmation of his diagnosis and treatment plan, and why the family were told he had cancer when he did not.

On August 24, Hakaraia said her father lost “almost all feeling” in his feet. She submitted another complaint.

She said an MRI showed his fracture was pressing on his spine and he had emergency surgery that night.

Hakaraia said she was initially told, on August 25, the operation went well.

She was therefore left confused when she found him in the Rotorua ICU unconscious and on a ventilator.

She claimed two health professionals gave conflicting information after the operation about his chances of survival.

She said one told them there was “nothing they could do” and he would die.

Hakaraia said another health professional informed the family a few hours later that there was a 50-50 chance of survival.

“It was just so confusing.”

She claimed a doctor “repeatedly” pressed their whānau to give them a time to turn off his life support.

She also claimed a doctor said her father was “using all the medication up for the surviving patients”.

He died on August 28.

Hakaraia said her father’s care was “horrific” at Rotorua Hospital.

“For me, it was disgusting, actually ... how the hospital treated us and my dad especially; he was in bed for over 21 days straight and he just never got up again.”

She, her two sisters and their children were with him when he died.

“My children are the ones who are finding it the hardest at the moment,” she said through tears.

“I see a lot of people out there who ... didn’t have a really good upbringing ... I tell my kids I was actually quite lucky to have a dad like mine.”

Her father was born in Rotorua and grew up in Ōhinemutu.

He was an “amazing grandfather” to his 10 grandchildren and a “happy, bubbly person”.

The Rotorua Daily Post put Hakaraia’s claims to Health NZ and asked what caused her father’s fall, what treatment he received, and if his death had been referred to the coroner.

Health NZ Lakes operations group director Kathy Rex said the agency extended its sincere condolences to Stacey Hakaraia’s whānau for their loss.

“We recognise this has been a very difficult time and acknowledge the distress reflected in the concerns raised about the care provided.

“We take these concerns seriously.”

Rex confirmed Health NZ had received correspondence and complaints from the whānau, which were being considered through its complaints process.

“We understand the whānau want answers about what happened during Mr Hakaraia’s care and the circumstances surrounding his death.

“We are carefully reviewing the care provided and are working to provide a comprehensive response.”

Rex said Health NZ was committed to providing safe, high-quality care and listening to patients and whānau when they raise concerns.

“We investigate these concerns to identify any opportunities to improve the care and experience we provide.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Twenty-six RNZ staff will leave the state broadcaster, starting from next month, union leaders say.

PSA and E tū members were told of the departures in an email update last night after union bosses and delegates met RNZ acting chief executive Mark Stevens, chief people officer Sarah Nielson and interim chief financial officer Richard Dellabacca.

“Management confirmed 23 FTEs (full-time equivalents) covering 26 people are already confirmed to be leaving the organisation through voluntary redundancies and fixed-term contracts ending, with departures starting from December.”

RNZ has been contacted for comment.

The broadcaster is grappling with an $11.8 million deficit after a series of financial blunders and overspends, with plans to cut the equivalent of 58 full-time roles by March next year – almost double the number RNZ initially planned to cut before the budget blowout was discovered last month.

Yesterday’s meeting with RNZ bosses was “tense and difficult” and the unions would “seek legal advice about the next steps”, PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons, E tū national secretary Rachel Mackintosh, PSA delegate Ella Stewart and E tū delegate Phil Pennington wrote in the email to members.

“It became clear some undisclosed change was planned but not fully shared with the unions.”

RNZ bosses made it clear they were under “severe pressure and are pushing ahead with a phased, team-by-team approach rather than publishing a single, clear organisational change proposal”, the union leaders wrote.

“We strongly challenged their approach as stressful, chaotic and contrary to the Collective Employment Agreement.

“We pressed on them the lack of transparent, orthodox change management and the terrible timing heading into Christmas.”

RNZ staff have already taken to the streets over the crisis, protesting in the past week outside their offices in Wellington and Auckland.

“What’s going to happen when there’s the next Cyclone Gabrielle? When people here are not here because they’ve lost their jobs and we need them to go out there?”, said Pennington, the E tū union delegate and a RNZ senior journalist, to a Wellington crowd.

RNZ’s chief executive for the past 13 years was Paul Thompson, who resigned in May with plans to leave at the end of this year.

After the broadcaster’s financial troubles were revealed, Thompson initially stuck with his planned departure date but last Saturday announced he would leave the role on Monday, six weeks earlier than expected.

Mount Maunganui landslide: Council halves Mauao remediation budget to $13.1m

New Zealand Herald November 20, 2026

The site of the fatal Mauao/Mount Maunganui landslide, pictured in October this year. Photo / Ayla Yeoman

The remediation budget for slip-hit Mauao/Mount Maunganui has been halved to about $13.1 million as Tauranga’s council slashes costs before the incoming rates cap.

On January 22, a storm caused 42 landslides on the mountain, including one that crashed into the Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park, killing six people.

The maunga, campground and damaged Mount Hot Pools have been closed since, with on-and-off closures of the Pilot Bay boat ramp and Adams Ave. The Mount Maunganui Lifeguard Service building recently reopened.

In a Tauranga City Council meeting on November 10, councillors agreed to cut the remaining budget for remediation work in the area from $26,245,000 to $13,122,500.

Recovery manager Charlie Rahiri told Local Democracy Reporting this would not impact the goal to partially reopen walking tracks on Mauao this summer.

“Work on remediating walking track slips is well underway and on track.

“Any reopening will prioritise safety and is likely to be partial in nature.”

The budget cut comes as council staff were asked to find $200m in savings across several major capital projects over three years.

The Local Government (Rates Capping) Amendment Bill passed its first reading in September. It would require councils to cap annual rates increases at 4% per capita.

Councils would have to consider the cap in their long-term plans from July, before it becomes mandatory in 2029.

Staff recommended the Mauao budget be reduced by 50% to save $13.1m across the financial years between 2028 and 2030.

Their report said the works would slow down and future development opportunities and slip remediation works would be deferred.

Rahiri said the council was still committed to remediation but wanted staff to investigate costs more fully, as well as external funding opportunities.

“We are currently engaged in a conversation with the community on the future of the Mauao Precinct, and therefore any funding decisions about those facilities are still to be considered.”

The council is seeking community feedback about options for the Mauao recreation reserve and Pilot Quay area – the Mauao Precinct. It includes the hot pools, holiday park and boat ramp.

The council, with the Mauao Trust, iwi and hapū, Bay Venues and Mount Maunganui Lifeguard Service, was exploring options for the future of this area.

This engagement did not include decisions about reopening walking tracks.

A survey asks questions such as how people have previously used and experienced the precinct, what they want its future to look like and whether the activities and amenities should be retained, enhanced or reimagined.

Mauao recovery community update meetings will be held at Huria Marae in Brookfield on November 24, Hungahungatoroa Marae in Matapihi on November 26, Club Mount Maunganui on November 30 and at the new Tauranga library on Willow St on December 9.

Public feedback closes on December 14.

Meanwhile, the council has recovered $550,000 from insurance for loss of profits from the holiday park since January’s storm.

A council Official Information Act response to Local Democracy Reporting in September said it had made a claim for $1.1m for the loss of holiday park profits.

The council sought $900,000 for loss of profit from the Mount Hot Pools, operated by council-controlled organisation Bay Venues. It received $450,000.

A specific claim for material damage had not been made at that point, but the council received $1.4m towards a future claim for the holiday park and hot pools.

The holiday park lost about $1.55m in profits as at August, and Bay Venues chief executive Chad Hooker confirmed the hot pools had lost an estimated $1.2m.

“We expect this to be covered by our business interruption insurance, with $450,000 already received,” he said.

The council had spent about $6.68m on its landslide response and recovery as of September 30. In October, it approved another $3.5m, taking forecast operational costs to $10.5m.

– LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

Ayla Yeoman is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based in Tauranga. She holds a Bachelor of Arts majoring in communications, politics and international relations from the University of Auckland, and has been a journalist since 2023.

A boy is traumatised after he was allegedly threatened with a fake firearm as he made his way home from school.

His shaken mother is warning parents to look out for their children after her 13-year-old son got off the bus Thursday afternoon near New World Mt Roskill, where he was called over by a boy the same age and a young adult.

The woman, whom the Herald has agreed not to identify, said her son asked them to let him go, and they eventually did after laughing at him.

He ran home and told his mum what happened. She called the police, who arrived within minutes.

They took his statement and later found those allegedly involved.

Officers told her they found a fake gun on the teen but no charges could be laid against the man because he “did not commit an offence”.

The mum said she was scared for her children and wanted to warn other parents of potential dangers on the streets.

“I’m scared. I am scared for my life. I’m scared for my kids. Nothing like this has ever happened to anybody in my family.

Auckland City west area response manager Senior Sergeant Guy Baldwin said the matter has been referred to Youth Aid.
