For weeks now, residents of a small Lockyer Valley town have watched as four gigantic decommissioned grain silos transform from a plain white eyesore into one of Queensland’s biggest pieces of public art.

The $1.85 million project, which includes a car park and viewing platform on the other side of the train tracks, is nearing completion on the old GrainCorp silos by the train line at Forest Hill.

Like the rest of the community, Anna Williams, whose sister runs Caffe Sorella in town, has been eagerly tracking the changes as the mural has taken shape over the past couple of months.

What was once a “bit of an eyesore”, as Williams described it, has become a towering tribute to the town’s pioneering past.

“It was all kept secret – we didn’t really know what was actually happening, and then all of a sudden it just developed, and it’s just beautiful,” she said.

“People have been coming [to check the progress]. The first time they saw it, it was painted a pink or brown colour, and then all of a sudden you see a sketch of a boy and a girl – all right, what’s coming next?

“And then there’s the train, all of that. So they come back and they see it take shape.”

What they have seen is their town reflected in paint, a young girl holding a Queenslander-style home in her hands, a boy playing with a steam train.

And the Lockyer Valley rolling off into the distance.

“It’s just beautiful,” Williams said.

The artists behind the mural are Brisbane-based Jordan Bruce, of the Brightsiders collective fame, and Joel “The Zookeeper” Fergie from the Sunshine Coast.

The Forest Hill mural is the fourth piece of giant silo art to be painted in Queensland, and the closest to Brisbane by some margin.

“It’s become a bit of a way for towns to share their identity, what they’re about, what’s a drawcard to the area, what they’d like to be known for,” Fergie said.

“We’ve had ‘big’ things around regional Australia [pineapples, bananas, merinos etc], and for the last 10 years, it’s big silos being painted.”

The pair have been on the job now since early October, with (weather permitting) a few weeks left until completion.

Both have temporarily relocated to nearby Gatton while painting the silos, about a 90-minute westerly drive from Brisbane.

It’s quite the job. The four silos are 26 metres tall and about 15 metres wide – a huge artistic canvas by any standard.

And it has been far from easy going, particularly when perched on an elevated platform atop a crane.

“There are certain areas on this job where, because of the power line in particular, you might need to park further away [from the mural] – then it gets a bit hairy, especially if the wind’s up,” Bruce said.

“We do have good machines that are safe, but there’s no way to stop being scared at different points – at above 20 or 22 metres, you start to feel it.”

Fergie said that was why the more intricate parts of the mural were closer to the ground than the top.

“A lot of the detail sits on the bottom two thirds, so we’ve tried to keep that top section quite sparse,” he said.

“That just means you’re not up there all day every day painting trees right at the top, partly because we don’t love being up there all day every day.

“It’s pretty scary when you’re 26 metres up on a machine that you just hope’s been serviced really well.”

Bruce said the design, which was a closely held secret before work commenced, came from a period of community consultation with the locals.

“The first time we came out here, Joel had a vision of a child playing with a train, and that created a bit of a jump-off point,” he said.

“It was partly about how to interact with what’s already happening, so you can imagine when the train comes past, if you get the photo at the right time, it’ll look like the boy’s playing with an actual train.”

Lockyer Valley Mayor Tanya Milligan said the mural was about seven years in the making – and she had high hopes for its potential as a drawcard to Forest Hill.

“For our council, it’s a once-in-a-generation opportunity. It’ll attract visitors. It will position Forest Hill and the Lockyer Valley as a must-see destination,” she said.

“I’ve seen a few murals in my time, and I’m trying not to be biased, but this mural will be absolutely magnificent.”

The GrainCorp silos were built in the 1970s and decommissioned in 1990. For decades now they have loomed over Forest Hill as towering, blank concrete monoliths.

“If you’re heading into Forest Hill, you used to have these four naked, huge silos, which are now going to be looking absolutely magnificent,” Milligan said.

“The community’s excited – and so they should be. It will bring with it some significant injection to the economy of our towns, but also our businesses.

“What’s been great is that the artists actually spent time in Forest Hill and spoke to our community to really get an understanding of our community.”

Fergie said what came out of that process was a local pride in the town’s pioneering history.

“Look around Forest Hill, and it’s filled with classic old Queenslander homes and architecture,” he said.

“It used to be a Cobb & Co staging post right in the middle of town, so there’s rich history that the community is really proud of here in town.

“That was the backbone of our design, essentially. How can we bring in some of that old history, put our own spin on it, and shine a fresh light on some of that interesting history?”

The answer, Fergie said, was to approach it through a young person’s eye.

“It’s a nice way of creating an imaginative, expressive artwork that multiple generations can connect with in different ways,” he said.

“We always want to try and make a work that speaks past, present, future at the same time, and that’s really the backbone of the artwork – young people at play, thinking about history, reimagining it, having fun, and they’re connected to the landscape that is really beautiful out here.”

As the work nears its final brushstrokes, both Fergie and Bruce are ready for a break.

“The thing about our work is, it’s very common that we don’t know what’s next. Luckily, I know that I’ll be doing something closer to home early next year, and other than that, there’s a whole lot of who-knows-what,” Bruce said.

“So, I intend to just spend some time with family, and also just create for the sake of creating. I’m looking forward to a bit of time doing that, and then get back into work in the new year.”

Fergie was also looking forward to completing the mural, even if he had no idea what was next.

“When you finish a project at this scale, which we’ve done a few times now, the last thing you want to do is actually make art when you finish,” he said.

“You just need to decompress and then that energy comes back – you get really excited again.”

Summer is coming. Here’s what you should know about sharks

Sydney Morning Herald November 21, 2026

Last summer was one of the worst on record for shark bites. With a hot season ahead, should swimmers and surfers be worried? One survivor and two experts weigh in what works – and what doesn’t.

GLENN ORGIAS, 51, is an energy trader and writer who lives in Bondi, Sydney. On February 12, 2009, he was bitten by a shark while surfing at Bondi Beach. He spent 10 days in ICU, more than five weeks in hospital, and lost his hand and part of his forearm. Since his attack, he’s written two books – a memoir called Man in a Grey Suit, and Teeth Kicker, a crime novel about – well, a loan shark.

“There was a lot going on the night I was attacked. Paul [de Gelder, a navy diver] was attacked the day before [by a bull shark in Sydney Harbour]; there’d been a huge amount of flooding in Queensland, which had pushed a lot of fresh water into the ocean; and it was really stormy here in Sydney, so the water was reasonably murky. It was dusk, and the light was getting low.

There would’ve been 20 or 30 guys out that night. It was big surf – very lumpy, not very nice – but it had been flat for two weeks, so no one had surfed for ages and everyone was keen to get out there. It was breaking a fair way offshore. I’d just got a wave and was paddling back towards the pack – about 80 metres from shore, 20 metres from the lineup – when I was attacked.

The shark just slammed into me from below. It knocked me right off my board and pulled me under by my left arm. I didn’t know what was happening. I couldn’t see anything – I never actually saw it – but I remember it shook me really aggressively, sort of ran me through the water. The whole thing was so quick – less than a minute, maybe less than 30 seconds – I didn’t really know what was going on. Then it suddenly let me go and I popped up.

The other surfers didn’t come for me. It was a difficult situation – they initially scattered, as you would, because I was screaming. I managed to get back on my board and got my arm – what was left of it – back onto the board. I just started paddling. I was very fearful it was going to circle back and come again. I felt like a sitting duck. I just went hell-for-leather and paddled really hard one-handed and caught a wave. Just on my stomach. It was the best wave of my life – the wave that saved my life, absolutely.

When I got in [to the shallows], my board got sucked back out behind me, dragging on my leash, and I couldn’t get out. I was there in the shallows, holding my arm, just stuck up to my thighs in the water. And then one of the local guys here who I know quite well grabbed me and helped me up onto the sand.

There were a lot of people on the beach that night. Someone called the ambulance, which took about 45 minutes to come. But Bondi’s one of the best places in Australia to be attacked by a shark: there were three doctors literally right there. I’d lost a fair bit of blood, and later on one of them – an emergency doctor from Prince of Wales [Hospital in Randwick] – told me that when he looked at me, he thought it was 50-50 I’d have a cardiac arrest on the sand and not make it.

Straight after the attack, when I woke up in hospital, I thought I’d never surf again. I remember my wife, Lisa – who was six months pregnant – saying, “I want to move away from the beach.” And I was the same – I didn’t want to even see the ocean. But by the next day, we’d both calmed down; we both decided we wanted to stay. And I knew I wanted to surf again.

Since the attack, I’ve learnt a bit about what happened, though of course you can’t be sure. I think it was a test bite from the shark. Another guy in the water that day got bumped just before I was bitten, and – I’m speculating – I think it was the same shark: I think it was noticing a lot of surfers, trying to figure it out. The teeth marks from my bite, and my wetsuit, suggest it was a juvenile white shark, maybe about four years old, about 200 kilograms – around the age where they transfer from eating finned fish to mammals, like seals. So they’re just learning, and with something big, they want to test it out. They’re looking for fat and meat. So when it got my arm it gave it a bit of a go, then it was like, “Yeah, feeling a bit weird … not worth my time”. So it let go.

I only learnt all that later, of course. When I think back, I think our understanding of sharks now is at a completely different scientific level than when I was attacked; and I didn’t understand the contributing factors towards shark attack the way I do now. For instance, the night I was attacked, there were the floodwaters and the runoff; it was dusk; it was overcast and cloudy and not easy for sharks to see. There were a lot of bait fish around; and it was February, which is a very common month for shark attacks. So there were lots of risk factors which the average Joe – including me – didn’t really know at the time.

Now there are drones and tagging and tracking and just a lot more information to help you. When I decide to go out these days, I think I recognise that I’m making an actual decision, consciously, based on a whole lot of factors. For myself, my basic rules are: if a beach is closed, I don’t go. I don’t surf at sunset or sunrise – basically, if the sun isn’t on the water, I don’t go. If it’s really murky after rain, I’ll give it a couple of days. I do sometimes feel fearful, but fear’s not something that will stop me doing it. It’s just a feeling, and I just try to manage it, accept it and let it pass. And usually it does. Often I’ll go out and I don’t feel any fear at all.

I’m not an expert and I’m not really capable of offering anyone advice. But my personal feeling is that what’s most valuable is the continuing development of scientific knowledge and education around sharks: their habits, behaviours, biology. Just in the past year, the drones have started putting out a lot of information, which I think is useful. I don’t love shark nets: they didn’t save me, and I think they trap a lot of wildlife. I’m not 100 per cent against them, but I’ve always questioned their value. I feel the same about drum lines. My major thing is I don’t really want a whole lot of wildlife getting killed unnecessarily when it’s not really having a very big impact on shark attacks. I think the biggest impact will come with people really understanding that “today is a potentially dangerous day”, based on the science. I think the scientists are doing a good job.

These days, sometimes I’ll surf every day of the week; sometimes, if it’s flat for a while, I won’t go at all. But I guess I average a couple of times a week. [Last summer, at the peak of the attacks] I stayed out of the surf for two weeks, probably longer than most people. I probably do take a more cautious approach than others. I certainly don’t feel immune. And if I did get attacked again, people are going to think I’m a real idiot! Like getting struck twice by lightning.

2:55

'I wouldn’t go back in time and not have the attack'

Long-time surfer Glenn Orgias reflects on the lessons of his 2009 shark attack.

Chris Pepin-Neff is an associate professor in public policy at the University of Sydney. For the past 20 years, they have worked in the sub-specialty of “human-shark studies”, looking at media coverage, policymaking, and public opinion and emotion surrounding sharks. They have worked on human-shark risk assessment and safety measures all over the world, including Australia, South Africa, Réunion Island and the United States.

“I always look at three things: shark activity, human activity, environmental conditions. Last summer was a perfect storm: warm water temperatures, record summer rain, superabundance of bait fish. It was a singularity – totally incomparable to any other time. And I’d suggest we’re not going to have another year like we’ve just had. But that said, there’s going to be extraordinary levels of unpredictability this year: we’ve got El Niño, it’s going to be hot – we just don’t know what’s going to happen.

It can be helpful to think in terms of attractants and deterrents. Attractants are things that attract sharks. So, say you have a harbour beach, with a jetty nearby. You’ve got boats, with sewage that attracts small fish: attractant. You’ve got fishermen gutting fish off the jetty: attractant. Then you’ve got high water temperature and low water clarity, environmental conditions that raise the level of bait fish: attractant. So a lot of attractants, which equals high risk. My mum’s passed now, but she was a big swimmer. Would I let her go swimming between the boats in that sort of scenario? No way. To me, it’s a disaster waiting to happen.

What you want is to remove attractants and add deterrents – things that trigger avoidant behaviour in sharks. So one thing I always recommend is that if you’re swimming at an unprotected beach, you should be swimming in pairs or groups. That’s particularly true for children: everybody needs a buddy. And that’s because we want to trigger sharks’ avoidance response by being more intimidating. Big multiple splashes, like swimmers between the flags – a great big mess in the water – that’s intimidating, because sharks don’t know what that is: it doesn’t read like potential prey. One swimmer is not intimidating. A surfer on a surfboard is not intimidating. So sharks come up and they’re curious, maybe defensive. That’s when they might take a bite.

You can also do a few things to make yourself less inviting. Don’t wear jewellery – your watch, your necklace – because it could look flashy, like fish gills that are moving. Don’t wear yellow: in the shark-bite community – and I’ve not seen a scientific study on this, but dear god, I know it’s true – it’s referred to as “yum yum yellow”. Don’t wear flesh-coloured clothes. You don’t want to look like a seal, but I’d rather be black than look like flesh. Or a fish. Don’t wear silvery, bluey things.

I’ve done assessments on Réunion Island, in Florida; the same rules apply. You just have to be mindful that the ocean is an active ecosystem. It’s wrong to assume that the ocean is like a resort pool that’s always safe, and the shark is always dangerous. The fact is, the shark isn’t always dangerous and the beach is really never safe. The ocean is the wild. We do ourselves a disservice when we pretend otherwise.

This is why the research on culling has shown that it doesn’t work. Because if the attractant is never removed, you have to kill every single shark in the ecosystem. And then you’ve got to kill every shark under that, and under that, all the way down. Apex predator, meso-predator, on and on: white sharks and bull sharks, then dusky sharks and bronze whalers. It would never end.

Netting is difficult. Not all nets are created equal. Enclosure nets in the right context work very well. I’ve seen them in operation in Capetown; I recommended one at Cottesloe in Western Australia. An enclosure net doesn’t kill anything, doesn’t catch anything. It’s not an environmental disaster. It comes right in to the beach – water on three sides, sand on the fourth. You put it out for three hours on a Sunday morning for Nippers or whatever, then you pull it back in. It’s completely safe – nothing can get in, nothing can get out.

I think other kinds of nets [such as the gill nets at many beaches, which sit off-shore in the middle of a water column as partial barriers, while leaving the majority of the area un-netted] are insane and dangerous. The reality is that when fish get caught in those nets, they struggle. Those struggles send out low-frequency vibrations that sharks can sense over long distances: it’s one of the ways they detect prey. So those vibrations are literally like ringing a dinner bell for sharks to come in toward the nets – and the beach. They are literally the last thing you should put in front of the flags.

The irony is that people don’t actually want [gill] nets. I’ve gone all over the world – and remember, I only go to beaches after clusters of fatal shark bites – looking for people who want them, and the highest number I can get is between seven and nine per cent. I did a survey here at Waverley at Bondi. The question was: “If a shark net was taken out and there was a fatal shark attack at Bondi afterwards, would you hold the politician responsible?” Six hundred people, scientific study; 70 per cent of people said, “No, we wouldn’t.” We also asked, “Would you go back to that beach if the net was taken out?” And three out of four people said, “Yes.”

But for politicians, that 30 per cent is too much of a risk. Politicians are trying to manage the public holding them accountable for shark bites – not the occurrence of shark bites themselves. What’s the threshold of risk and courage a politician would need to take shark nets out, pray to God there are no incidents, and if there is, be able to sustain nine weeks of front page coverage blaming them? That’s a very, very hard question. I’ve seen it asked all over the world, but never more than in Australia. And the fact is, no politician is courageous enough to take that risk.

And so the state government has been entirely disingenuous on the subject of shark nets in NSW. There were shark nets in the water when at least three of the last shark attacks here occurred, and yet the government has doubled down on the effectiveness of shark nets. I’m not talking about my friends at the DPI [Department of Primary Industries] or my scientist colleagues, I’m talking about the politicians who said, “Oh, well, this cluster goes to prove that we need more shark nets.” It has not proven that. It has proven that shark nets are less effective and potentially more dangerous even than we thought. They’ve had 100 years to find one study that says they work and they can’t. And I can find five studies that say that gill nets catch sharks and other marine life, and attract sharks closer to the beach. And not only studies: DPI pictures and videos show that 40 per cent of sharks are caught on the inside of the nets. The fact is, shark nets don’t protect beachgoers. Shark nets protect politicians.

One of the major political off-ramps for governments wanting to stop using nets is drumlines. The old kind are baited buoys that basically drown the shark. The new kind, smart drumlines, have a pinger that alerts people, who come and drag the shark out to sea. The response has to be quick, otherwise there’s an 80 per cent mortality rate – but it’s potentially an excellent resource for tagging and other scientific data collection; and the research shows that dragging a shark away is traumatic enough for the animal that it stays out of the area for between three and six months. So it’s a very effective non-lethal measure. Although there is some bycatch, it’s very low – far lower than nets.

Drones are another effective measure – in the right context, they allow us to see what’s really happening in the water. Drones show shark nets don’t work: you can see the sharks swimming over and under and around the nets. So the government’s investment in drones is, in fact, funding the largest study ever proving that the government’s investment in nets is ineffective.

Colin Simpfendorfer is an adjunct professor of Marine Biology at James Cook University. He is one of the world’s foremost scientific experts on sharks. From 2012 to 2020, he was co-chair of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Species Survival Commission Shark Specialist Group – the leading global authority on the conservation, management and extinction risk assessments of sharks, rays and chimaeras.

“When we talk about shark-human interactions in Australia, we’re really talking about three species: white sharks, bull sharks and, to a lesser degree, tiger sharks. But mostly bull sharks and white sharks.

So for bull sharks, at this time of year they’re coming south from places like Queensland into NSW, sometimes even Victorian waters. The females are going into rivers – always the same river, often the place they were born – to give birth to their young. And the young bull sharks will live in those rivers for several years before they leave.

White sharks are a bit less predictable. This is a roaming species, and so the adults in particular can be anywhere between here and New Zealand, or all the way down to Tasmania. We’re talking about an apex predator: one of their characteristics is they have a massive range they travel over. There’s no point staying somewhere for a long period because they’d eat out all the food resources.

Australia works very hard to identify and manage our shark populations and our fisheries, and we do an extremely good job. And that’s important, because sharks are intensively fished in many parts of the world, including many of our immediate neighbours. This idea that “Oh, there are way more sharks now than there were” – that’s simply not the case for these species. White sharks, for example, are long-lived and have few young: we certainly haven’t seen a sudden explosion in their numbers. On the other hand, there are certainly more people in the water now than there have ever been – especially with things like sea-changers in northern NSW, where there are a lot of juvenile white sharks.

When it comes to shark-human interactions, the most fundamental thing for people to understand is that even in bad years, a shark biting a person is an extremely rare event. Given the millions of hours people spend in the water, and the fact that there are always sharks in the water, bites are really extraordinarily unusual. So the fluctuation of numbers we see – as with NSW last year, for instance – can actually be just random chance.

The number of encounters do seem to go through cycles – and we don’t fully understand what drives those cycles. Certainly things like temperature, food, water quality do play a role for sharks; for people, the numbers of swimmers, their behaviour, and their location may be factors. The “rogue shark” idea [of individual sharks that repeatedly bite humans] has had very little science done on it, which makes it hard to dispel scientifically. My take is that it developed from this observation that shark bites sometimes occur in groups. But that’s more likely due to local conditions making sharks more common in a particular area than a single shark biting lots of people. The idea itself first emerged a long time ago, when abattoirs were discharging offal directly into the ocean and rivers in places like Cairns and Townsville. Those conditions attracted many sharks, and groups of bites occurred.

Being conscious of conditions is one of the ways we, as individuals, can mitigate our risk. Swimming at dawn and dusk is probably a bad idea: sharks’ vision isn’t necessarily always great, and it’s worse in low light. Don’t swim in the middle of the school of fish. Don’t swim alone.

There are also a number of technologies that can help, at least theoretically. Many of them are snake oil, but there’s very good scientific evidence that some types of electrical devices reduce your risk. Not eliminate it altogether – but significantly reduce it. [A study in Nature in 2024 found that two such devices reduced the probability of bites by 54 per cent across bull, white and tiger sharks.] The idea of those devices is to interfere with the shark’s electrical sense. Sharks have seven senses to our five: they have cells that can detect changes in water pressure along their bodies; and they can detect very small electrical voltages from the muscle movements of their prey. If we interfere with that electrical sensitivity, it confuses them, so they pull out of [potential] bites, swim away, avoid the scenario.

So that’s all personal stuff we can do. Then there’s the question of deterrents at community or government levels. The first possibility is fully netted enclosures: keeping sharks and people separated by a physical barrier. Enclosures don’t catch or trap sharks – or anything else – they just provide a barrier in the water. They work well in calm water, but not in high-energy environments where you’ve got storms or waves.

Then you’ve got measures like [gill] nets or drumlines. If we take netting, the obvious question is, is it successful? That’s a good question. It depends on what your metric of success is. Does success mean nobody getting bitten by a shark, ever? In that case, it’s clearly not working. Has it reduced risk? Maybe. The science is very hard to do. What we have known for a long time that these nets will also catch turtles, dolphins, a whole range of different fish. They don’t catch necessarily a lot of them, but they can still have very big impacts on what are relatively small populations of some of these species.

The third type of protection is the shark cull approach. Is that effective? It certainly isn’t a panacea. What we do know is that you can never get rid of all the sharks; and the consequences to the environment would be devastating. You’re going to kill a whole lot of other things along the way, impact a complex ecosystem, and affect things you can’t even begin to predict – including things like commercial fisheries.

So in the end, the benefits of these deterrents are very hard to quantify, and the costs are clear. That being said, I think governments are starting to wake up to the fact that just going out and killing sharks isn’t the answer; many people don’t see that as the answer. What we’ve seen over the last decade or so are some changes towards lower environmental impacts, still with appropriate risk mitigation. Are those changes happening fast enough? Hard to say. People think science will provide the answer. Actually, science can advise, but it can’t make the decision. It would be nice to see some real, consistently science-based decision-making.

The reality is that, at the beach, there’s always a shark somewhere not too far away. It’s their environment. It’s where they live. It’s not that they’re coming to stalk you. They’re just going about their normal daily lives. So they swim along beaches. They hang out wherever. Ultimately, you can never eliminate risk 100 per cent if you’re in the water. Everyone has to reach their own accommodation of these very small risks. People will do the things they love, and they should. Ultimately, we all have to take responsibility for what we do.

‘You hold hope and fear at the same time’: Living in the limbo of incurable cancer

Sydney Morning Herald November 21, 2026

Lisa Briggs often wonders what it would be like to wake up and feel normal, just for a day.

Each morning, she checks for changes to her breathing and mentally scans her body for any unfamiliar pain. Subtle shifts can trigger panic. Could this be a side effect of a medication? Has the cancer spread?

“There is this whole psychological element of it,” the 44-year-old says.

“This process of analysing, overanalysing and worrying. It is almost like a tab that’s open on a computer. It’s running silently in the background all the time.”

When the anxiety feels paralysing, she closes her vivid green eyes and settles her mind by focusing on her gratitude for being alive, and her love for her two children, Jasmine and AJ, and her husband, Kirk.

Briggs has stage 4 incurable metastatic lung cancer.

The disease was detected four months after she gave birth to her son in 2014.

By then, the cancer had spread, invading her liver, spleen and lymph nodes, and riddling her bones. The prognosis was devastating: a 3 per cent chance of surviving five years.

Yet, 12 years later, Briggs is still here. The whiteboard in the kitchen of her home in Doreen, in Melbourne’s north-east, is a testament to that. There, she scrawled the defiant words “I am not a statistic” in big, bold, black letters.

Briggs is one of a growing number of Australians living for years with incurable cancer. She is not imminently dying, nor is she ever likely to be rid of the disease.

“You’re holding on to hope and fear at the same time,” she says.

Not so long ago, a stage 4 cancer diagnosis was a death sentence, meaning the disease had metastasised and spread far from where it first formed, attacking distant parts of the body.

Now, revolutionary advancements in new targeted therapies alongside pioneering immunotherapy and novel drugs mean rising numbers of people are living with incurable cancer for longer.

For some, like Briggs, the disease has become a chronic illness of sorts, kept at bay by a brutal regimen of drugs.

She takes at least 10 tablets a day to stay alive and be well enough to care for her children. They are a mix of targeted cancer therapy drugs, cholesterol and heart medication, probiotic supplements, and pills to counter debilitating side effects such as reflux or sudden changes to her mood.

Professor Michael Jefford, director of the Australian Cancer Survivorship Centre at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, describes the rise of long-term survivors as “a new paradigm”.

“Since the emergence of immunotherapy and targeted cancer therapies there’s been a much bigger number of people living longer term,” the oncologist says.

“But because they are relatively new treatments, we’re assuming some people may actually even be cured eventually. We just don’t know yet.”

More than 2.6 million Australians are forecast to be living with a cancer diagnosis by 2050 – an increase of almost 1 million people over the next 25 years.

About 44 per cent of those are expected to have a cancer that is not yet cured and will require ongoing treatment.

Researchers also predict that breakthroughs in immunotherapy, a treatment that boosts the body’s immune system to fight cancer, and targeted therapy, which targets specific features of cancer cells to stop the disease growing and spreading, will continue to propel survival rates higher than ever before.

Researchers also predict that breakthroughs in immunotherapy, which boosts the immune system to fight cancer, and precision oncology, such as targeted therapy that blocks malignant cell growth, will continue propelling survival rates to record highs.

While early detection and treatments have improved dramatically, it remains difficult to determine who will be a long-term cancer survivor.

Questions remain about why individual responses to these transformative treatments can vary so profoundly between patients, though the differences are thought to be driven by a complex mix of biological, genetic and lifestyle factors, and even the specific type of tumour.

“There’s an enormous amount of uncertainty people have about whether the treatment will work for them, and if it does, how long will it last?” Jefford says.

Sydney cancer researcher and oncologist Professor Bogda Koczwara says the distinct human experience of living indefinitely with advanced and incurable cancer is increasingly being recognised as its own unique form of cancer survivorship.

“When you are first diagnosed, people are happy to cheer you on for a short haul, but running out of stamina later is a real thing,” she says.

“People want to return to normal. But for survivors living with advanced cancer, the old normal never returns. There is a new normal, which is completely different.”

Koczwara says those living in the limbo of incurable cancer have been left floundering.

“These individuals have significant, unique needs, and so do their caregivers,” she says.

While people cured of cancer linger in dread of a relapse, Jefford says those surviving for years while enduring relentless treatment face a different kind of fear.

“For both groups of people it is marked by persisting physical issues, but overwhelmingly psychological concern,” he says.

“They might have ongoing consequences from their treatment. They might be worried about developing another cancer. They might feel that they’ve changed as a person.”

At the moment there are glaring gaps in cancer survivorship support for people like Briggs.

“The cancer system has been set up to do a good job of diagnosis and treatment, but it is almost like a conveyor belt of diagnose, treat, and then off you go,” Jefford says.

“We’re leaving people lost in transition. If you have a knee replacement or a heart attack, you automatically get rehabilitation afterwards. We don’t do that with cancer.”

The breathlessness began during Lisa Briggs’ second pregnancy. Her chest felt tight, like she could never get enough air in.

Then she developed a wheeze and a severe fatigue she had never felt before. She estimates she went to the doctor 16 times in 10 months.

“I kept saying, ‘Something’s wrong – I can’t breathe,’” she says.

Her GP put her symptoms down to exhaustion and pregnancy-related asthma – a woman stretching herself too thin. She was working as an osteopath and exercise physiologist, running her own sports medicine clinic. She was pregnant and had a lively toddler at home. But months after her son was born, she still had a persistent, throbbing pain in her back.

Skin cancer doctor

One morning, as she was buckling her young daughter into a car seat, she coughed up blood into a tissue.

The days that followed are a blur. She is rushed to hospital in an ambulance. She is put in an isolation ward when doctors suspect she might have tuberculosis. Her world comes tumbling down as an oncologist tells her gently, but frankly, she has terminal lung cancer.

“He just said, ‘The cancer has spread, and there is no cure,’” Briggs recalls.

“I don’t remember a single word that came out of his mouth after that. I went into shock. Then the panic kicked in. I started to think about my kids and my family, and what was going to happen to them.”

She remembers Kirk sitting beside her in the hospital, holding her hand, reassuring her that they will get through it, promising her she will see her daughter start school.

For Briggs, the precariousness is always there. Her life is a cycle of waiting for the results of her scans every three months.

“What happens to a lot of people in my situation is things pop up, and it’s so unexpected,” she says.

“You can literally go into a scan feeling fantastic. Then you walk out being told you’ve got a tumour in your brain. That’s the reality we face.”

In Australia, five-year survival rates for advanced cancers including melanoma, lymphoma, prostate, breast, lung and some blood cancers, such as multiple myeloma, have all increased.

“To think that people with diseases associated with such a poor prognosis, like advanced melanoma or advanced lung cancer, may even be cured with medication is incredible,” Jefford, who has worked in oncology for almost 30 years, says.

“That didn’t exist when I started out as a doctor.”

Yet, despite the extraordinary strides to extend life, survival gains remain stubbornly uneven.

Immunotherapy, for example, works for only a small fraction of bowel cancer cases, Jefford says.

Survival rates for advanced types of cancer, including pancreatic, brain and ovarian, have also lagged behind as they are notoriously difficult to detect and often diagnosed in the very late stages when treatment options are limited.

“Ideally, what we want is to have highly effective treatments that are very well tolerated and that they work for the vast majority of people,” Jefford says.

But promising research is on the horizon.

Earlier this year, the US Food and Drug Administration fast-tracked approval of a new drug, daraxonrasib, for the most common form of pancreatic cancer after a clinical trial showed it can block a mutated protein that spurs tumour growth.

Patients who took the drug lived notably longer, for an average of 13.2 months, compared with 6.6 to 6.7 months for patients who had chemotherapy, the researchers found.

In a world-first trial this year, CAR T-cell therapy, a specialised immunotherapy in which a patient’s own immune cells are genetically modified in a lab to hunt down cancer, extended survival rates by about 40 per cent in people with advanced gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer, when compared with standard care.

The results, published in medical journal The Lancet, sparked cautious optimism globally about the potential of immunotherapy on solid tumours.

“The boom of immunotherapy is kind of just taking off,” Koczwara says.

“We’re going to see some really exciting developments. The challenge remains that access to treatment is very inequitable. Not every treatment is affordable. The costs of these drugs are huge and getting higher by the minute.”

As doctors closely monitor the toxicity of cancer treatment on the body, Koczwara warns our systems of care remain poorly equipped to help people cope with the fallout of living with cancer for years.

“We know less about survivors living with advanced cancer than those who have completed treatment, and that’s a real gap in the research and the support,” she says.

Koczwara wants a shift in how society views advanced cancer, arguing there is much to learn from the management of chronic conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

But Koczwara, who also leads the Australian Research Centre for Cancer Survivorship in NSW, says one of the most challenging realities of living with incurable cancer is that it is so unpredictable.

“We can say, ‘You’re likely to be alive longer,’” she says.

“This is a really good thing. And yet, what sits underneath all of that is for a lot of people they will eventually die of it. This uncertainty is incredibly difficult to live with.”

People are left agonising over life choices. Should they have the child they yearn for? Is it safe to travel overseas? Should they keep contributing to their superannuation? There are difficulties in maintaining employment and finances.

Invisibility can be a hallmark of metastatic cancer too.

“People might look terrific, but they don’t necessarily feel that terrific,” Koczwara says.

“It is so hard for people to comprehend what they are going through behind closed doors and the energy it can take to do things.”

Briggs says: “This is the space where I live each day. It’s where life persists, but the systems around us are still figuring it out.”

Some days, Briggs is well enough to clean the house, do the washing, complete the shopping and pick up her children from school. On rarer days, she can be bedridden. Her body has weathered a gruelling clinical trial and years of endless treatment. Some medications have rendered her violently ill or sent her pulse racing so rapidly she thought she was having a heart attack.

Briggs grapples daily with her children having to grow up faster than they should. There is a quiet tenderness between her and her husband, both wanting to carry the weight of it all for each other.

“There’s been times when I’ve purposely tried to mask or hide how I’m feeling because I’m trying to protect him,” Briggs says.

“He does the same for me. But he does it way better.”

More than a decade ago, too ill to rise from the couch while her infant son lay nearby, Briggs vividly remembers asking her daughter Jasmine, now 15, to always take care of her little brother.

“I remember her little face, and I’m going to cry as I say this, but I just said to her, ‘I need you to be a mum to AJ because Mummy’s really sick,’” Briggs says, her eyes filling with tears.

“She’s so nurturing. She is just the most beautiful kid. I said, ‘Promise me you’ll take care of him forever.’ She said, ‘OK, Mummy’, and she did.”

There is a piercing clarity that comes with confronting your own mortality. Your world shrinks. Briggs savours picking her children up from school and hearing about their day on the car ride home. She finds solace in nature. The walls of her home are full of photographs of precious family holidays to Disney World. This year, she was well enough to travel to Italy to surprise her parents.

“Nobody can tell you what’s going to happen between today and tomorrow, let alone in 12 months’ time,” she says.

“But these are the moments I live for.”

Every summer, they pack their car and caravan and drive to the coastal town of Mallacoota in East Gippsland.

Briggs rises while it is still dark and sits outside to bask in the sunrise.

It was in this caravan years ago where AJ, arms outstretched, called his mum for the first time from his bed.

“I could hear him calling ‘Mama’, and I just sat, and I listened to that because it was not a moment I ever thought I’d live to see,” she says.

“Kirk said, ‘Aren’t you going to go pick him up?’ I said, ‘I just want to listen for a moment.’ I let him call my name over and over again because it was the most beautiful thing I had ever heard.”

Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:04:46 GMT

African ministers say they ‘didn’t come here to beg’, with civil society groups calling it the ‘worst Cop ever’

Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.

The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.

On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.

Several Cop insiders said Saudi Arabia was one of the countries playing an obstructive role. The petrostate has gained a reputation over the decades for using the Cop process to slow action. Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in the final agreement as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at the advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there”. He said: “It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests.”

Eight countries called for reference to “a clear transition away from fossil fuels” to be restored into the text of any agreement. Panama, Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, the Solomon Islands and Sweden outlined vital issues they said must be addressed, including ensuring polluting countries paid into funds for developing countries to adapt to the climate crisis.

Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, said: “It is not acceptable to have a Cop or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly.”

Panama had sent an open letter to the president of the negotiations, Chris Bowen, with a list of demands the country said were not negotiable.

“Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work,” said Bowen. On Friday afternoon, he said: “There is still a spirit of making it work. People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, let’s give up and go home.”

In a dramatic press conference on Friday morning, African ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone said African people were being asked to pay for a crisis they did not cause. They accused rich countries of simultaneously attempting a third exploitation of the continent – after slavery and colonialism – by using carbon taxes to prevent Africans from making use of their wealth of critical minerals to industrialise.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who was ministerial chair of the African group of negotiators, said: “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them. We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries, that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

A vital request of African nations was for discussion of climate finance. All week civil society observers have accused richer countries, led by the EU, of obstructing progress in talks on money.

The chief climate negotiator for Europe said on Friday that it was already the world leading climate finance donor. A senior EU official said: “We, together with the EU member states, are providing €32.3bn [£27bn] from public sources and mobilising €9.3bn in private finance in 2025 to support developing countries. We’re doing by far the most.”

The last Cop meeting to finish on time was in Italy in 2003. Some talks have dragged into the Sunday after the scheduled Friday finish.

Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:18:20 GMT

Christmas comedy hit is set for a follow-up from the point of view of the father with Seth Rogen as writer and producer

A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return.

According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni, Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline, will be from the father’s point of view.

The film will also recruit Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg as writers and producers and they will work with Culkin to craft the script. Rogen and Goldberg recently worked with Disney on a Muppets TV special.

Home Alone was a major box office hit upon release in 1990, grossing $476m worldwide and becoming the year’s second-biggest movie. Culkin returned for the sequel Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which made $359m two years later.

The franchise continued without the actor for three further movies and then in 2021, after Fox had been bought by Disney, there was a straight-to-streaming reboot.

Culkin later reprised the role in a 2018 commercial for Google and this year has once again returned as Kevin for a new McDonald’s advert.

Last year, he was asked about a sequel at an anniversary event.

“I kind of had this idea,” he said. “I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard and I’m not really paying enough attention and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me and then I get locked out.”

In his pitch, the character’s son won’t let him in and would be the one setting the traps with the house as “some sort of metaphor for our relationship”.

The original film’s director, Chris Columbus, who later went on to direct the first two Harry Potter adventures, has spoken out about a possible sequel. “I think it’s a mistake to try to go back and recapture something we did 35 years ago,” he said. “I think it should be left alone.”

Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:00:37 GMT

Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners

Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

after newsletter promotion

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.

Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, especially in troublesome times. He will love the pageantry and event glamour of Old Trafford. And he will love having Ferguson in the crowd for the matches.

Pochettino first encountered him in January 2013 when, in his second Southampton game, he went to Old Trafford to face Ferguson’s United, who won 2-1. Pochettino has mentioned that this week. And the meal at Scott’s. And how he was at the Camp Nou for Ferguson’s finest hour: the 1999 Champions League final victory against Bayern Munich. Pochettino was an Espanyol player at the time, together with Toni Jiménez, who is part of his coaching staff, and they watched the first half from so-so seats before blagging their way into the directors’ box for the second period.

When Solskjær scored his iconic late winner, Pochettino and Jiménez celebrated wildly. They were caught up in the moment. It was the first time Pochettino felt a connection to United and he began to pay more attention to them. And Ferguson. Pochettino described him this week as “the best coach in the history of the sport” but it was not a soundbite of convenience. He has always maintained this and said so on the record after the lunch at Scott’s.

How can Pochettino position himself in terms of the Glazers and Ratcliffe? The first thing to say is that he does have experience of unpopular and/or difficult owners. At Spurs, Daniel Levy was forever maligned by the fans, and Pochettino had problems with the American ownership at Chelsea. Between times, the Qataris at PSG were not easy. Pochettino worked to build a relationship with Levy, regularly saying nice things about him in the press and famously including him on a staff-bonding trip to Argentina.

It featured white-water rafting and ended with Pochettino having to fish Levy out of the Manso River. A repeat of the adventure with Joel Glazer feels unlikely but Pochettino’s starting point at United has been to stress unity; the need to create chemistry with everyone, including “the directors and the owners”.

And so to Anfield, where Pochettino first managed with Southampton in September 2013 when his team won 1-0. He has not tasted victory in his eight subsequent trips; seven with Spurs, one with Chelsea, the record shows two draws and six defeats. No United fan expects anything this time but Pochettino considers it a great game to have. He will certainly learn a lot about his players.

The Super Bowl of F1: how Las Vegas GP has hit the jackpot after turbulent start

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:00:37 GMT

George Russell calls it the biggest race on the Formula One calendar bar Monaco – and the numbers back him up

That Formula One has achieved a palpable success in hosting a race in Las Vegas is impossible to ignore. Even with this year’s outing a dead rubber and with the city in perhaps its least flattering light, the cold drizzle of a Thursday afternoon beneath gunmetal-grey skies, the fans who have flocked to Nevada were irrepressibly enthusiastic.

Long queues stretched out into the streets before the gates were even open and it seems even many locals who were initially cool to the somewhat disruptive F1 circus have embraced the fans, their fervour for the sport and the positive impact of the race.

Kimi Antonelli might have tied up the title with Mercedes in Mexico but this weekend’s race in Las Vegas retains an unmistakable celebratory atmosphere that the organisers have assiduously cultivated and is, quite literally, paying off. When darkness falls and the city truly comes alive, adorned in all of its garish neon beauty, F1 in Vegas really begins to make sense as part of a burgeoning sport riding a wave of commercial success.

Las Vegas is now entering its fourth year on the calendar with a deal to continue until 2037. It is – for all that purists may dislike its emphasis on being, whisper it, entertaining – here to stay.

As Mercedes’ George Russell observed this week: “With where the sport is now, I think you need a race like this on the schedule. I guess it’s the biggest one, bar Monaco, from an entertainment perspective for the people who come here and for F1. This just feels like the Super Bowl.”

The “biggest bar Monaco” is praise indeed and exactly what F1 had in mind when it brought the race to the city in 2023, spending £500m to build the facilities and circuit. It was a turbulent opening. Quite apart from the well-documented issues on the opening day when running was curtailed because of a loose water valve cover, there was opposition from locals unhappy with the disruption to their work and businesses, including some legal challenges. Yet it has proved to be an absolute success story.

Emily Prazer, the chief commercial officer for F1 and the president of the Las Vegas GP, accepts it has been a challenging process. “We have to admit where we perhaps were a little bit bull in a china shop about it,” she said. “We had a very small amount of time to get this thing up and running for 2023 but now we spend hours talking to people making sure we’re answering those questions.”

This has involved working closely with the administration of Clark County and the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, which has allayed much of the local disquiet, not least by bringing in so much money. Over the previous three years, the meeting has generated $3.2bn (£2.4bn) in economic impact in Southern Nevada. In the past two years the race has generated $45m and $43m respectively in tax income.

In 2024, research into the race weekend indicated that the average visitor spent $2,400, excluding race tickets. The meeting has transformed what was traditionally the quietest weekend of the year in Vegas into one showing a healthy return. Despite the race being initially unpopular, these are numbers with which it is hard to argue and Vegas is about nothing if not numbers.

In the first year of the race a local tour guide told me it would succeed if the people who worked here felt it was benefiting them in tips and spending, that the returns outweighed the disruption. A threshold that appears to have been met.

It is also increasingly where the business of F1 is being done. This week the sport announced a new partnership with the wearable fitness technology brand Whoop, which will mean some drivers having their heart rates broadcast live to fans and media, and another with Nike as part of the expanding and lucrative commercial partnerships F1 is embracing. Another, with Lego, is represented in the paddock by 4ft-tall minifigure versions of each driver outside their respective hospitality units, while celebrities will race Lego cars before the main event on Saturday. None of which feels in the slightest bit out of place here.

Alongside which F1’s management would doubtless have been equally pleased by the feelings among fans. The season has been marked by the low grumble of driver dissatisfaction with the new engine regulations, which has at least partly been behind the FIA pushing for a return to 2.1-litre, V8 engines for 2030. An agreement on which was formally concluded when it was announced by F1 and the FIA in Las Vegas. The new engines will utilise a smaller electric element, half of which will be limited to overtake-mode use, with the purpose being lighter and cheaper engines to put an emphasis on “attack-orientated racing”.

F1 has nonetheless been robust in its defence of the new formula all season, insisting that for all the driver disgruntlement, fans were enjoying the racing more than ever. In the bustling East Harmon fan zone , lit by red and white neon reflecting from billowing clouds of dry ice and throbbing to pounding music, even as the rain continued during practice and there was only limited running in the first session, spirits were high and they were shifting merch hand over fist.

Gemma, 24, had come in from New York state with two friends for their first F1 meeting. “We love the cars,” she said. “Love the drivers. It’s fun, exciting, there’s so much action and coming to Vegas, even in the rain they look amazing here.”

Which chimes with F1’s position on both the regulations and this race, which has proved successful perhaps beyond even what the sport had in mind. Making money amid the spectacle. What could be more Las Vegas?

No competitive lap times were set during first practice with the rain and cold temperatures making for immensely tricky conditions. The teams were unwilling to risk much running, given conditions are expected to be dry for the rest of the weekend.

In the second session, the track was still wet but running was possible, albeit on the intermediate tyres. Russell topped the timesheets for Mercedes, from the Alpine of Pierre Gasly, benefiting from being out last on a drying track, with Charles Leclerc in third for Ferrari.

Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:00:37 GMT

The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player

Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”
