Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:00:36 GMT

The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist?

There was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang, a saga that may or may not have involved some kind of adulterous 63-year-old honey trap spy dynamic.

The latest suggestion being punted about is that, whatever his raw human frailties, Huang is in fact “irreplaceable” as the president of Nvidia. Only this guy can do it. Only this leather-jacketed human visionary, who looks in every available photo like your GCSE chemistry teacher’s profile pic on TerrifiedUkrainianSinglesWantToDateYou. com, can manage this key artificial intelligence mission.

Funny isn’t it? Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can literally make every other person on the planet’s job vanish overnight, because, like, we don’t actually need humans any more. We have a fake version that’s cheaper and less annoying. Except, of course, in this case where it turns out humans are in fact creative, delicate irreplaceable things. Hal. Open the airlock doors, Hal.

It’s obvious what the best solution is here. Scrape his data and make an AI Jensen Huang instead. Get the robots in. Nothing personal, Jensen old boy. It’s just the necessary march of progress. And if I can offer some helpful advice during your period of soul-crushing obsolescence, I’d say maybe look at industries AI can’t vaporise beneath your feet while you’re working yourself thin just trying to survive.

Develop your soft communication skills, yeah? Work for free. Try to become a hot new middle-aged gimmickfluencer, like two billion other desperate units of human alienation around the world. Stop drinking flat whites. Whatever. Sorry, Jens, you’re breaking up. I’ve got RobodeathbotExec5000 on the other line, I’ve got to take this.

All middle-aged men must have views on AI. In fact this may be what kills it in the end, endless scrolling legions of men with beards mansplaining the future. You want slop. We’ll give you so much slop your servers will melt. My own theory is that AI might be the thing that saves the human race, not the rogue element that kills it. AI doesn’t crave things, or have daddy issues. The real threat to humanity isn’t some kind of deranged robot consciousness. It’s deranged people, lone egomaniacs, actual human elements like greed and despotism.

At which point, enter sport. Or in this case, Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. Shah remains a compelling figure. Don’t be deceived by the pictures from the meeting in Bali, in which he’s wearing his usual glazed facial expression, like a man who’s just been hit in the head with a rock and it’s the greatest thing that’s ever happened to him.

In reality this is another moment of triumph for this super-talented administrative prodigy, whose rise to supreme overlord of all cricket is all the more remarkable given he also happens, by pure coincidence, to be the son of the Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s oldest political ally.

Otherwise, this was widely seen as a disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. But one thing did stand out. Proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues have been postponed to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. And this is a shame, because something is cooking here, something we really should be keeping a closer eye on.

I’m talking Major League Cricket. And specifically the San Francisco Unicorns, who may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now, but are also carrying a potentially significant contagion. I first heard about it in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine, where he talked up the Unicorns’ use of artificial intelligence, not just to decide which players to sign, but in making mid-match decisions on the field. Hmm. Is this … OK? Is anyone actually paying attention here?

The Unicorns are this kind of entity, brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is “treating a cricket team like a startup”. At this point we’re back in Nvidia territory. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are, like Huang, Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area-digital-rainmaker types. At the Unicorns they’re applying the same innovative, unregulated tech to sport.

The key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data, player guff, plus the combined predictive power of every T20 game ever played, spitting out tactical nudges at hyper-speed, that can be carried out mid-match by actual people via a process described, depressingly, as “Human-in-the-Loop Execution”.

Star human bat-skill unit Finn Allen talked enthusiastically about the effect of all this in the season just past, explaining in detail how real-time decisions were powered through a centrifugal loop of data-fed robo synergy or some such, and actually it’s all just fine. “It’s not all AI or no AI. It’s the perfect amount of contribution,” Allen reassured local reporters after an eight-wicket win against Washington Freedom, speaking from inside his exciting new super-sentient iron maiden-style compliance pod.

And there are some obvious problems here. First, it’s incredibly boring. If I want to watch a robot play cricket I can go to the Oval when Dom Sibley’s batting. Mainly, however, it feels like cheating.

If fiddling with the ball or wearing tape on your fingers is against the spirit of cricket, so is using a machine to make captaincy decisions. Captaincy is a skill. Sport is a live test of human capacity. This is, at best, pushing the boundaries. At worst it’s a kind of brain-doping. It should obviously be regulated, understood, debated, and capped at source until everyone involved knows what we’re dealing with.

Because really this smells like the death of sport, and in more ways than one. It’s cricket as tech entrepreneurialism. The entire Unicorns backstory reads like a pitch for an app, with its roster of celebrity endorsements (Pat Cummins! Wow! How’s that working out?) and its endless giddy chat about scaling up the product. “This is at the level of human civilisation. I don’t think you can keep these kinds of ideas contained,” one of the founders says in its in-house blah. “It’s cricket for now, but why not the NFL, football, soccer” or indeed “the broader sports space”.

Well, I have an answer to that. Which is: no thanks lads. Because this is a genuinely horrible prospect, a hungry and acquisitive entity that’s going to creep in at the edges, make a great deal of money for a small amount of people, and in the process destroy the entire point of this precious, brittle, defiantly human thing.

There is a theory big tech companies have begun to buy into sport – see Bezos at Liverpool – as a hedge against AI. New technology is going to destroy so many existing industries. Whereas sport, the human spectacle, is seen as safe from this, like buying gold when currencies go haywire.

Well, maybe not. The capacity of AI to process data is potentially devastating to sport. Formula One is already a machine-led activity, now eagerly embracing the possibilities of robo-integration, raising the ultimate boss-level dream of self-driving race cars for a self-spectating crowd, streamed live to an auto-depressed TV audience.

AI is already present in elite football scouting systems, with various degrees of success. But zoom out and so much of football is essentially guesswork, sniff-test, hunch-based, all of the stuff artificial intelligence exists to replace. These are also the elements that give it value. These aren’t actually oversights or glitches, they’re food for the brain, nourishment for the soul, drivers of the stories and narratives human crave, the things that make this still feel like art, beauty, pleasure, collectivism.

Artificial intelligence would undoubtedly be better at managing Manchester United than the lost souls currently passing through those gates. But would you actually want to watch it? Would it have value, or cultural weight, or the capacity to surprise and delight and ping the levers in your brain? These are rhetorical questions. The answer is very obviously: no. This is instead a process that will destroy sport, reduce its vital human heart to another commodified digital product.

This might sound like Luddite talk. But, well, the Luddites actually had some pretty good points about the industrial loom. Are humans enchanted by mass production? Are we happier now? Is our lace of higher quality? Or is there just more of it and it’s all the same? Does the Unicorns’ future-verse seem warmer and more compelling? Will we ever have the will and the collective backbone, to resist, to regulate this stuff, to police its limits?

This isn’t what the digital age was supposed to look like. The 20th century gave us visions of a flowering of culture, the death of human drudgery, like one of those Star Trek planets where serene future-people wear robes and walk around Palladian gardens while a robot prepares afternoon tea.

As opposed to the current version, in which four people become incredibly wealthy while the rest of us live in an asbestos box, face clamped into a smartphone, trying to remember what that thing we once really valued andcared about was for. Resist the machines. Release Finn Allen from the Phantom Zone. Sport is always out there riding just ahead of the tide-line. First, they came for our bowling changes.

Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:00:11 GMT

Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

A chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Her trial heard she wore short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

After her conviction she was granted bail and was due to be sentenced at Harrow crown court on Friday.

But Bowen, from Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to court in the morning, and the judge, Karim Ezzat, issued a warrant for her arrest, “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall had earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from Scotchbrook was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, said: “Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn’t answer.”

He had earlier said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

In an update on Friday afternoon, the Met said: “On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing.

“A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.

“At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.

Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful Euro throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:53:21 GMT

The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company.

“Dear, dear Andy,” said António. “Dearest Andy, my adored Andy,” added Ursula. Neither could quite get enough of the prime minister. Andy fluttered his eyelashes bashfully. The feeling was mutual. It was hard not to feel a little bit sorry for Keir Starmer at this point. The deal that was being agreed was basically the one he had spent much of his last year in office negotiating. Now he had been totally airbrushed out of history.

It wasn’t all about Andy’s devastating good looks, mind. Though the physical chemistry was unmistakable, there had always been something a bit reserved about Keir. Withholding even. Starmer always had one eye on Reform and was wary about starting a new relationship with the EU. He had too much of the uptight Brit in him.

Andy was far more passionate. Spontaneous. No qualms about stating the obvious that Brexit had been a disaster for the UK and he was keen to experiment with closer ties. Fair to say, the EU have always preferred to negotiate with someone who isn’t afraid to rush in. This wasn’t to be just a one-night stand. This could be the start of something lasting. Once everyone had done with their trust issues.

Costa went first. We were as one. Andy was always welcome in the EU. Mi casa, su casa. We want the closest possible relationship. We were hurt when you ditched us in 2016 and we are ready to love again – if a little circumspect. Even in a throuple, there are rules that must be observed. Von der Leyen was even more open. This could be the start of something big. Not just dinner – waffle had been on the menu. It was the most perfect night: youth mobility, food standards and trading emissions today. AI and defence tomorrow.

Then it was over to Andy. He made no apologies for his rapture. His was the love that dared to speak its name. This was a win-win for everyone. Good for Britain, good for Europe. Three-quarters of Brits wanted closer ties with Europe and he would try to make that happen. This was the love affair that would make the country £17bn better off.

The questions from the media almost felt like an intrusion on the burning passion of first love. Could they clear up one thing? Would the deal on youth mobility and red tape be dependent on agreeing tuition fees for EU students? It didn’t seem entirely clear …

“There is absolutely no confusion,” said Burnham. Laughter broke out in the media room. Andy looked hurt. No one likes people making fun of them when they are in the first bloom of love. Andy thought everything had been agreed; António and Ursula thought there were some finishing touches to be made. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. We seemed to have heard this one before.

Finally, the question we all wanted an answer to. Was this the limit that could be reached with an incremental approach? Or was now the time to think about formalising a new long-term relationship? With one voice they all expressed the desire that this was the start of something big. Something permanent. None of them were the same as they had been in 2016. Time to start again. With that they rushed to embrace one another. Were they wedding bells chiming in the distance?

But there are always some who can’t stand the sight of other people’s happiness. Former lovers. Those who aren’t even allowed inside the EU’s headquarters in Brussels because they are the only former MEP to be refused a legacy pass. Step forward, Nigel Farage. Just hours after the throuple had left the media centre to peel grapes for one another, Nige was standing in front of a wobbly camera to trash the new romance.

“I had never seen Burnham look so tense and shifty,” he said. Which was weird. Because the rest of the world had seen unadulterated happiness on his face. A man who had waited 10 years for this moment. But if Nige is miserable, the rest of us have to be too. The same with the Tories. They couldn’t quite say why they hated the new relationship but they just knew they did. The only pleasure to be had was in creating division and discontent. Divorce their only language of love.

So Nige reinvented reality to suit himself. Andy had directly reneged on the Labour manifesto. Completely untrue. This wasn’t a reset but an overturn of the relationship. Three-quarters of the country might want what’s on offer, but three-quarters of the country were being fooled. With the youth mobility scheme we were back to open borders. Almost as if Nige was deliberately making things up. Visas will still be required.

What really stuck in Nige’s throat, though, was Burnham calling this a moment of hope. Nige only trades in grievance and despair. No Brit should ever consider a relationship with a foreigner because no foreigners can be trusted. Best to stay single and unhappy. As so often, it sounded as though the person he was really talking about was himself. Forever the bridesmaid, never the bride.

Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:22:50 GMT

PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”

For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.

More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.

While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.

Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:13:24 GMT

It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

Mr Burnham is on to something: polls consistently show that many voters think that Brexit has not worked out well and rejoining the bloc has gained popularity. The rise of the European radical right also probably changes the EU’s calculation about Britain. Building closer ties with a broadly pro-European British government could mean the terms of future agreements allow for Britain’s preferential access to the bloc. However, Brussels won’t offer something for nothing. As the Swiss ambassador to the UK told a Lords committee earlier this year: “If you want to have access to the common market, you will need to pay some cohesion money.”

Horse-trading is a feature of geopolitical life for Brexit Britain. The EU is using public borrowing and procurement rules to encourage defence production within Europe, create economies of scale and strengthen European supply chains. Britain balked at the financial contrib ution Brussels wanted in order to join up. With British defence manufacturers in danger of losing access to an expanding European market, both sides have made noises about getting around the table – but so far a deal remains elusive.

Brussels’ “Made in Europe” industrial strategy poses another challenge. Britain imports cheap Chinese electric vehicles while the EU seeks to protect its producers. British carmakers, however, depend on European demand. Under proposals advanced before this meeting they risked being shut out of the market. The summit recognised this danger, promising closer cooperation on electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require Britain to align its policies with Brussels – without having a vote over them.

This week Labour’s Stella Creasy, and Bernd Lange, a senior German MEP, proposed a Swiss-style deal to restore Britain’s economic and diplomatic influence without rejoining the EU. But greater market access without membership means accepting rules that Britain cannot influence. Mr Burnham’s reset pursued selective agreements – allowing Brussels to press for concessions. Switzerland offers a warning: frustrated by more than 120 bilateral deals, the EU insisted on a new framework. Down the line, Britain could face the same dilemma. Mr Burnham must calculate how long the country can negotiate the benefits of membership without confronting the costs of staying outside.

The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:12:47 GMT

A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today

The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026, but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it, even given their extravagant headgear.

A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in time.

“While standing in front of a painting by Jan van Eyck we … believe he succeeded in rendering the inexhaustible wealth of detail that belongs to the visible world,” the art historian Ernst Gombrich wrote in Art and Illusion (1960). An exact replica is unachievable to a painter “however patiently he worked with a magnifying glass” – artistic virtuosos are only human too. From 15th-century Netherlandish paintings to 19th-century Victorian novels to the hyper-realism of Grand Theft Auto VI, mimetic art, at its best, immerses us in artificial worlds so absolutely we forget the hands that created them.

“Jan van Eyck was here, 1434” the artist playfully reminds the viewer in an inscription on The Arnolfini Portrait, a treasure of the National Gallery’s permanent collection. Despite centuries of speculation it remains a mystery. Is the woman pregnant? Who are the figures glimpsed in the mirror? Might it be a self-portrait of Van Eyck and his wife, as a catalogue essay suggests? Or is that the artist under swathes of vermilion cloth in another portrait? What is truth and what is fiction, these pictures ask.

It is no wonder that single portraits have inspired whole novels. Maggie O’Farrell’s The Marriage Portrait (2022), partly based on a painting of a 16th-century Italian duchess, explores this slippery relationship between art and artifice. Vermeer’s masterpiece Girl with a Pearl Earring sparked Tracy Chevalier’s bestseller and an acclaimed film. We long for such luminous figures to step out of their canvases and tell their stories.

With their mottled skin and sideways glances, Van Eyck’s faces are as revealing as Lucian Freud’s unflinching portraits or Jenny Saville’s colossal nudes. If, as Oscar Wilde observed, “Every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist and not of the sitter,” it is also a portrait of the viewer. These strangers confront us with our own humanity and mortality: “Look, we were once flesh and blood like you!”

The Cambridge dictionary editors had something more 21st century in mind when they defined “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”. To come face to face with Van Eyck’s portraits, often barely the size of a laptop, is a timely reminder of human creativity. This is what “human” means, warts and all.

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:11:25 GMT

Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.

The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe.

There has been speculation over Farage’s future in light of police and parliamentary investigations of Reform’s financial affairs. The Commons standards watchdog is due to report soon on whether he should have declared a £5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. If he gets a substantial suspension from parliament, he could face a second byelection, contested by other main parties, in his Clacton constituency.

However, Farage sounded a note of defiance in an interview with the Sun, saying: “These are very thoughtful moments, but, you know what, if I’m not here doing this job right now, who else could? Who else would? I don’t see that person. So I’m gonna do it.”

A number of other Reform UK politicians are potential contenders to succeed him, including the party’s economics spokesperson and former Conservative, Robert Jenrick, the home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, and the former leader Richard Tice. Another possibility is the return of Rupert Lowe, who left Reform in acrimonious circumstances and founded his own party, Restore Britain, but who is popular on the online hard right.

The party is going through a difficult period after slipping from first place in the polls to second or third behind behind Labour and sometimes the Conservatives.

Asked by the Sun if he had “blown” his chances of reaching No 10, Farage said: “No, far from it.”

He admitted there had been “self-inflicted wounds” in the past year but said he still had a chance of becoming prime minister.

He told the newspaper that he would fight the next election as Reform leader if he was “still here and fit and healthy”.

He also batted away questions about the £5m, which he has insisted was to pay for his personal security despite the fact the party has been providing this.

“What’s it got to do with you? Drugs, sports cars, desert islands. It’s a gift,” he said, adding that although the party had had “ebbs and flows” and had made mistakes after growing “too far and too fast”, he was confident it was “more than through the worst of it”.

On the prospect of another battle over Europe as Andy Burnham weighs the case for rejoining the EU, the Reform leader said: “If you ask me, have I got the energy and the enthusiasm to do this again? I would say to you, hold my jacket. I’m ready for it.”

‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:04:15 GMT

Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’

Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting.

While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida. GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments.

From the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia to the painstaking world-building of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictional take on Florida, players have shared their wide-ranging experiences with the Guardian, revealing what has surprised and challenged them about this long-awaited release – and what this all means for the series’ evolution.

Pete Langhelt, 39, from Colchester, pre-ordered GTA VI “as soon as I could”, and has been looking forward to its release for a long time. “Out of my group of friends I’m probably the only one really nerding out about it,” he says.

While Pete hasn’t been able to take time from work in the civil service, he’s still clocked “about 10 hours” of gameplay already. “The core of the missions themselves are pretty similar,” he says. “You turn up somewhere, shoot a load of people and escape. But the development of the characters has changed an awful lot. I have enjoyed the dynamic between Jason and Lucia. I never thought you could make comfortable domesticity into an enjoyable side activity in a video game.”

Pete has played all the installments of GTA franchise from the first, when he was “probably too young to be playing”. “I think Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favourite Rockstar game going into this, and it seems to have developed the things that I really liked about Red Dead.”

The game encourages exploration, he says. “The day and night cycle seems a lot less intense than GTA V, meaning you don’t feel rushed to get things done. I can let Jason take a slow start to the day before taking a slow drive or boat ride to whatever criminal activity needs completing.”

His partner is less keen. “She’ll have to put up with me being on the Xbox for the next few weeks,” he says.

A 59-year-old MBA retiree from Venice, Florida, was also struck by just how much of the experience revolves around everyday life. He described it as the “most beautiful, real, open-world game that’s ever existed”.

“I was surprised that, with about 10-plus hours of play, most of my time has been spent performing mundane tasks like home repair, grocery shopping, personal grooming and trying to open a bank account. The realism is incredible, but perhaps too real,” he said.

“It’s as fully realized as a game world could be. I never expected to see anything more fully developed,” he added.

Rob Smeraldo, 28, from Dundee, took the day off work yesterday to play the game on his PlayStation 5. “I made sure I had loads of snacks and Domino’s,” he says. And already, Rob believes that “GTA VI must be the greatest game ever made”.

“I think the realism and just the detail put into it is absolutely astounding. The shadows, the way the hair moves when people move around … They took their time, but it’s definitely been worth it,” he says.

Rob is a longtime GTA fan and wore a GTA VI T-shirt and drank from a GTA mug to mark the occasion. “I purchased the physical copy [of the game] as soon as it became purchasable – I just wanted the memorabilia, you know?”

Ella Delancey, 35, of Berkshire has been playing GTA since she was a child. “GTA III is a huge core memory for me. My brother and I were much too young to be playing it and I definitely wouldn’t let my daughter play it now, but at the time we were obsessed.”

So far, the social and brand director has been surprised by how much there is to do aside from pushing the story forward. “I’m not very far into it yet, but I’m already struck by the graphics and the sheer depth of what you can do. It’s very violent, obviously, but I play by the rules, which probably makes me a bit boring. I’ve been birdwatching and exploring, and there’s so much to do outside the main story.”

There is one thing she is struggling with, however, and that’s Lucia, one of the main protagonists, leaving her child in a cafe and going to prison, only to come out and start committing more crimes. “As a mother, that doesn’t sit comfortably with me. I know it’s a game and you have to suspend your morals to a degree, but that part has given me pause,” she says.

“I do think it’s a step forward that you can no longer hire sex workers as in previous games. GTA still has a complicated relationship with misogyny – and it’s far from perfect, but that change feels significant.”

While Ella hasn’t taken any time off work to play, she has set aside time on Friday to play or watch her partner play. “It’s so immersive that it doesn’t feel like a chore, and I can see it replacing our usual after-work TV downtime for a little while,” she says.

Clint, 36, who works in the music industry in Chicago, describes the game as “truly one of one”, pointing to its unexpectedly domestic moments and the relationship between Jason and Lucia as some of its biggest draws.

“The story is just downright cute. I just had my character build an Ikea table with his girlfriend, and loved it. I typically skip some cutscenes, but now I’m rewatching them when I miss something,” he says.

Clint says Jason and Lucia’s relationship is particularly significant, describing it as an example of healthy masculinity that could resonate with younger players.

“The main character’s relationship is healthy (at least so far, at six hours in – and ‘healthy’ for a GTA game), which I see as such a positive. Positive both because I can relate to caring for one’s partner and because I love that real, healthy masculinity is being portrayed. I love that you are incentivized to complete menial tasks to make Lucia happy in between the wild and chaotic portions of the storyline. I’d like to hope that this might show young and/or disaffected men that misogyny is super lame and unmanly, at least in some small way,” he says.

Beyond the relationship dynamics, Clint praises the game’s approach to world building, which he says “feels so deep and textured”.

“Also refreshing are the built-in guardrails that make the game feel so lifelike … The player cannot just go steal a car or engage in indiscriminate violence without consequence. Every fight comes with police scrutiny, even speeding got me chased until I slowed down. It moderates what was a free-for-all melee atmosphere in the previous titles. This both enhances a sense of realism and immersion and makes me wonder if that doesn’t have some, albeit minor, benefit towards the ‘video games breed violence’ crowd,” he says.

The Guardian’s own team is also getting in on the action. The US’s deputy sport editor, Bryan Graham, says “it’s been a strange 24 hours” since the game dropped.

“Maybe we’ve been starved of genuine monocultural events for so long that we’ve forgotten how to handle them. The first sign the discourse might be getting a little carried away came when the New York Times invoked Jean Baudrillard, Jorge Luis Borges and bell hooks in their suite of GTA 6 think pieces (a dream blunt rotation I’d be sure to remember later),” he said. “Meanwhile, the day’s sanest take came from Glenn Beck, of all people, who went viral for pushing back on the strange spectacle of gen Xers scolding younger generations for getting excited about a video game.”

Graham continued: “Then came midnight. Really, it should be called Florida: The Game. With apologies to Sean Baker, I’m not sure there’s ever been a piece of media that is more of a love letter to America’s weirdest state, or more affectionate in its ridicule.

“Having played only a couple of hours before passing out, I’ve mostly been poking its version of the Florida Keys, where shimmering waterways give way to sun-bleached houses, shabby strip malls and alligators in the reeds. But that small sampling has been enough to see that Rockstar has created something both exquisitely observed and gloriously unhinged, a funhouse mirror held up to an America that increasingly resembles its own parody. Make no mistake: this is art!”

Tom Johnson, the Guardian’s vice-president of audience and strategy, says he was “probably lying to myself when I fired up my PS5 at six thirty this morning to ‘make sure the game installed properly’.

“I blinked and nearly an hour had passed and I had to remind myself I did not in fact have the GTA flu and needed to start getting ready for work,” he quips.

Of the game, Johnson said “the stunning graphics and well-paced storyline sucks you in immediately by allowing you to play as both characters, drive a car, captain a boat and even fly a small plane.

“Even the more mundane side quests are enthralling – I spent a few minutes doing a kettlebell workout and painting a room before wondering if I was just playing a sexier version of The Sims.

“I grew up in Miami, far away from the more glamorous parts of the beach, and I can’t wait for this workday to end so I can head west towards Kendall in search of my childhood home. At this point, given the game’s commitment to realism, it wouldn’t surprise me if an accurate replica of my parents’ car will be there waiting for me, parked in the driveway.”

Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:57:10 GMT

Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees

Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

But the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Burnham rejected suggestions there was any confusion over the deals coming into force: “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” he said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.

Hailing the “historic” agreement Burnham said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe,” as he argued that the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

The prime minister said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, while also reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal. The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those might be. It will be to inform the next parliament.”

Burnham also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who was in Brussels on Friday to hold a retaliatory press conference, to justify why they would reject a deal which, he said, would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity. “Why would anybody turn their back on that?”

The prime minister said the deals, which were initiated by Keir Starmer, would add 0.5% to British GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Farage said Burnham had been naive and the EU had “used this moment to strongarm the British prime minister over tuition fee cuts for hundreds of thousands of EU students”.

EU leaders sought to play down differences over tuition fees. “We are heading in the same direction and that is what matters,” the European Council president, António Costa, said of the broad relationship. He described the UK as “our closest neighbour, a reliable ally and a natural partner”.

Von der Leyen said it was up to the UK to decide where the journey was going, adding: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

In a sign of tension in the negotiations, the EU agreed a declaration that the three deals would not come into force without equal treatment on fees for EU students at British universities.

“The [EU] Council and [European] Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students,” stated the confidential statement seen by the Guardian. The EU would not adopt the three agreements before “the conclusions of the negotiations … providing for equal treatment on tuition fees”, it added.

Another potential flashpoint could be the UK’s status as a rule-taker. The food and drink and emissions trading deals require the UK to align with EU rules. British experts will be invited to relevant EU meetings, including dealing with potential animal health emergencies. But Britain will not have voting rights. Burnham rejected suggestions this was a fig leaf, saying it would be “quite a moment” to have British experts back in EU meeting rooms.

France was said to be instrumental in shaping Britain’s exclusion, although Paris argues its position was widely supported and reflects the reality that a non-member state cannot be a decision-maker.

The UK hailed a joint decision to create a “partnership for economic resilience”, as an answer to its concerns over the EU’s Made in Europe plans. The EU is still finalising legislation that will give EU companies preference when public money is spent on the key technologies, such as renewables and electric cars. But questions over whether the UK needs to align with EU trade defences remain open. Burnham said the two sides had reached an agreement “to work together where we have common threats”.

After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:52:43 GMT

From predatory male celebrities to ordinary men who connive to abuse women, there is no doubt where the problem lies – and the solution too

The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men.

That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by David Walliams, accusations Walliams denies. There was earnest discussion of the enabling power of celebrity, how stardust blinds people from seeing what’s in front of them. Some suggested the problem was narrower still, with abuse cast as a function of the way British comedy operates, lacking a recognisable HR structure or protection for junior workers from big names with clout. In parallel, a debate began about staggering the age of consent, addressing the particular dynamics of older men who target younger women, including those who would be regarded as children by any definition except the letter of the law.

All of those are valid questions, by the way. But if, underlying them, is the consoling hope that we are facing a limited problem, one confined to, say, high-status men or those whose victims are very young, then Thursday’s verdicts should dispel it. The grimmer truth is that this problem is wider and deeper: the guilty were ordinary men, carpenters and cabbies, ready to violate a middle-aged woman who was audibly and visibly unconscious.

Even this especially shocking crime – in which a man recruits other men online to rape his sedated wife – may not be as rare as we imagine. A similar case is now being tried in Manchester and, according to Wiltshire police: “This may be a significantly under-reported crime type.”

Of course, there are specific elements and contexts that make rape and sexual abuse more possible. Just as the entertainment industry provided a hospitable environment for Brand, so Philip Young could advertise for fellow rapists thanks to online forums such as Craigslist and Reddit. The internet made it easier for him to secure sedative drugs. But these things facilitate rather than drive the impulse. They are not the heart of the matter. Which is, to state it plainly, male hatred of women.

Of course, such hatred is not universal; not every man is infected by it. But it is embedded in our world and sits deep in our culture. (After Pelicot and Young, you look again at Sleeping Beauty: what exactly did we think was going on in a story that, in its 17th-century telling, had the king discover the unmoving, unconscious body of a woman, rape and impregnate that woman, and then flee?)

In Afghanistan, the Taliban have imposed gender apartheid, prohibiting girls and women from learning, singing, taking a bus without a man or walking to the park. According to Human Rights Watch, one directive ordered the removal of windows, lest Afghan women, “imprisoned in their homes, might see the outside world”. Closer to hand, you look at the manosphere, whose leading lights delight in the degradation and humiliation of women, treating their girlfriends as, at best, unpaid domestic servants or, at worst, property and chattel. You contemplate the rates of femicide, which include three women killed every fortnight in England and Wales by a current or former partner. You look at the rape statistics, including the estimate from the Centre for Women’s Justice (CWJ) that only 15% of all rapes get reported and that, of those that do, only a tiny percentage ultimately ends in a conviction.

Women have been saying all this, loudly and clearly, for years. When cases such as Brand or Walliams or Philip Young erupt, it tends to be women who lead the debate and make the arguments, in print and on the airwaves. On one level, that’s obvious – in the same way that, say, Jewish voices are given the floor when there is a murderous attack on Jews. But it’s also incomplete. Because it misses out, and risks letting off the hook, those who have most work to do. In this case, men.

The logic of that was encapsulated well by a small sign – no more than an A4 piece of paper – held up by a woman protesting in New York earlier this year over the case of the Cornell seven: the fraternity brothers at Cornell University accused of gang-raping a female student they’d incapacitated through ketamine, and doing so over the course of seven hours. The protester’s sign carried three words that had been crossed out: Protect Your Daughters. In their place were three different words: Educate Your Sons.

This shifts responsibility to where it should lie. It honours the principle articulated so concisely by Gisèle Pelicot herself who, like Joanne Young, waived her right to anonymity, believing there was no need to hide herself since she had nothing to be ashamed of. Or, as she put it, “Shame has to change sides.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

That makes moral sense, but it might make practical sense too. Take the kind of young man susceptible to the example of Andrew Tate and his fellow denizens of the manosphere. If such a man hears a woman condemn misogyny, if they hear a woman speak of the necessity of consent, they will hear those as messages that stand in opposition to manliness. They will understand their own sexual desires as manly and restraints on those desires as their opposite, as unmanly or feminine. For a man such as this, it is perhaps only condemnation by other men, framed in terms of maleness, that will cut through.

A useful precedent could be what was, in a different era, called wife-beating. Not so long ago, the culture all but countenanced such behaviour. Think of the Beatles’ song, Run For Your Life, both its title and lyric: “Well, I’d rather see you dead, little girl / Than to be with another man”. But attitudes moved. “The norm did shift,” CWJ founder Harriet Wistrich told me on Friday. These days, if a man were hitting his partner in sight of another man, that second man would, she hopes, step in.

This, then, is how fathers might best heed that protester’s call to educate their sons. To tell them that the kind of behaviour that has been revealed in courtrooms and on front pages these last two weeks is wicked and inhuman, but also pathetic, inadequate and weak – and, yes, worthy of shame. That to prey on those who have less power, or no power at all, is the mark of someone who is not merely a failure as a person – but no man at all.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Death threats to Bowens revealed after De Boinville security incident

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:40:16 GMT

Abuse and threats are becoming a grimly familiar part of daily routine for riders, confirms jockeys’ association

When Nico de Boinville received a security escort back to his car after racing at Plumpton on Monday, following a telephone threat to harm the jockey received at Nicky Henderson’s stable, it was the first time that such a move had received widespread media attention.

It was not, however, the first time that it had been felt necessary to give a rider additional protection at a racecourse. James Bowen said on Friday, in a blog for the bookmaker Dragonsports, that he and his brother, Sean, the champion over jumps, “were both the subject of death threats” during a meeting at Ffos Las in October 2025, “to the extent that we had security accompanying us between the paddock and weighing room for the next three or four days.”

Threats and abuse have become a sadly familiar part of the daily routine for racing’s participants in recent years. “Unfortunately, it’s the way of the world at the moment,” Paul Struthers, chief executive of the Professional Jockeys Association, said on Friday. “The incidents with Nico and James are different, because they were both phone calls and not social-media driven, so I don’t want to conflate the two things. But abuse is part and parcel of day-to-day life for jockeys, for trainers and for pretty much every other professional athlete.”

Struthers began his racing career working in betting shops in the 1990s, and is therefore no stranger to the language and anger that punters can vent on jockeys and trainers. “What you’re seeing on social media is an amplified, more aggressive version of what you used to hear in a betting shop,” he says. “You’d hear abuse all the time, with people screaming at the TV, but no one heard it other than the people in the betting shop.

“What you’re seeing on social media is far worse. It’s one thing to be a professional sportsperson or a jockey and deal with criticism of your performance. That just comes with the territory. But the majority of it isn’t about that. It’s really gratuitous, abhorrent comments aimed at them and their families.”

Both the PJA and the National Trainers’ Federation (NTF) work with Sean Memory, a former police superintendent and specialist in online abuse, to support individuals that have suffered abuse and also to attempt to track down persistent abusers.

“A lot of the work is behind the scenes,” Struthers says, “supporting trainers and jockeys, and trying to find the individuals carrying out the abuse and getting them to stop. But you can only take complaints to the police with the consent of the individual who has been abused, and while it’s not that the police don’t take it seriously, they’re under-resourced and too busy. It isn’t a priority for them.”

The PJA has also recently developed Social Protect, an app for jockeys that aims to filter abuse from their social media feeds before they, or anyone else, can see it.

“It’s a brilliant piece of software,” Struthers says, “that integrates with an individual’s social media accounts and deletes abusive comments in real time. It takes five minutes to download and link to your account, and then it’s up and running. It doesn’t just hide the messages, it deletes them, and it works with Instagram, which is actually the social media channel of choice for jockeys now.

“The reality is that too many people have forgotten how to behave and it’s going to be part and parcel of athletes’ lives, unfortunately, so it’s about how best we can support and help them.

“Through Sean’s work, and through using apps like Social Protect, we can support jockeys who suffer from abuse and help prevent them being abused in the first place.”

Paul Nicholls has set his sights on becoming the first trainer to saddle 4,000 winners in Britain after finally overhauling Martin Pipe to become the country’s most successful jumps trainer when Knappers Hill provided his 3,931st British win at Warwick on Thursday.

Nicholls started out as a trainer at the late Paul Barber’s stable at Ditcheat in Somerset in 1991 and finished runner-up behind Pipe in seven successive championship races before finally taking his first title in the 2005-06 season.

He dominated the jumping game for the next decade, when his biggest stars included Kauto Star, Denman, Master Minded, Big Buck’s and the 2012 Grand National winner, Neptune Collonges, and took the title for the 14th time in the 2022-23 season.

“When I started I just wanted to train winners and run a successful business,” Nicholls said, “and then in 1999 I had three winners at Cheltenham [Flagship Uberalles, Call Equiname and See More Business in the Gold Cup] and everything took off from there.

“I’m very proud of all we have achieved as ‘Team Ditcheat’, I’m just the frontman for a great team.”

“The fire still burns and it won’t stop. The day it does stop then I will give up, but I can’t see that happening. 4,000 winners is not too far away and after that it will be 5,000, simple as that!”

It can be a long way home up the Haydock straight when the ground is heavy, but it remains good, good-to-soft in places ahead of the Grade One Betfair Chase on Saturday and that could see the front-running Affordale Fury (3.00) emerge as only the second Irish-trained winner of the race in its 21-year history.

Like Grey Dawning, the favourite to repeat his success last year, Affordale Fury is making his seasonal debut, but he has run well fresh in the past and been given plenty of time to get over the injury in the Irish Gold Cup in February that curtailed his 2025-26 campaign.

That was the only blip in an otherwise progressive season and there is just 1lb between Noel Meade’s eight-year-old and Grey Dawning on Timeform’s ratings.

The betting, though, rates Dan Skelton’s runner nearly twice as likely to land the spoils, at around 11-10. That simply feels too short given that Affordale Fury could well have the run of the race, and he makes far greater appeal at around 3-1.

Ascot 12.55 With Lulamba, one of last year’s top novices, missing due to the ground, Steel Ally will be hard to beat. Sam Thomas’s runner looks more than ready for this step up in trip and the trainer has few peers when it comes to getting them ready first time up.

Haydock 1.15 Cheekpieces coaxed a little more application from North Shore at Cheltenham last month and his seven-length win there is the strongest form on offer, albeit in a field full of potential.

Joanne Young’s faith in justice system is sign of real change, but courts are still catching up

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:39:06 GMT

Young’s abusers were convicted through suspect-centric prosecution, though much more needs to be done for victims

Hope can be found in the darkest of places. Joanne Young stood outside Winchester crown court on Thursday and said she was relieved – not just for herself and her family – but for women in the future.

Young, who was subjected to years of drugging and rape by her husband, who invited other men to assault her, waived her anonymity to speak out.

She said she hoped her case meant those who had experienced similar abuse could have more faith in the criminal justice system, and that all women and girls who had been abused by men would hear the message that they could be believed and understood.

Given the powerful dignity of Young’s address, it was easy to miss the significance of another remarkable statement, made on the same day by a prosecutor in the case.

“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse,” said James Foster, a specialist prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service’s Wessex complex casework unit.

Suspect-centric. The fact that a criminal investigation and prosecution is focused on the suspect of the crime should, of course, be unremarkable. But, until quite recently, in cases of rape, sexual assault and domestic abuse, that was rarely the case.

There are some signs, some small green shoots of optimism, that suggest the lumbering criminal justice system is moving in the right direction. Those words from a regional prosecutor indicate a shift that was unimaginable a decade ago, and for people who have spent their lives trying to reform the criminal justice system, it is a sign that change is possible.

In 2018 the Guardian ran a series of stories about a sharp drop in the number of cases that CPS prosecutors were willing to take to trial, prompting concerns about the de facto decriminalisation of rape. Prosecutions fell 60% from 5,190 in 2016-17 to 2,102 in 2019-20, even as the number of incidents reported to police increased.

At a time when the issue was getting little coverage, the Guardian revealed how the CPS held training events for prosecutors, advising they “take the weak cases out of the system” to boost the conviction rate.

In March 2019, Theresa May’s government launched a review into rape investigations. When it reported in 2021, the conclusion was stark: victims were not only being let down, but made to feel as if they were the ones under investigation.

The Conservative administration – which had inflicted budget cuts resulting in a 30% reduction in CPS staff and the loss of about 20,000 police officers – issued an unusually frank mea culpa. The policing and crime minister at the time, Kit Malthouse, said “it simply has not been good enough”. The then justice secretary, Robert Buckland, said he was “deeply sorry”.

The response to the review was radical. The Home Office funded Operation Soteria Bluestone, under the leadership of academics and criminology experts Betsy Stanko and Katrin Hohl, to review a number of forces’ cases and unflinchingly reveal their failures.

Police officers and prosecutors were told to change in six key areas by focusing investigations on suspects, disrupting repeat offenders and engaging with victims, and by improving learning and development, officer wellbeing and the use of data and digital forensics.

after newsletter promotion

They were also told to stop indiscriminately trawling victims’ personal data, and instead request only information that was relevant and proportionate.

It is clear that in many forces, things have changed – pushed and encouraged by Sarah Crew, the clear-eyed police lead for rape in England and Wales, a role newly created in 2021. Police referrals and CPS charges for rape were back up to 2016 levels by 2024, with the change hailed by independent sexual violence advisers such as Rape Crisis England & Wales.

Nevertheless, charities have continued to warn against complacency: despite the recovery, about 97% of reported rapes never make it to court.

Fears have also been raised that process of change could stall. The courts backlog means rape survivors and complainants are waiting an average of 423 days for trial, with many waiting far longer.

Experts argue that the use of rape myths is still prevalent in courts, noting that during the trial of Russell Brand – in which the celebrity was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others – his barrister, Ian Winter, said Brand’s accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Hohl, now the government’s independent adviser on rape, worries that as the police and the CPS move in the right direction, the courts system is being left behind. Last month, she published a report suggesting sexual assault cases prepared under the improved standards come up against a “cliff edge” once they get to trial.

Despite the horror of her experience, Young has shown us a sliver of light in a criminal justice system that has failed too many victims for too long. But the work to fully transform it is far from complete.

‘It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic!’ How Australian TV conquered the world

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:34 GMT

From Colin from Accounts to a certain blue heeler dog, Australian TV has swept the globe – so much so that many kids have picked up the accent. Homegrown stars and creators explain how down under went overground

About four years ago, parents around the world began observing a strange phenomena in their children: Australian accents. Bluey – the charming cartoon about a dog and her family that is currently one of the most watched shows in the world – had children saying words such as “dunny” and “brekky” without thinking twice.

“When I was a kid, I would do an American accent when I played with my toys,” says Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, which makes Bluey. “So this is like the colony taking back over!”

In the last five years, Australia has staged a global cultural invasion via television. Count just the recent successes: Colin from Accounts, My Brilliant Career, Fisk, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, Dalliance, The Newsreader, Reckless, Goolagong, Territory, The Twelve, Apple Cider Vinegar, High Country, Love on the Spectrum, Last Seen, Mix Tape, Do Not Watch This Show, The Airport Chaplain, The Artful Dodger, Dog Park, Gnomes, Austin, Deadloch – and of course, a certain blue heeler. In the coming months, Brits will also get the outback thriller Treasure & Dirt (BBC), the true-crime documentary 2.6 Seconds (Netflix), the Anna Torv-led mystery Dustfall (BBC), as well as more Austin and Scrublands (BBC).

“It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic,” as Amanda Duthie, Netflix’s head of content for Australia and New Zealand (My Brilliant Career, Apple Cider Vinegar), puts it.

“There’s people looking over the fence at us, saying: ‘What’s in the water in Australia at the moment?’” says Jennifer Collins, director of screen at the ABC, Australia’s national broadcaster (Love on the Spectrum, Bluey, Fisk, Austin, Dog Park). “Back in the day, kids’ shows and one or two dramas would do really well for us – but now all of our shows are cutting through.”

“I’ve been in the industry quite a while – some may say too long – but I remember the olden days when it was hard to get a pitch meeting with the UK commissioners and there weren’t that many Australian shows picked up there,” says Ian Collie, founder of production company Easy Tiger (Colin from Accounts, The Twelve, Scrublands, Territory). “But definitely in the last three or five years, there has been an upward trend, which is great.”

The question is: why? Is Australian TV getting better? Is there more of it? Or are international broadcasters and streaming services finally catching up to a good thing?

After speaking to more than a dozen producers, stars, directors and executives across Australia’s TV industry, the consensus is that something started changing 10 years ago, but really sped up around 2020. Covid lockdowns meant that the many talented Australians who had left for entertainment jobs in Hollywood and London fled home as work dried up. Everyone who used to moan about having to live in Los Angeles realised they didn’t need to any more.

“Actors now audition from a distance. Writing teams are scattered across the globe. Shows that are shot in England can be edited in Australia, or vice versa,” says Andy Ryan, head of drama at Australian streamer Stan (Scrublands, The Killings at Parrish Station, The F Ward). “That’s an unintended benefit of Covid for Australians – you don’t have to travel halfway around the world to have a meeting any more.”

Suddenly, Australia had a brain gain: all the expertise built overseas began being shared on masse. Meanwhile, the international streamers – Disney+, Netflix, Prime Video – had set up shop and were funding local productions; Australia’s domestic streamers and broadcasters geared up to compete. Then the Hollywood strikes of 2023 happened, which coincided with the start of a huge, ongoing decline in TV production in the US and the UK. The streaming giants and big broadcasters started hunting furiously for readymade hits abroad that they didn’t need to fund.

“There’s been a massive contraction globally in the number of shows being made, so all buyers are looking for shows that they think stand out,” says Carly Heaton at Fremantle Australia (Heartbreak High, Wellmania). “Everywhere, we’re seeing different content than what we might have normally seen – the Brits are seeing more Aussie content, and vice versa.”

Shrinking budgets have also made Australia a lot more attractive to foreign streamers and broadcasters looking for co-productions, rather than funding a show themselves: Colin from Accounts, for instance, was produced by Easy Tiger and CBS – but that means it was shown on CBS in the US (as well as the BBC in the UK).

“Australia is very cost-competitive internationally,” says Ryan at Stan, which regularly partners with UK broadcasters. “We make TV for a great price.”

Australia has also benefited from one international success: Squid Game. When the South Korean show became a massive global hit, all the old wisdom around commissioning went out of the window.

“People thought that Brits wanted to see Brits, Aussies wanted to see Aussie,” says Heaton at Fremantle Australia .“But Squid Game was a massive hit globally, and with subtitles – who would have thought that would happen? No buyers would have braved that before.”

“Everyone is watching so much more international TV,” says Duthie at Netflix (the brave buyer of Squid Game). “We are open to subtitles now! Nobody can quite believe it – ‘Honey, come and watch this show, it’s called Squid Game!’ The audience has muscled up, along with the sector.”

As Australian TV spreads, there seems to be a growing realisation that we don’t just make soaps. We have our own period dramas (My Brilliant Career) and office comedies (Fisk) and war stories (The Narrow Road to the Deep North) and romcoms (Colin from Accounts), plus a wealth of entirely unique First Nations stories. Australia is exotic enough to be interesting, but not so foreign that it’s challenging. “We feel quite distinctive, a bit fresh – just like Scandi noir did 10 or so years ago,” says Collie. We’re having our time in the sun.”

“There is an inherent curiosity about who we are as a nation, as a culture. We are not here making a watered-down version of a British or American show,” adds Nakul Legha, head of scripted at Australia’s multicultural public broadcaster SBS (The Airport Chaplain).

Frankly, though, some of Australia’s recent international successes simply can’t be explained. “None of us knew that Fisk would take off in the way it did,” laughs Collins at ABC, which sold the show to Netflix internationally.

Liz Doran was the showrunner on Netflix’s My Brilliant Career, which reached the Top 10 in 72 countries this year. The drama features a storyline where one character is implied to be part of the Stolen Generations – Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families by the state – a historical point that is well known in Australia but not always abroad. “But we were never asked to add more dialogue to explain that, because we’re just treating the viewers like adults – if they’re curious, they’ll chase it,” Doran says. “Which is exactly what we have always done for shows from America.”

Australia is done explaining itself to the world: you figure out what a smoko or a bogan is if you care, hooroo. But the world seems to like that. When I recently interviewed Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, the married creators and stars of Colin from Accounts, they recalled being asked by US executives to tweak an “arvo” in a script to “afternoon”. “And we were like … no,” Dyer told me. “It stayed in.”

“When Bluey took off, it felt like nobody cares any more – in a really great way,” says Pearson at Ludo. “People don’t need you to change things, they get it. That’s the stuff we loved about The Simpsons or John Hughes or the Beatles – they never pandered to you. People not only are happy to watch Australian stuff, they maybe even prefer it the more personal you go, the more foreign it feels.”

“What we’ve seen is when we’re hyperspecific in Australian content, that travels particularly well in the UK. Humour is an obvious shared sensibility,” says Alexandra Gilbert, head of content at Prime Video Australia and New Zealand (Deadloch, The Narrow Road). “Take something like Deadloch – a British audience might need a dictionary to translate half the words, but it travels incredibly well.”

“I’m quite sure most people don’t understand half the things the Heartbreak High kids are saying,” adds Heaton at Fremantle, which made the show for Netflix. “But you get the tone and, because of the specificity, it’s funny. And as long as you get the intent, you get the humour.”

“Specificity is hugely appealing,” adds Dena Curtis, head of Indigenous commissions and production at NITV, Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander channel, which made Reckless. Although the show was based on a Scottish series (Guilt), Reckless is told from an Aboriginal perspective – “[which] is appealing overseas because that isn’t something that has been easily available,” Curtis adds. “It just takes one show to break through and then people say, OK – what else have you got?’ And I think it’s becoming anticipated that something coming out of Australia will be good.”

“I’m really mindful of the narrative that says: ‘Well, Australia is only starting to get good at making TV now!’ No!” says Legha. “We’ve had stories like The Flying Doctors, Wentworth, Rake, Kath & Kim, McLeod’s Daughters. We have an amazing history of great storytelling, I don’t think that’s changed. It is just that international buyers are seeing there is a real point of difference in the stories we’re telling here.”

“Everyone’s like, what’s the difference? It’s money,” says Doran. “I think one of the reasons some of our dramas haven’t travelled well in the past is because we are working on lower budgets than other countries. Australian crews and creatives are incredibly fast-paced and have initiative and we’ll work our arses off – but you can only make a low budget go so far. The international streamers mean we can make a show that has a polish and style on par with international shows.”

“Higher budgets don’t mean greater success; if only it was that easy!” counters Jo Porter, of production company Curio Pictures (High Country, The Artful Dodger, The Narrow Road). “But I think we’ve had to compromise in the past because we haven’t been able to finance at the level a particular story needed. Now we are able to prove our shows will sell globally, distributors have more confidence taking risks.”

A familiar face tends to inspire the UK to buy in particular: think Anna Friel in The F Ward, Ciarán Hinds and Jacob Elordi in The Narrow Road, David Thewlis in The Artful Dodger or Juliet Stevenson in Dustfall. Feral, a new Netflix drama, is filming in Queensland with Downton Abbey’s Michelle Dockery and Baby Reindeer’s Jessica Gunning; next year Sheridan Smith will lead Two Birds, a Stan and ITV co-production made in Western Australia.

“Marquee cast members do help sell the show internationally,” says Ryan. “And we’re not asking for them to come out to Australia for six months, more like four weeks. So it’s much more achievable from a logistics point of view. Also, 15 years ago, if you brought Anna Friel into an Australian medical show, you’d probably make a story point about why an English-accented doctor was in your hospital. Now we don’t explain it at all.”

So it is a bit of everything: a bit more money, a bit of pain overseas, a bit more openness internationally, and a lot of talent finally getting their dues. The phrase most often repeated was: “A rising tide lifts all boats.” Duthie at Netflix calls the current situation “a self-saucing pudding of confidence and opportunity: the more you do, the more you learn, the more you can deliver”.

“The Aussies are coming, watch out!” Collie laughs. “More than 200 years ago, the Brits sent all their riffraff to Australia. Now we’re coming to get them!”
