Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:34 GMT

Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets

Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world. On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg).

People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi.

Yet there’s good reason to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate different varieties into our diets. Here’s what experts say about the health benefits of mushrooms.

“The selling points for mushrooms for many years were that they taste good, and they don’t have any bad stuff in them,” says Dr Robert Beelman, professor emeritus of food science and director of the Center for Plant and Mushroom Foods for Health at Penn State University. “There’s very little fat, no sugar, very few calories.”

Mushrooms’ savoury, umami flavor also makes them a particularly good option for anyone looking to eat less meat. “I often recommend replacing up to 50% of ground meat with chopped mushrooms for meatballs, tacos or meat sauce recipes,” says Marisa Moore, a registered nutritionist based in Atlanta.

Unlike meat, mushrooms are not a robust source of protein. But they provide a healthy mix of different types of fiber, including beta-glucans, a kind of soluble fiber also found in oats and barley, which “has been shown to help reduce cholesterol levels”, says Moore, and chitin, an insoluble fiber that supports good bacteria in the gut. Beta-glucans have a particularly interesting composition that the human body recognizes as “something a little foreign”, notes Zuniga, “which can help stimulate and activate the immune system”. In studies, beta-glucans have shown promising anti-inflammatory effects.

It’s becoming easier to buy a variety of mushrooms, especially at specialty grocers. While different varieties contain vitamins and minerals in slightly different concentrations, most mushrooms offer healthful compounds, including potassium, which helps in the regulation of blood pressure; selenium, which supports thyroid health; and B vitamins, which play an important range of roles in, for instance, cellular function and metabolism.

In addition to fortified milk and fatty fish, “mushrooms are one of the few sources of vitamin D that we can easily get in our diet,” adds Moore. “Vitamin D is essential for healthy bones, helps regulate the immune system and plays an important role in regulating our mood and sleep.”

Yet vitamin D deficiency is considered prevalent in the US, especially during winter, when our bodies naturally produce less of it through sun exposure. Some mushrooms have even been treated with UV light, which converts a compound called ergosterol into vitamin D.

The average person needs about 15 micrograms of vitamin D per day, and while you would need to eat an impractical quantity of mushrooms to reach that threshold, about one cup of these UV-treated mushrooms or wild mushrooms exposed to sunlight will get you most of the way there (and a cup of mushrooms cooks down significantly).

“Mushrooms are the only thing in the produce aisle that can actually increase their vitamin D content just by being exposed to sunlight,” says Moore. In fact, you can boost the vitamin D in mushrooms yourself by placing mushrooms gill-side up under direct midday sunlight for 15 minutes to an hour, after which the vitamin D benefits appear to plateau and subsequently decline, according to research.

after newsletter promotion

Some studies have correlated higher overall mushroom consumption with lower incidence of certain cancers, including breast cancer. But more research is needed to ascertain whether they have an effect on cancer risk and why.

It’s very difficult to isolate the effects of a specific food in this type of observational research, says Zuniga. “Someone that’s consuming mushrooms is likely also consuming other fruits and vegetables.”

One part of cancer prevention recommendations for all cancers is to eat a diet rich in plant foods, which lends the benefits of a range of nutrients and phytochemicals, she says. “Mushrooms are a food that you can consider as part of our general recommendation to consume more plant foods to lower your risk of cancer,” Zuniga says. Some researchers think that beta-glucans can increase immune system activity in ways that improve the body’s recognition of, and response to, cancer cells.

Mushrooms also contain some unique compounds “with a high antioxidant capacity”, meaning they combat the cellular damage underlying many health conditions, says Zuniga.

For instance, mushrooms are the most significant dietary source for an antioxidant called ergothioneine, which may have a role in “potentially controlling or preventing chronic diseases, especially neurodegenerative diseases”, says Beelman. Some researchers have observed a link between lower blood levels of ergothioneine and a higher risk of cognitive impairment, neurodegenerative disease, cardiovascular disease, frailty and all‑cause mortality. These researchers consider ergothioneine to be a “promising nutritional intervention” to support cognitive resilience, though long-term trials proving a direct causal relationship are lacking. Beelman suggests aiming for 10mg of ergothioneine a day – about one cup of oyster mushrooms. Lion’s mane, porcini and shiitake varieties are also good sources.

Mushroom supplements are widely available. But Zuniga cautions that in the US, “because of the poor regulation of dietary supplements”, you can’t be sure what they contain. Some mushroom supplements may be vetted, but Moore generally recommends “starting with whole foods whenever possible”.

“You’re bound to find a mushroom that you like,” adds Zuniga. “There’s such a variety to choose from.”

Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:54:57 GMT

Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018

French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot.

The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes.

Two sources following the case confirmed to Agence France-Presse on Friday that a police investigation was under way.

The investigative website Mediapart reported this week that an actor, given the pseudonym Alexandra, had made a complaint to police in 2025.

Alexandra, an eastern European actor and dancer who was 32 at the time and working in France, told Mediapart that she was attacked by Depardieu and Houellebecq as they pinned her down during one scene and while cameras filmed.

Mediapart reported that Alexandra described being “in a state of stupefaction and disconnect”. In her police complaint she had spoken of “deep humiliation” and “indescribable shame”.

The film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, had been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, AFP reported.

Nicloux told Mediapart that at the moment of filming he had not “noticed any constraint”, but he had “apologised” to Alexandra.

Alexandra’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Depardieu’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian contacted Houellebecq’s publishers, who did not respond.

This week Depardieu, 77, dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a different film set in 2021, and apologised to them.

At his trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021. His suspended sentence will now stand and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register.

after newsletter promotion

After Depardieu’s apology this week, the assistant director whom he sexually assaulted said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”

Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.

He has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.

In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

Houellebecq, 70, who is among France’s most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

We should be free to call ourselves Black English

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:48:37 GMT

Readers respond to an article about categories on the census form

It’s about time we fixed the Black English category in the census, whether popular or not (It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose, 14 November). Categories count. They make citizens, politically engineer belonging and allow people to be seen and to see themselves. The excuse that the Black English category is simply unpopular doesn’t wash. I remember in the 1990s when the Black British, or Black African categories were all the rage, they were never particularly comfortable to tick, but we all got over ourselves and stomached the flattening of our complex identities for what we believed was a good cause.

A Black English category would also help me out enormously, living as I do in France, where people don’t believe me when I say I’m English, but simply think I’m deluded and can’t speak French properly – which I can. Having left Scotland when I was three and grown up in London, I felt I couldn’t legitimately call myself Scottish – but English, I could. Years ago I stopped calling myself Britannique, because Black or otherwise, it just didn’t really translate well.

Les Anglais is what the French know well and love to hate. It’s also a source of pride for me to be able to say that I’m Black and English in a country that has refused to include racial or ethnic categories in its census, believing them to be anti-republican and divisive. But as the recent street protests and rioting in towns and cities have shown, official attempts to deny French citizens visibility in all their diversity merely creates a cauldron of discontentment among the “just French” that sadly, one day, boils over. Kathryn Nwajiaku-Dahou Paris, France

Debates about whether Black English can be a legitimate census category are certainly absurd, as Calum Jacobs argues. They are also riven with confusion and hypocrisy. There is no single academically agreed definition of ethnicity, so it is presumptuous, at best, to claim absolute certainties, let alone proprietary rights. Those who would deny Englishness to others who aren’t white are, in effect, insisting that “English” is a racial category despite claiming it is an ethnic one.

Whatever reservations some Black people may have about an English identity, they are not based on issues of entitlement. They are the product of complex historical struggles to resist being defined from without.

But whatever the motives or inclinations of those who would police them, ethnic identities are potentially available to all who inhabit and are shaped by the cultures that are often ethnicity’s most powerful determinants. Moreover, there are as many different types of English sensibility as there are accents to speak it, places to claim it and histories to shape it, so reducing ethnicity to some kind of genetic essentialism is as futile as trying to capture memory in a bottle. Paul McGilchrist Cromer, Norfolk

I am instinctively sympathetic to recent calls to represent categories such as Black English and Asian English on the census ethnicity form. As someone from London, but with a Palestinian father and an English mother, I can only select “Other” on these baffling forms. (For unexplained reasons, “Arab” already comes under a separate “Other” subheading – a fact media coverage on this question has conveniently ignored – making me some kind of Other to the Other.)

But I am also not sure any of this is what representation should look like. I feel I am British, English, and Palestinian, and all of these words mean very different things to me. I suspect they mean different things to you, too. I hope we can find ways of talking about ethnicity which do not reduce it to an item on a list. Michael Rizq Cambridge

Calum Jacobs’s article makes a good case for census forms to include a Black English category in England. But what about me? Born and bred in Scotland, I emigrated to England when I was 22 and am still here at 83. So how about a Scottish English category for me and my fellow missionaries? Jim Michie Chester

White supremacist convicted of planning bomb attack on asylum seekers in Hull

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:48:31 GMT

Mikka Anderson stockpiled weapons and tried to recruit accomplice for attack on Royal Hotel

A white supremacist has been found guilty of planning a firebomb terror attack on asylum seekers in Hull.

Mikka Anderson, 24, stockpiled weapons including napalm, knives and a crossbow for an assault designed to kill as many people as possible, Newcastle crown court heard.

The British man, from Hull, tried to recruit an accomplice for an attack on the city’s Royal Hotel, which housed asylum seekers until September this year. However, his plan unravelled when that man went to the police.

Anderson had denied preparing an act of terrorism but was found guilty on Friday. The judge, Mrs Justice Lambert, told the defendant he should expect a “very significant” prison term when he is sentenced next year.

Anderson first made contact with his intended accomplice through social media, knowing that the man – who cannot be identified by the media – had been involved in anti-migrant disorder in the city.

On a secure messaging platform, Anderson told the man he was in a group of “white Christian nationalists” whose “main objective is fighting back against Islam, paedophile elites and Jews”.

The two men met in the city centre when Anderson outlined his plan to attack Hull’s Royal Hotel “and to kill as many of the migrants who were housed inside it as possible”, said Adam Birkby, prosecuting.

During the trial, the intended accomplice told jurors Anderson explained his rationale for targeting the hotel, saying: “He said it was full of nonces, rapists, people that shouldn’t be in our country.”

After the informer told police about the plot, Anderson was arrested. Knives, a crossbow and petrol bombs were found during a search of his home.

He had made or attempted to create napalm, gunpowder and fuses, the court heard, and carried out reconnaissance on the hotel, which housed migrants until September this year.

The trial heard that Anderson, who grew up in France and Spain before moving to the North York Moors, had previously tried to join the Royal Marines.

Anderson had also tried to buy a piece of land in Devon with fellow rightwingers, who planned to use it as a shooting ground and a site to practise tactics.

Earlier, the trial heard, he had looked into Islam but turned away from it and had also previously been a Mormon.

He then developed an interest in the extreme-right following the Southport riots, finding a sense of “brotherhood” with others after experiencing an isolated childhood, jurors were told.

Judges, juries and rape myths in trials

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:47:13 GMT

Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham

In your report (‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind.

It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted.

Examples of the full direction can be found in the published crown court compendium, which observes that “There is a possibility that juries will make and/or be invited by advocates to make unwarranted assumptions. It is important that the judge should alert the jury to guard against this.”

The court of appeal has stated that “We accept that the effect of each direction may be to bolster the evidence of a victim; but it only bolsters their evidence to the extent necessary to prevent unfairness to the victim caused by the stereotypical thinking against which it warns.”

This does not prevent the defence relying on this unattractive and out‑of-date tactic, but, given that the jury can receive these directions in writing to take into the jury room, it may well backfire if they do. Paul Keleher KC London

Gaby Hinsliff is right to ask questions about the role that the law is playing in keeping serious allegations of wrongdoing out of the public domain (Don’t just blame the culture for keeping powerful men’s dirty secrets. Blame the law too, 13 November). Many academics share her concerns.

While not perfect, the law of defamation contains free-speech protections that have been developed over centuries. They seek to strike a delicate balance between protecting individual reputation and allowing genuine allegations of serious wrongdoing to reach the public consciousness.

Like Hinsliff, numerous legal commentators have challenged the idea that powerful people should be able to dodge those free-speech protections by bringing actions in privacy, harassment or breach of confidence instead. Prof Nicole Moreham Co-editor, The Law of Privacy and the Media (fourth edition)

Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:47:05 GMT

Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit

Cop31 live – latest updates

The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster.

double quotation markI. Global progress and context 1. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilateralism and resolves to remain united in the pursuit of efforts to implement the Convention and achieve the purpose and long-term goals of the Paris Agreement; 2. Recalls that the Paris Agreement will be implemented to reflect equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances; 3. Acknowledges that the Paris Agreement is working and that the global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development is irreversible, and that significant collective progress towards the Paris Agreement temperature goal has been made, from an expected global temperature increase of more than 4°C according to some projections prior to the adoption of the Agreement to an increase of around 2.6°C based on the full implementation of national climate plans; 4. Emphasizes the importance of promoting the economic and social benefits and opportunities of action on climate change, recognizing the significant drop in the cost of mature renewable energy and zero- and low-emission technologies, and the role of the energy transition in strengthening energy security, affordability and availability;

This reaffirms the Paris agreement and defends it against charges that it is not working, by acknowledging the progress made in bringing down the world’s emissions trajectory that would have taken us well above 4C. But 2.6C is still far too high, and would violate the limit of “well below 2C” set in Paris in 2015, and the 1.5C temperature goal that was set as an aspiration.

It is the first mention of an “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”. Some countries – chiefly the Arab group, led by Saudi Arabia, but also including Russia and some developing country allies – want this much weaker phrase to replace the commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” that was set at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.

double quotation mark5. Commends the 167 Parties that, as at 18 November 2026, had communicated their new nationally determined contributions, the 81 Parties that have communicated long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies, and 96 Parties that have submitted their national adaptation plans, and urges Parties that have not yet made such submissions to do so as soon as possible;

Nationally determined contributions (NDCs) are the bedrock of Paris. Each country crafts their own, setting out their core emissions-cutting goals and actions to be undertaken to meet those goals. For developing countries, NDCs can operate as development plans, inviting investors to put money into renewable energy or low-carbon technology, as well as help them improve their resilience to the impacts of extreme weather.

double quotation mark6. Also welcomes the implementation of the enhanced transparency framework, including submissions of 140 first biennial transparency reports, 112 technical expert reviews, 80 Parties undergoing facilitative, multilateral consideration of progress and the 2026 synthesis report of the first biennial transparency reports; 7. Encourages Parties that have not yet submitted their first biennial transparency report to do so as soon as possible and invites all Parties to submit on time their biennial transparency reports due on 31 December 2026, taking into consideration paragraph 4 of decision 18/CMA.1.

The transparency reports were a central focus at Cop29 in Baku: they lay out commitments on spending of climate finance.

double quotation mark8. Encourages enhanced support for the implementation of national adaptation plans, and urges Parties to implement the UAE Framework for Global Climate Resilience and to mainstream climate change adaptation into all relevant national plans and strategies, taking into account national circumstances and priorities;

National adaptation plans are the counterpart to NDCs – they show what countries need in order to protect themselves against extreme weather and can also operate as investable plans to attract private companies or to gain access to climate finance from public sources.

double quotation mark9. Expresses deep concern that global peak warming is projected to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels; 10. Underscores that the risks and impacts of climate change will be much lower at the temperature increase of 1.5°C compared with 2°C; 11. Recognizes that 1.5°C overshoot and every increment of warming above current levels will increase the frequency and intensity of loss and damage and result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems; 12. Reaffirms resolve to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C, to limit both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot, and to close adaptation gaps, reinforcing the need for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions, and to enhance action and support to enable countries and communities to better prepare for, adapt to, respond to and recover from adverse climate impacts;

Cop31 is the first Cop to acknowledge that the 1.5C temperature limit has already been breached. These paragraphs, if adopted, would be the first ever in an official UN framework convention on climate change (UNFCCC) agreement to recognise this “overshoot” and set out an attempt to deal with it.

Dealing with the overshoot, and making it as brief and shallow as possible – that is, ensuring temperatures rise as little above 1.5C as possible and for as short a time as possible – is vital to low-lying countries in particular, but is also important more broadly, as temperatures rising above 1.5C can quickly start to trigger tipping points that could have irreversible effects on the climate.

double quotation mark13. Recognizes the urgency of enhancing action and support in relation to adaptation, means of implementation and mitigation to address the gaps in the implementation of the Paris Agreement as a whole; 14. Recalls with concern the pre-2020 gaps in both the mitigation ambition and implementation of developed country Parties and that the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) had previously indicated that developed countries must reduce emissions by 25–40 per cent below the 1990 level by 2020, which was not achieved; 15. Also recalls with concern that the carbon budget consistent with achieving the Paris Agreement temperature goal is now small and being rapidly depleted and acknowledges that historical cumulative net carbon dioxide emissions account for at least four fifths of the total carbon budget for a 50 per cent probability of limiting global warming to 1.5°C; 16. Urges Parties, while implementing their NDCs, to strive to overachieve their targets, in light of national circumstances, recognising that developed countries should take the lead; 17. Reiterates that support shall be provided to developing country Parties for the implementation of Article 4 of the Paris Agreement, in accordance with Articles 9 to 11 of the Paris Agreement, recognizing that enhanced support for developing country Parties will allow for higher ambition in their actions;

More on NDCs. Note that in climate agreements, mitigation always refers to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, or steps taken to curb future emissions growth. It does not mean mitigating the impacts of extreme weather – that is known as adaptation, or resilience.

This notes that NDCs at last year’s Cop, which was the deadline for them, were inadequate to keep temperatures in line with the Paris agreement. NDCs are submitted every five years, but there is also a mechanism whereby countries can submit improved NDCs without waiting five years. However, almost none have ever done this, and the current round of NDCs is likely to remain unchanged before the “global stocktake” in 2028, which is the mechanism by which NDCs are assessed.

double quotation mark18. Highlights that costed needs reported in nationally determined contributions of developing country Parties are estimated at USD 5.1–6.8 trillion for up until 2030 or USD 455–584 billion per year and adaptation finance needs are estimated at USD 305 billion annually for up until 2035 and notes with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs, particularly for adaptation in developing country Parties; 19. Recalls the invitation in paragraph 36 of decision 1/CMA.7 for Parties to develop implementation and investment plans for their nationally determined contributions and to align their nationally determined contributions with their broader economic development strategies and plans, and encourages Parties to accelerate their efforts in this regard;

This is an important paragraph for developing countries, which are angry at the insufficient finance on offer to help them. However, Cop31 was never intended to be a finance Cop – that was done at Cop29 in Baku, when developed countries agreed to provide $300bn a year by 2035 from public sources, and to help ensure $1tn a year flows to developing countries from private and other sources by the same date.

double quotation mark20. Notes with deep concern that the adverse impacts of climate change are increasing in frequency and severity, with far-reaching consequences for people, livelihoods and ecosystems, including oceans, mountains and the cryosphere, and further expresses concern over the potential of the ongoing El Niño event, compounded by long-term climate change; 21. Recognizes the growing impacts of climate change on physical and mental health, and underscores the need to strengthen climate-resilient health systems through the integration of health into national adaptation plans and other relevant processes; 22. Recognizes the vulnerability of mountain regions, ecosystems and glacier-dependent communities to the adverse effects of climate change, and decides to establish the Work Programme on Mountains and Climate Change under the Nairobi Work Programme on impacts vulnerability and adaptation to climate change, with a view to enhancing adaptation action, disaster risk reduction, resilience building, data observations and early warning systems, using support through existing channels and building on existing work under the Convention and the Paris Agreement; 23. Requests the Chair of the SBSTA to convene the [XX] [Mountains and Climate Change] Dialogues at SBSTA66 and SBSTA68 with a view to elevating scientific understanding and awareness of the impacts of climate change on mountain regions, ecosystems and glacier-dependent communities, and further requests the Chair of the SBSTA to prepare, with the support of the secretariat, a report upon the conclusion of the [XX] [Mountains and Climate Change] Dialogues for consideration by [SBSTA69][at CMA10]; and decides that a high level dialogue on mountains and climate change is to be convened at COP32 under the guidance of the COP32 Presidency;

The first mention of this year’s El Niño, which is threatening food price rises and food shortages and having a disastrous impact, particularly on developing countries.

double quotation mark24. Further decides to hold a high-level dialogue at the ninth session of the CMA focused on scientific findings around 1.5°C overshoot, its implications, and the complementarity between equity, science and sustainable development; 25. Recognizes that systematic observation underpins early warning systems and the assessment of collective progress towards the Paris temperature goal, and expresses concern regarding threats to continuity and sustainability of long-term observational records and networks, both in situ and satellite, of the Earth system, including support for the Global Climate Observing System and for the Global Ocean Observing System, and encourages support for addressing persistent monitoring gaps in under-observed regions, including through the Systematic Observations Financing Facility;

This section is about the early warning systems against climate disaster that were championed by the outgoing UN secretary general, António Guterres, and could save millions of lives globally. Their potential importance was illustrated by the glacier collapse in Nepal in September.

double quotation markII. Accelerating implementation A. Concrete solutions 26. Recognizes that end-to-end multi-hazard early warning systems are among the most effective solutions for saving lives, strengthening adaptation and resilience, and reducing loss and damage; 27. Recalls the call of the Secretary-General of the United Nations to ensure universal coverage of early warning systems for all people on Earth by 2027 and recognizes the contribution of the Early Warnings for All initiative towards achieving this goal; 28. Recognizes that electrification has significant benefits to emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access, and underlines universal access to clean, reliable and affordable energy, sustainable energy, clean cooking and means of implementation for developing country Parties can help realise these benefits;

29. Also recognizes that reductions in anthropogenic methane and other non-carbon dioxide emissions provide significant opportunities to slow the rate of global warming in the near term and to limit peak warming and the duration of overshoot, alongside accelerated action to reduce all greenhouse gas emissions, and the importance of technical assistance and support for developing countries to support these efforts;

Addressing methane could be an “emergency brake” to help bring down global temperature rises in the short term.

double quotation mark30. Expresses deep concern about the impacts of climate change on the ocean, livelihoods and biodiversity, including through ocean warming and sea level rise, and recognizes the important contribution of sustainable ocean-based climate action to strengthening adaptation and resilience and advancing mitigation efforts while delivering benefits for communities and biodiversity; 31. Recognizes the need to enhance means of implementation and support for sustained global ocean observing and early warning systems, enhanced access to ocean data and technologies and capacity-building; 32. Also recognizes nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches as essential climate solutions that can contribute simultaneously to mitigation, adaptation and resilience, including through the conservation, protection, restoration and sustainable management of forests and other natural ecosystems;

This inclusion of oceans in the draft text has been one of the few bright spots. Australia had promised to highlight the needs of its Pacific island neighbours.

double quotation mark33. Recognizes that carbon dioxide removal has a role, as assessed by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), in achieving the long-term temperature goal, but should complement, and not substitute for or delay, deep emission reductions, and stresses that its deployment should ensure environmental safeguards, and respect the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities; 34. Welcomes efforts that contribute to urgently and rapidly scaling up the development, dissemination and deployment of Carbon Capture Utilization and Storage and Carbon Dioxide Removal technologies; 35. Recognizes the importance of resource efficiency, sustainable consumption and production, waste reduction and circular economy as important elements of climate action, in accordance with national circumstances and priorities;

The inclusion of carbon capture and storage here make these paragraphs controversial. Some civil society groups deride CCS as a “false solution” that helps the fossil fuel industry to continue to have a role. However, they are likely to be insisted on by Saudi Arabia and the Arab Group, which can point to findings by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and UN Environment Programme (UNEP) that CCS will be needed to bring down the overshoot of 1.5C. They could be used as a bargaining chip with Saudi Arabia – if these commitments stay in, Saudi must agree to allowing stronger language in other parts of the text. Whether that works remains to be seen.

double quotation mark36. Calls for global cooperation across all actors to strengthen implementation, finance, investment, technology transfer and capacity building for concrete solutions to accelerate the irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience, and to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, recognizing that countries will take different pathways and solutions in accordance with their national circumstances and development priorities, including through, inter alia: (a) Strengthening and expanding the deployment of end-to-end multi-hazard early warning systems linked to early action, and delivering on the Early Warnings for All initiative and the 2027 target for universal coverage, including in all least developed countries and small island developing States; (b) Strengthening climate risk monitoring, forecasting, preparedness, anticipatory action, and adaptation planning; (c) Accelerating, in line with national circumstances, the uptake of clean, secure, affordable, accessible and resilient energy systems, including through the accelerated development, deployment and diffusion of renewable energy and other zero- and low-carbon energy technologies and fuels, energy efficiency, the accelerated expansion, modernization and improved resilience of electricity grids, transmission and distribution networks; (d) Increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, complementary to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030 and alongside storage, system flexibility and modern and resilient grids, and improving energy access; (e) Accelerating action to reduce anthropogenic methane and other non-carbondioxide emissions through practical and cost-effective solutions, recognizing that mitigation pathways, opportunities and implementation approaches vary across sources, sectors and taking into account different cultural practices; (f) Strengthening and accelerating the implementation of sustainable ocean-based action in national climate goals and plans, including, but not limited to, NDCs and NAPs, in a nationally determined manner; (g) Encouraging enhanced efforts to halt and reverse deforestation and forest degradation by 2030; (h) Accelerating Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) [to at least 500 MtCO2 reflecting current policies by 2035, and to work towards 1.3 to 2.5 Gt] [working towards 2.5 Gt] carbon dioxide per year by 2035 and encouraging all actors, including industry, to scale up research and development and deliver on committed projects, recognizing the role of CCUS, particularly in hard to abate sectors;

These paragraphs about the “transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions” are significant. As well as repeating the substitution of the “transition away from fossil fuels” with the much weaker phrase, they also weaken the planned target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 by making it one of a suite of voluntary options, rather than a firm and binding commitment.

double quotation mark37. Encourages locally led and ecosystem-based adaptation and integrated adaptation programmes that combine sustainable land management, ecosystem restoration, drought resilience and climate-resilient livelihoods, supported by finance, technology transfer and capacity-building; 38. Recognizes the important role of domestic energy planning, capacity building, policy strategies and frameworks, as well as cooperation between different levels of government, in creating enabling environments to expand electrification and sustainable fuels use and to attract financing for energy transitions; 39. Calls for the full and expeditious implementation of NDCs and NAPs informed by the outcome of the first global stocktake, as set out in decision 1/CMA.5, across mitigation, adaptation and means of implementation;

Adaptation is central to developing countries, but these paragraphs fail to recognise their need for strong funding measures to allow that to happen.

double quotation markB. Enabling action, including through means of implementation 40. Underscores the commitment towards the effective implementation of the new collective quantified goal and the call for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 in the context of this goal, and resolves to accelerate delivery thereof; 41. Reiterates the importance of reforming the multilateral financial architecture and underscores the need to remove barriers and address disenablers faced by developing country Parties in financing climate action, including high costs of capital, limited fiscal space, unsustainable debt levels, high transaction costs and conditionalities for accessing climate finance; 42. Expresses concern at increasing adaptation impacts and costs and stresses the urgent need for scaled-up provision and mobilization of adequate, predictable, public, grant-based and highly concessional finance for adaptation in developing country Parties, especially LDCs and SIDS and others with significant capacity constraints; 43. Recalls decision 1/CMA.7, paragraph 53, and requests the Standing Committee on Finance to prepare for consideration at the ninth session of the conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement a technical report identifying options for the baseline of the call for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 in the context of decision 1/CMA.6 and to include in the report referred to in paragraph 30 of decision 1/CMA.6 information on the progress on the call for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 in the context of 1/CMA;

The new collective quantified goal on finance mentioned here was the name given to the settlement made Cop29 for $300bn a year to come from public sources in the developed world to the developing world by 2035, along with $1tn from other sources, to help poor countries cut emissions and cope with the impacts of extreme weather.

Developed countries regard these financial negotiations as having been settled and closed; some developing countries would like to reopen them, finding them insufficient.

double quotation mark44. Further agrees to discuss, under the work programme on climate finance referred to in paragraph 54 and 55 of decision 1/CMA.7, an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035 that responds to and accelerates delivery of the call for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 in the context of decision 1/CMA.65 for consideration at CMA 9; 45. Decides to launch, under the guidance of the COP31 and COP32 Presidencies, in consultation with Parties, the “Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap on Adaptation and Resilience Finance”, aiming to identify predictable and scaled-up sources of finance for adaptation, including for responding to loss and damage, including through innovative sources, and mechanisms for access, including in the context of decision 1/CMA.6 and paragraph 54 and 55 of decision 1/CMA.7; and requests the Presidencies to produce a report summarizing the conclusions of the work for consideration by the CMA at its ninth session (2027); 46. Recognizes that improved, efficient and equitable access to climate finance is essential to support implementation, including through the measures outlined in the new collective quantified goal, acknowledges progress by multilateral development banks and multilateral climate funds to improve access, and encourages finance providers to take into account country-led programming and ensure the meaningful engagement of vulnerable communities and groups; 47. Encourages enhanced readiness support, institutional capacity-building and technical assistance for developing country Parties to strengthen national financial institutions, including national and public development banks and other entities seeking direct access to climate finance, and invites the operating entities of the Financial Mechanism, funds serving the Paris Agreement, bilateral climate finance providers, and multilateral development banks, upon request and in a country-driven manner, to support funded project preparation and capacity-building; 48. Invites climate finance providers, including the operating entities of the Financial Mechanism, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and the Special Climate Change Fund, and multilateral development banks and other international financial institutions to improve access by taking measures that simplify and expedite approval and disbursement procedures, such as mutual recognition of accreditation across funds, readiness and project preparation support that extends beyond the preparation of strategies and pipelines to support implementation, reduce co-financing requirements and transaction costs, and to enhance transparency on efforts taken in this regard as appropriate; 49. Requests the secretariat, in collaboration with multilateral development banks and multilateral climate funds, including the operating entities of the Financial Mechanism, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and the Special Climate Change Fund, to organize annual workshops from 2027 to 2030 to facilitate the exchange of views on efforts, progress made and next steps on enhancing access to climate finance, with a view to support meaningful engagement of Parties and further requests the secretariat to prepare technical reports on these workshops as inputs to the biennial report by the SCF on the implementation of decision 1/CMA.6 and as inputs to the special assessment of access to climate finance referred to in paragraph 34 of decision 1/CMA.6; 50. Reaffirms paragraph 16 of decision 1/CMA.6, including with regard to pursing efforts to at least triple annual outflows from the operating entities of the Financial Mechanism, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and the Special Climate Change Fund based on 2022 levels by 2030 at the latest, and encourages consideration of these efforts in future pledges and replenishments to these institutions; (a) Welcomes the initial pledges received to date towards the 9th replenishment of the GEF Trust Fund, notes with concern the decline of the resources allocated to GEF-9 compared to GEF-8, including resources allocated for climate change mitigation focal area, and encourages further pledges to the GEF-9 replenishment; (b) Underlines the importance of an ambitious 3rd GCF-replenishment and encourages the GCF to actively reach out to potential contributors; (c) Urges developed country Parties to provide financial resources for the third replenishment of the Green Climate Fund, notes the importance of converting pledges to contributions in a timely manner and also urges the conversion of pledges as soon as possible;

Here the text plans yet another roadmap – the “Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap on Adaptation and Resilience Finance”. But it takes more than a roadmap to deliver climate finance. One of the main problems for developing countries is that the finance available is often hard for them to access – it involves not only complex form filling but also proving that the country can handle the money, use it efficiently and meet its stated objectives with it. Donors are quicker to make promises than they are to follow through with cash, and disbursements have been too slow and too focused on the larger and middle-income developing countries rather than the smallest, poorest and most vulnerable, who need it most.

Last year at Cop30, countries agreed to triple adaptation finance, but they did not set a baseline or say how this would happen. Developing countries would like to see that fleshed out in Turkey.

double quotation mark51. Recognizes the importance of multilateral climate funds having predictable and ambitious replenishments and contributions that scale and align with increasing programming capacity and allow the funds to respond to growing developing-country needs and continue leveraging additional public and private finance at scale; 52. Notes the establishment and operationalization of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, the ongoing progress made by its Board to implement the Barbados Implementation Modalities and the progress achieved in operationalizing the Santiago network and by the Executive Committee of the Warsaw International Mechanism, and stresses the importance of enhancing collaboration, coordination, complementarity and coherence across funding arrangements for responding to loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change; 53. Notes that funding requests under the Barbados Implementation Modalities total approximately USD 2.8 billion against allocations of approximately USD 342 million, that only 50 per cent of USD 822 million in FRLD pledges has reportedly been converted into contributions, and that the Santiago Network and WIM ExCom remain under-resourced; 54. Takes note of the 21 per cent increase in climate finance from multilateral development banks over the prior year in view of reaching their 2030 climate finance estimates announced at COP29, of delivering $120 billion per year and mobilizing a further $65 billion in private capital; 55. Emphasizes the importance of Parties and the international financial architecture to implementing policies, plans, measures and actions which mobilize public, private, bilateral, multilateral and alternative sources of finance, for developing country Parties, in a manner which supports climate resilient development and enhances developing countries’ capacity to 7 attract and absorb climate finance, reduces cost of capital, optimizes the use of grant-based and concessional finance, and crowds in private investment;

Loss and damage here refers to funds for the rescue and rehabilitation of countries stricken by climate disaster. A loss and damage fund was agreed at Cop27 in Egypt in 2022, but it has been slow to fill and to disburse cash. Nepal received only $21m this year after its glacier collapse disaster.

double quotation mark56. Affirms that the resolve to pursue efforts to keep 1.5°C within reach and to limit both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot, and to close implementation and financing gaps, requires the full implementation of Article 2, paragraph 1(c) of the Paris Agreement, in a nationally determined manner reflecting different national circumstances, which is complementary to and not a substitute for the provision and mobilization of financial support to developing countries under Article 9 of the Paris Agreement; C. International cooperation and collaboration 57. Underlines the urgent need to address, in a comprehensive and synergetic manner, the interlinked global crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, desertification, and land and ocean degradation in the broader context of achieving sustainable development;

Addressing the overshoot referenced here will be vital, but this language is not strong enough for the countries most vulnerable to its effects.

double quotation mark58. Encourages Parties to enhance cooperation and synergies in the implementation of the Convention, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification and other relevant multilateral environmental agreements, as appropriate, in a synergistic and efficient manner, in accordance with national circumstances and priorities and in a manner respectful of the respective mandates of these agreements, without creating new obligations for Parties, and notes the work of the Joint Liaison Group of the Rio Conventions in this regard; 59. Requests the co-facilitators of the 2027–2028 biennium Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue to develop the Antalya Ocean Current, a multi-year plan for future Dialogues, taking into account the ambition cycle of the Paris Agreement with a view to supporting continuity between dialogue sessions, identifying entry points for ocean action across relevant UNFCCC processes, and enhancing uptake of the Dialogues key messages; and invites submissions from Parties and non-Party stakeholders on such a multi-year approach, with updates on progress to be delivered through the Dialogue;

More good news on the oceans, with a catchy name for a new ocean talking shop. Cop presidencies love to name new initiatives for the cities where their Cop took place, but frequently fail to follow up afterwards with the funds to keep these initiatives going.

double quotation mark60. Also requests the co-facilitators of the Dialogue, with the assistance of the secretariat, to develop the Blue Imece Synthesis report to be published by 1 June 2028 as an input to the technical assessment of the global stocktake, drawing upon: (a) How Parties have considered ocean-based climate actions in their latest national climate policies, including but not limited to nationally determined contributions, long term strategies and adaptation communications, as relevant; (b) Voluntary submissions from Parties on progress and challenges in implementing their ocean-based climate actions; (c) The best-available science relevant to climate impacts on the ocean and the ocean’s contributions to mitigation, adaptation and resilience; (d) Updates on how work programmes and constituted bodies under the Convention and the Paris Agreement have integrated and strengthened ocean-based action in their existing mandates and workplans, as per the invitation in decision 1/CP.26; and (e) The outcomes of the Ocean and Climate Change Dialogues;

Calling for a new report on the oceans, which will also please Pacific islands.

double quotation mark61. Notes the concerns regarding measures that have negative cross-border impacts, particularly for developing countries, reaffirms that Parties should cooperate to promote a supportive and open international economic system that would lead to sustainable economic growth and development in all Parties, particularly developing country Parties, thus enabling them better to address the problems of climate change, and also reaffirms that measures taken to combat climate change, including unilateral ones, should not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade; 62. Recognizes that international trade can promote innovation and sustainable economic growth and development, support effective, equitable, cooperative, and inclusive climate action, and create opportunities for value addition, diversification and participation in low emissions value chains; 63. Welcomes the convening of the first dialogue on trade and climate change at the sixtyfourth sessions of the subsidiary bodies and encourages continued engagement at the next two dialogues [involving relevant international organizations: World Trade Organisation, United Nations Trade and Development and the International Trade Centre], and invites the SB chairs, supported by the secretariat, to produce a summary report of the next two trade and climate dialogues to be presented in conjunction with the subsequent session of the subsidiary bodies; 64. Also invites Parties, at their discretion, to share relevant information relating to the potential cross-border effects of trade measures through the trade and climate dialogues;

Here the anodyne language disguises one of the hottest disputes at Cop31 about trade. Many developing countries now face tariffs from the US and the EU in particular, and a new carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) from the EU.

The EU’s CBAM is intended to stop carbon leakage – it imposes costs on imports to the EU of goods, in particular high-carbon industries – chiefly steel, chemicals and other heavy industrial goods – if the exporting countries cannot show that they have taken measures to reduce their carbon emissions. This is because, the EU says, it requires its heavy industries to pay for the carbon they produce. So imports of such goods from abroad where carbon emissions were unconstrained are, they argue, undercutting EU prices.

The CBAM was mainly aimed at, and mainly affects, China, which is now taking additional measures to reduce its carbon, including through an emissions trading scheme. India is also worried about the CBAM, regarding it as a means of protectionism from the EU.

But some smaller developing countries object to it too. The EU says that small countries will not be affected by the CBAM, as help is available to them. Many are unconvinced – although some might also be objecting in order to cement their relationships with China and India, rather than out of real fear that their exports will be hit.

double quotation mark65. Encourages engagement in the related high-level event referred to by decision 1/CMA.7, paragraph 56; 66. Recognizes the particular vulnerabilities of small island developing States, including to climate change-related sea level rise, and the leadership of Pacific island countries and other small island developing States in requesting an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice on the obligations of States in respect of climate change; 67. Recognizes also the importance of advancing intergenerational equity and meaningful participation of children and youth in climate action and decision-making processes, and invites relevant work programmes and constituted bodies to integrate responses to impacts on children and youth in undertaking work within their existing mandates and in their activities and outputs; 68. Acknowledges the role and contributions of Indigenous Peoples and of local communities in nature stewardship and climate leadership, as well as the disproportionate effects of climate change on Indigenous Peoples and on local communities;

Indigenous people have received less attention at this Cop than was hoped, particularly after their protests at Cop30 in Brazil last year, storming the conference centre to have their voices heard.

double quotation mark69. Encourages Parties, in accordance with their national circumstances and priorities, to strengthen multilevel arrangements with local and regional governments for the implementation of their climate actions; 70. Recognizes the central role of equity and the best available science and of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), whose assessment reports are the most robust and comprehensive assessment of climate science, in the effective implementation of the Convention and the Paris Agreement, highlights the importance of the IPCC reports for the global stocktake, and expresses appreciation and gratitude to those involved in preparing the reports of the Seventh Assessment Report for their contributions, and invites the IPCC to continue to provide policy-relevant information to UNFCCC processes, including all three working group contributions of the Seventh Assessment cycle to the next Global Stocktake;

Rows over the IPCC have spilled over into this Cop. Some countries – mainly Saudi Arabia, but also Russia, India and Kenya, have objected to the proposed timetable by which the IPCC would present the findings of its latest assessment report in 2028. They say this is to allow for more developing country science to be included in the IPCC. Some believe that in reality it is because they wish to weaken the global stocktake. The row is unlikely to be resolved at this Cop.

double quotation mark71. Welcomes the launch of the second global stocktake as a comprehensive, facilitative, inclusive and Party-driven process, recognising it is an integral part of the ambition cycle of the Paris Agreement to assess collective progress towards the Paris Agreement goals, and encourages the meaningful participation of non-Party stakeholders in the process; 72. Recognizes the value of a diverse range of knowledge systems and encourages further efforts to enhance contributions from all regions, underscoring such contributions strengthen the robustness and comprehensiveness of scientific assessments;

The global stocktake will take place at Cop33, which first India, then China, was expected to offer to host. India decided against offering in April and at this Cop China decided it would not offer to host either.

Indonesia, Uzbekistan and South Korea are said to be considering a hosting bid.

double quotation mark73. Recognizes the important role and active engagement of non-Party stakeholders, particularly civil society, workers, business, financial institutions, farmers, cities and subnational authorities, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, people of African descent, women, youth and children, and research institutions, in supporting Parties and contributing to the significant collective progress towards the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement, in addressing and responding to climate change and enhancing ambition and implementation with a view to keeping 1.5 ℃ within reach; 74. Recognizes the increasing complexity and breadth of the UNFCCC process and the need to maintain an inclusive, transparent, predictable, consensus based, Party-driven UNFCCC process that can effectively fulfill the objectives of the Convention and the Paris Agreement and resolves to continue to strengthen the UNFCCC process to fulfil the objectives and goals of the Convention and the Paris Agreement; 75. Requests the Chairs of the Subsidiary Bodies to convene a dialogue on this matter at SB67and SB69, and requests the Secretariat to prepare a summary report containing options for strengthening the consensus based, Party-driven process as an input to the dialogues, and further requests the Chairs of the Subsidiary Bodies to prepare a summary report of the dialogues for consideration at COP34 and CMA11;

This might have been a good place, while acknowledging the role of workers, to slip in a reference to the just transition – by which workers in high carbon industries are helped to move to low-carbon jobs. But the just transition is missing from this text, although it has a separate negotiating stream at this Cop.

double quotation mark76. Recognizes the important role of voluntary cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, as a vehicle to promote international cooperation, in enabling higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation actions, promoting sustainable development and ensuring environmental integrity, and the potential of high-integrity international carbon markets to mobilize investment, accelerate emission reductions and contribute to achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement, and encourages the secretariat and its regional collaboration centres to continue providing technical assistance and capacity-building support to developing country Parties to participate in cooperative approaches, the mechanism established by Article 6, paragraph 4, and non-market approaches;

Article 6 of Paris is about carbon markets, which have not had much attention at this Cop.

double quotation mark77. Welcomes the full operationalization of the voluntary Global Implementation Accelerator initiative at its eighth session and welcomes the related report of the Presidencies of the seventh and eighth sessions of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement; 78. Emphasizes the voluntary nature of the Global Climate Action Agenda in scaling up and strengthening voluntary efforts, initiatives and coalitions and mobilizing non-Party stakeholders to accelerate implementation and recognizes its role in supporting implementation and enhancing international cooperation, including through the recent organisation of its work around six axes: (a) Welcomes the voluntary BRIDGE initiative of the Presidency of the thirty-first session of the Conference of the Parties, to support country owned implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions and National Adaptation Plans, consistent with national priorities and circumstances; (b) Invites Parties to appoint voluntary implementation focal points by informing the secretariat to receive regular relevant information on engagement with the climate high level champions, Marrakech Partnership and the Global Climate Action Agenda; (c) Welcomes the launch of the COP31 Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, developed by the COP31 Presidency with the support of the United Nations Environment Programme-hosted secretariat of the Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction, and its voluntary collective global ambition to reduce the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by at least 25 per cent by 2035, relative to 2020 levels; (d) Welcomes the Zero-Waste Initiative as a voluntary contribution to advancing resource efficiency, circular economy approaches and sustainable consumption and production, including through its potential to contribute to methane emission reductions from waste, and notes its aspiration to halve the projected increase in annual global waste generation by 2035, recognizing different national circumstances, priorities and approaches, and the importance of international cooperation and support; 79. Requests the SBSTA to initiate, at SBSTA 66 (June 2027), the first review and update, as appropriate, of the modalities, procedures and guidelines referred to in decision 18/CMA.1, paragraph 2; 80. Invites Parties, non-Party stakeholders, transparency practitioners and experts to submit via the submission portal by 31 March 2027 their views on experience with reporting, technical expert review and facilitative, multilateral consideration of progress, as input to the review and update of the modalities, procedures and guidelines, and requests the secretariat to prepare for consideration by SBSTA 66 a synthesis report on the submissions to be made available no later than three weeks prior to that session.

The reference to waste is another nod to a pet project of the host nation, Turkey, which is keen on zero waste initiatives – despite being home to a large number of uncapped landfill sites which, as the Guardian recently revealed, are leaking vast quantities of methane.

It’s time we all made healthy food go further

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:44:42 GMT

Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas

Rachel Dixon’s article (The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten.

It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year.

With food prices still rising, WRAP’s research found the majority of people are cost-conscious at Christmas. The government’s Be Ready campaign asks us to stock up, but that only works if we use what we store.

Another F is for fridge: keeping most fruit and veg below 5C keeps it fresher for longer. Making the most of what we already have adds up – for our pockets, our health and the planet. Estelle Herszenhorn Director of food system transformation, WRAP

Thanks for an inspiring article on root-to-tip cooking. I recommend drying out banana peels in an oven or dehydrator as they make an amazingly cosy tea with a pinch of nutmeg. My friends love it so much it’s become a gift routine! (To save the faff of doing each one individually, stock up on peels in the freezer and dry in bulk when you have enough). Lily van den Broecke London

One tip in your article is using peach and cherry pits to make a drink. That should be fine if they are left whole, but don’t be tempted to grind them up: you could end up with a nasty case of cyanide poisoning from the toxic amygdalin they contain. I speak as someone with a lifetime aversion to bakewell tart and amaretto, which have the same flavour. Charlie Wartnaby Cambridge

The best way to avoid winter illness

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:44:19 GMT

Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter

“Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments (Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation.

It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told that “it’s fine”, but as a long-Covid sufferer for 2.5 years, I can tell you this disease is vile: I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy, certainly not my loved ones. I am unable to go for a walk, be social or stay active. If people feel ill (even “just a cold”) they should stay at home and avoid spreading their germs to everyone they meet, because they probably won’t know who is vulnerable. Sally Billenness Hounslow, London

In your article, Dr Philip Barber advocated a hot toddy at night, which included lemon and sugar: both of these ingredients are extremely bad for teeth, especially at night, when the saliva flow decreases substantially. This a recipe for rampant tooth decay (sugar) and erosion (lemon juice). Caroline Clitter Retired dental hygienist and dental therapist, Lymington, Hampshire

Anthropic shares slump on second day of trading as markets reel from AI sell-off

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:26:07 GMT

Nasdaq erases 2026 gains and Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Anthropic’s shares fell at the start of its second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

As they dropped, the wider stock market fell with them, with the Nasdaq Composite erasing all its gains for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly entered correction territory.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2.9% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1.66% in morning trading in New York.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital. com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell by 7% after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:08:42 GMT

Thomas sentenced to 15 months after admitting to criminal damage to vessel that had been carrying asylum seekers

The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail after slashing a dinghy that had been carrying asylum seekers in the Channel.

Judge Newton-Price KC described Thomas as a “publicity seeker” who had interfered with the work of law enforcement officers and lifesavers.

The judge said: “This offence amounted to a flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption of the legitimate activities of the border force, the coastguard and RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution] volunteers.”

He added: “Those organisations perform essential roles in policing the maritime border. They do necessary, highly sensitive and very difficult jobs. Their work should not be interrupted by a publicity seeker slashing with a knife at a boat that they were trying to recover.”

Thomas, the founder of the anti-migration group Patriot Platform, had taken a boat out into the Channel and observed asylum seekers in a dinghy being assisted by the RNLI, Border Force and French coastguard on 22 September.

He asked for his boat to be steered towards the rigid-hulled inflatable boat, and armed himself with a knife as rescue crews approached the dinghy and a French man boarded it.

Newton-Price said Thomas had slashed the boat about eight times and his actions would have alarmed anyone close at hand.

The judge said the fact the incident was livestreamed meant there must have been a “high degree of planning or premeditation”. He said the video was intended to be seen by a large audience on social media and replayed.

Thomas appeared from Winchester prison in Hampshire via video link. He made the sign of the cross at the start of the hearing and did not watch the livestream when it was shown in court. He slumped in his chair as the sentence was handed down.

Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said aggravating features of the offence included that it took place on the “high seas” and while law enforcement officers were investigating potential immigration offences and RNLI volunteers were carrying out humanitarian work.

Smith said Thomas had five previous convictions, including public order offences, being carried in a stolen vehicle and fraud, and had been sentenced in 2016 to two years in jail for kidnap. Simon Pentol KC, defending, described it as a “unique” case but said Thomas had not been charged with a racially motivated, terrorist or public order offence.

Pentol said: “The political element or landscape should be viewed though a very narrow prism.”

He told the court the incident began as “reportage” and the criminal damage was what Thomas had called a “spur of the moment opportunity”. Pentol said: “It was not premeditated. This was performative activism.” He added that the knife was not Thomas’s but was part of the boat’s equipment.

Pentol said Thomas had four children and was the sole provider for the family, and ran a successful business.

After slashing the dinghy with the knife, Thomas could be heard saying: “This is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats. Right, you’re on English territory. This is England; this is not France any more. Get off the boat; you have time to get off the boat. This is not France. Take them back.” He also said: “Traitors.”

The incident was captured on Thomas’s livestream and the 37-year-old, also known as Danny Tommo, admitted criminal damage when he appeared at Portsmouth crown court via video link from prison.

After footage of the incident emerged, Thomas’s actions were condemned as violent and dangerous by the refugee charities Stand Up to Racism and the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants.

According to the RNLI, the rescued asylum seekers had been onboard the dinghy for 36 hours, which was thought to be the longest time small-boat passengers had spent crossing the Channel.

The RNLI said there were concerns for their deteriorating health and fears of a “catastrophic failure” of the dinghy. The French coastguard said about 60 people on a small boat had spent more than 33 hours at sea “in precarious conditions” and refusing help as they were “determined to take all risks to reach the United Kingdom”.
