Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson to become Britain’s next big Hollywood power couple

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:00:33 GMT

Duo’s fame set to soar after Pattinson announced as next James Bond – but they will take newgen approach to power

He is the next James Bond. She is a successful model/actor/singer-songwriter. Together, they are set to become the next big British power couple in Hollywood.

This week Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse, who have been in a relationship since 2018, were thrust into the global spotlight after the news that he had landed arguably the biggest and most glamorous role in film.

RPatz is well known – this year alone he has starred in The Drama, The Odyssey and Primetime.

Alongside modelling, Waterhouse has played a leading role in Daisy Jones & the Six, the TV adaptation of Taylor Jenkins Reid’s Fleetwood Mac-inspired novel, and is touring Loveland, her third album, which includes a cameo from Mick Fleetwood. She previously opened for Taylor Swift at Wembley.

However, the 007 news means the couple’s level of fame will receive a turbocharged jolt, catapulting both of them into household names.

The last British twosome to transform into a power couple on a global level were the Beckhams. In May their empire, which spans football, fashion and property, passed the £1bn mark.

Instead of following the Brand Beckham blueprint, Pattinson, 40, and Waterhouse, 34, are taking their own newgen approach to power. Rather than trying to turn themselves into a joint brand for commercial gain, the couple are focusing on their own individual careers and successes.

It’s a master plan created by fellow big screen stars Tom Holland – who, like Pattinson and Waterhouse, also hails from west London – and Zendaya, who, despite their global fame and estimated combined net worth of £85m, have garnered a reputation as Hollywood’s most low-key couple. Pattinson previously worked with Zendaya on The Drama.

“For decades Hollywood power couples have leveraged their relationships to build joint brands, attract media attention and pursue lucrative business opportunities,” said Shaun Harper, a professor at the USC Marshall school of business at the University of Southern California. “But there is also tremendous business value in keeping their professional identities separate.”

When the Beckhams got engaged in 1998 they held a press conference. A year later, OK! magazine bought the exclusive rights to their wedding photos in a record-breaking £1m deal. They also sold the first photos of their oldest son, Brooklyn. In January, he published a statement in which he accused his parents of prioritising Brand Beckham. He is now estranged from the family.

Pattinson and Waterhouse are navigating fame in a more restrained way. They take a zero-sharenting – in other words no sharing on social media – approach to their daughter, who was born in 2024.

Pattinson has been an ambassador for Dior for more than 10 years and in September signed a deal with the Swiss watch brand Jaeger LeCoultre. Waterhouse has her own deals with Michael Kors and Miu Miu.

The duo were four years into their relationship before they made their red carpet debut at a Dior show in 2022 and since then, they have done so only a handful of times. When they do, it is fruitful for brands. According to the fashion data platform Launchmetrics, their joint appearance at the 2026 Venice film festival, where Pattinson wore Dior and Waterhouse Saint Laurent, generated £4m in media impact value for the luxury houses in one week.

Harper said the couple realised that success did not rely on their relationship becoming a commercial enterprise. “Their approach allows each to build a career, pursue business ventures and maintain a fanbase without being overly dependent on the other,” he said. “It also protects their individual brands from some of the reputational and financial risks that come with being marketed as a couple.”

Holland and Zendaya have starred in the Spider-Man film franchise together and regularly support one another on the red carpet, but they have never done a brand deal. Instead, Holland runs his own alcohol-free beer brand. Zendaya is an ambassador for brands including Prada Beauty and Valentino, and she owns properties separate to Holland. They have never shared their wedding photos.

Zoe Gaffney, a brand director at the marketing agency Leopard Co, points to how a shifting media landscape is influencing this new generation of celebrity couples. While the Beckhams rose to fame during the tabloid era, when “audiences eagerly awaited the latest glimpse into their glamorous lives”, today, owing to social media, they can be more in control of their own narrative.

This new age of optional exposure created a paradox, said Gaffney. “Perhaps being less visible can actually make you more desirable,” she said.

Holland and Zendaya use their platforms solely to promote their latest projects. Pattinson doesn’t have any social media accounts, while Waterhouse has almost 6m combined followers on Instagram and TikTok where, alongside promoting her work, she posts self-deprecating behind-the-scenes posts but never shares images of husband, whom she refers to as her “favourite weirdo”.

Gaffney said this made the couple “all the more compelling”. While the Beckhams do multiple congratulatory posts on any family achievements, Waterhouse has so far remained stumm.

However, it hasn’t stopped Bond fans from weighing in. “Can’t believe this was filmed by James Bond,” reads one comment below a video of her sipping a cappuccino. “Privacy creates intrigue and intrigue can be more powerful than exposure,” Gaffney said.

Harper describes the way they have kept their relationship away from public intrusion so far as impressive. “Sometimes the smartest business decision celebrities can make is to keep their romantic relationships out of their businesses,” he said.

Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:38:39 GMT

The first lady’s two-part TV documentary is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. Calling it thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry

Previously on Melania: earlier this year – either because it found her a compelling subject, or because it wanted to flatter the president before a potentially destructive upcoming antitrust trial – Amazon spent $75m (£57m) to make and market a theatrically released documentary about Melania Trump.

I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. Nobody did, except for journalists who sat in otherwise empty cinemas and (if reports are to believed) people who responded to Craigslist ads offering them $50 to see it. The second reason is because Melania is a series now.

And, listen, I tried. I really tried to go into the series with an open mind. The first rule of criticism is that you should review what something is, and not what you want it to be. I was unable to do this, because I wanted it to be watchable, or to have any form of identifiable substance. In both cases, Melania came up wildly short.

Even calling it a series requires a wild stretching of the imagination. What we actually have here are two episodes, neither of which make it to the 40-minute mark, consisting of nothing but junky little offcuts that fail to tell us anything about anything. A lot of these episodes consist of Melania Trump flatly intoning the sort of empty platitudes found on AI-written CVs. For example, she understands that “meaningful action is driven by change”, which I’m sure will be a great relief to us all.

What a legitimately bizarre thing this is. Even its presentation is weird. Both episodes are full of the sort of faux-lifestyle shaky 8mm footage you’d expect to find on something like With Love, Meghan. It’s a trope you see when someone wants to inject a sense of homemade glamour into proceedings, except here a lot of this cutesy footage is actually of Arlington National Cemetery, home to thousands of dead American soldiers.

Then – and I promise that this isn’t an exaggeration – there is a sequence in the first episode where Melania deliberates about the exact placement of a brooch. This sequence goes on for so much longer than you would expect it to. While it was on, and she was agonising over the exact millimetre position of the brooch, I put the episode on 1.5x speed, and it still took for ever to finish. I ended up falling into a catatonic fugue state, watching it. I might still be watching it now. The show has robbed me of my capacity to discern the boundaries of time and space.

In truth, there is a single grain of substance here. The second episode sees Melania travel to North Carolina and California to meet victims of Hurricane Helene and the wildfires. When the camera pans around to hear the stories of the people who lost their homes, the series momentarily becomes human.

But that doesn’t last long, because it turns out that this was simply used as a way to leapfrog into a discussion about Melania’s work with foster children. Inevitably, her contribution to this involves saying the name of her website out loud in full, twice, then wanging on about the blockchain. Everything unstoppably, inevitably, goes back to her. At one point, the first assistant director shows Melania how his brother’s house was affected by the California fires. “This is all he packed,” he tells her sadly as he swipes through photos on his phone. “His guitars and his Maga hats.”

Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry. There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up. He asks Melania how she unwinds, leading with a base-pleasing question about whether or not she prays. She shrugs it off with some woolly talk about how God is inside us. Does she go for long walks? “I don’t.” Instead, she reveals, she just goes to the spa a lot. “The first priority is to take care of yourself, so you can take care of other people,” she tells us, exactly as someone who tends not to care about other people very much would say. The exchange is Melania in microcosm.

But you’re not going to watch this either. Why would you? Melania is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. It will leave you bored and depressed in equal measure. But, hey, so long as it helps with the antitrust trial.

Melania is on Prime Video

Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:35:15 GMT

The actor’s new role as James Bond could be bad news for DC, as a new owner, new chief and new director already threaten to shake and stir Gotham’s distinctive hero

Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007. The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments.

Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap, delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around.

Four years ago, when The Batman hit cinemas to a chorus of critical acclaim for its brooding blend of detective noir and superhero spectacle, there would have been little question that the studio was all in. The film took more than $770m worldwide and seemed to promise a trilogy that might one day give Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight triptych a run for its money. But much has changed since then.

For one thing, Matt Reeves is no longer directing the remainder of the sequel’s principal photography, having stepped away from the production in October to focus on a family matter. Steven Soderbergh has been drafted in to finish filming, though Reeves says he remains committed to the project. Nevertheless, the unexpected change of director adds another layer of uncertainty to the franchise.

Meanwhile, the takeover of Warner Bros by David Ellison’s Skydance has brought a changing of the guard at DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran departing and former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham taking charge. The new regime wants to get DC’s superhero universe moving rather faster, which may not bode well for maintaining two separate versions of Batman. Gunn and Safran had envisaged a new, non-Pattinson caped crusader appearing in a project titled The Brave and the Bold, alongside Reeves’s standalone films. Whether Latcham maintains that enthusiasm remains to be seen.

You can see why the new management might want to cut the number of Batmen in half. Gotham’s defender of the night has been something of a law unto himself for decades, with successive directors allowed to reinvent him, while Warner Bros struggled to establish a coherent universe featuring Superman, Wonder Woman and the rest of the Justice League. For a studio desperate to emulate Marvel’s success at interconnected storytelling, maintaining a separate, apparently incompatible Batman might seem like an unnecessary complication.

But would anyone really want Reeves’s Batman sharing a universe with Superman? His dark knight inhabits a grimy, rain-soaked city of corrupt politicians, mobsters and serial killers, where he is unlikely to encounter a rampaging alien warlord. The introduction of Superman would risk puncturing the film’s carefully constructed atmosphere. Reeves has managed to make Batman feel like a detective again, rather than a billionaire who occasionally takes time off to investigate local crime.

None of this necessarily means Pattinson cannot play both roles. Bond is likely to occupy a substantial chunk of his working life for the foreseeable future, but it is hardly as though Reeves’s films have been arriving at a furious rate. And Harrison Ford managed to play both Han Solo and Indiana Jones, after all. The bigger question is whether the actor really wants to spend his time leading two of the most demanding franchises in cinema, particularly when he is no longer contractually obliged to complete the Batman trilogy.

It would be ironic if Warner Bros ended up sacrificing one of its few genuinely distinctive superhero franchises just as the wider DC universe was beginning to find its feet. Pattinson may yet be persuaded to return – and the studio and Skydance should be going all out to make this happen – but after years of delays, upheaval and changing priorities, nobody can assume he will. James Bond is well known for having a licence to kill. It would be a strange turn of events if his first victim turned out to be Batman.

Expect a fearsome backlash from cornered All Blacks – but England must play with freedom

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:08:22 GMT

New Zealand want to ease the pain of defeat by Wales but England’s squad depth will make them formidable opponents

I’ve heard it said that in New Zealand, 65% of people are rugby fans but 95% are All Blacks fans. Regardless of how accurate those numbers are, the sentiment is clear, and it explains why Dave Rennie said his players had “let the country down” by losing to Wales. A backlash is coming at Twickenham.

I spent some time with Kieran Read this week, one of the greatest All Blacks to play the game. He enjoyed some fine wins over England during his career but also suffered two defeats and clearly still carries those scars. The pain and anguish remain and, after last weekend’s chastening defeat in Cardiff, the All Blacks will be burning.

It is worth remembering they have been mourning the sudden death of their head of security, Logan Cadwallader, on this tour. The emotional toll of that is enormous. I’m not looking for excuses for the loss to Wales, and I wouldn’t expect them to either, but they are human and there is no way such a tragedy has not had an impact.

The response to defeat will be fearsome. Speaking to Read gave me an idea of how high the standards are that the All Blacks set themselves. The All Blacks of his day did not just want to win, they wanted to dominate, to transcend the sport. They wanted to be talked about like the Chicago Bulls, like Argentina’s football team – as one of the greatest sporting sides on the planet. So it is easy to see why there has been such soul-searching this week and why a response is inevitable.

What fascinates me is that the All Blacks find themselves in a place where England tend to thrive. Against Australia England felt cornered, with their backs against the wall, and in keeping with recent history they produced a fine performance. That is where New Zealand will be on Saturday but for England there is both a sense of expectation and, if they can cope with it, a sense of freedom too.

Expectation is not something England have been able to carry lightly. Many international sides will try to claim underdog status but I think it is fair to say when England come into these clashes against the very best sides, on the back of some good form, they do not always deal with the expectation. They are far happier when under the pump.

But there should be a freedom to Steve Borthwick’s side because, as much as any Test against the All Blacks matters, especially with the World Cup less than 12 months away, it does not feel like one of those crossroads moments that England have experienced plenty of in recent times. We live in an era of polarisation but defeat for England would not derail their revival since the Six Nations. Nor would victory install them as World Cup favourites. I’m not saying they have a free pass but victory would simply be the next step in their progression. It wouldn’t be anything more. That should be liberating for the players: go out and show the best of yourselves without a crushing level of pressure.

This is such an intriguing matchup because the All Blacks are fully loaded and so are England. The teams are at different stages of their respective journeys but in the past 12 months, both have shown themselves capable of some incredible stuff, while lacking consistency. New Zealand won the first Test of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series against South Africa but lost the next three. They were dominant in the Bledisloe Cup but lost to Wales last week. England were shocking in the Six Nations but after four consecutive wins they look comfortable with what they are doing again.

One of the most significant reasons for that is the strength in depth Borthwick has on his bench. We can go back to this fixture two years ago. The match got away from England in the final quarter because Borthwick did not have enough quality among his replacements. Last year he did. And in naming a bench featuring players such as Ellis Genge, Luke Cowan-Dickie, George Martin and Marcus Smith it is clear that Borthwick has high-class replacements at his disposal once more.

The All Blacks, on the other hand, are coping with a sizeable injury list but have called on the big guns and, as much as Beauden Barrett’s achievement of 150 caps should be recognised, it is his brother Jordie I am most worried about. He is a world-class operator at inside-centre. It’s not just the flashy stuff, it’s not just his kicking game, it’s his ability to make try-saving tackles, to make crucial interventions at key points. Keep him quiet and England will go a long way to getting the job done.

Banish the big light: 12 interiors hacks for a cosy winter (and not a candle in sight)

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:00:32 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From your bath to your bedroom, an experts’ guide to making your home a stylish sanctuary

We are in the midst of “staying-in season”, enduring cold days and long nights. But if your attempts at hibernation aren’t working, maybe the ambience is off. The gloomy winter months call for soft mood lighting, warmer textures and sunny colours to bring more joy into your home. From accessories that tell a story to the trending fabric trick to hide clutter, here are ways to create that elusive sense of cosiness this season. And I promise none of them involves buying yet another candle.

The secret to a snug home is a scheme that looks lived-in without feeling cluttered, and curated without appearing staged. Gallerist Gennaro Leone, a co-designer behind one of London’s cosiest cafes, Cremer in Hoxton, explains how to achieve the effect. “Layering warm woods, alongside vintage objects, textiles and lighting, rather than relying on any one element, will help everything feel collected over time rather than overly designed,” he says.

If you choose to add new textiles, Leone suggests mixing and matching “stripes, checks and small floral motifs, especially in warm, earthy colours like rust or ochre”, for a timeless feel. A little feng shui is often enough. “Move a lamp to a darker corner, or hang up a textile to immediately make a room feel warmer and more enveloping without buying new furniture,” he suggests.

One way to up your lighting game for winter is to switch up your shades. British interior designer Isabella Worsley says: “Swapping lampshades from lighter, fresher fabrics in summer to richer materials is an effective way to instantly change the mood of a room. Rich silks in autumnal tones bring warmth and depth to the palette, but also beautifully alter the quality of light in the space.” Worsley’s Arcove collection features olive- and russet-hued lampshades (from £130), or for patterned options, try OKA (from £50).

Worsley’s Arcove lampshade, 18in

OKA Roa lampshade, 16cm

Raise the bar before you’re even inside the house by decorating your path or entrance with low-level lighting. “I like to use floor lanterns leading up to the front door, as well as some dotted about the terrace at the back of my house,” says designer Susie Atkinson, founder of the eponymous design studio. The Danes (£15.50) and Ben Simpson Furniture (from £15.99) make aged bronze and antique brass versions that are sturdy and should be able to cope with British weather.

Aged brass table lantern

Nothing soothes winter aches like a good bath – and even if your tub is far from Instagram-worthy, stocking the shelf with some beautifully packaged products will make it look like somewhere you want to be. Invest in spa-like formulas that smell comforting and feel cosseting. I like Commune’s aromatherapy bath salts (£80), and the fragranced oil body cleansers by 39BC (£39) inspired by Cleopatra and Mark Antony. The Denarii scent with frankincense, patchouli and sandalwood is perfect for a cold snap.

Commune aromatherapy bath salts

Tea and coffee breaks are non-negotiable when there’s a chill in the air. To make them into more of a ritual, Jo Kornstein of Tides Studio in Kent recommends investing in a handthrown pottery mug. “Not only will you feel happy every time you have a hot drink, but you’ll be supporting a local potter or artist.”

Lucy Rutter (£35) is Kornstein’s favourite maker of the moment, while I have my eye on a Nerikomi mug by London-based Fern Taylor (£35).

You could also add some coasters with a handmade feel. I like using tiles, and am coveting the folklore-themed collaboration between Ashby and Bert & May (£6 each).

Nerikomi mug by Fern Taylor

Mansaa tiles by Ashby and Bert & May, each

“I like having something ‘living’ in a room, especially at this time of year when the outside can feel a little more bleak,” says Atkinson. Alongside ferns and succulents from your local garden centre, if you have already planted bulbs in pots in readiness for spring, she says her trick is to put them somewhere cold like the garage until shoots appear, and then bring them inside to “force” them to bloom earlier. “I keep them in the garage, knowing they will be perfect to bring into the house in January, when it is especially chilly,” she explains. Bowls, foot baths and other curiosities that you can find at flea markets will also make interesting containers for winter plants. “I have a very large old pestle and mortar, which I plant with paperwhite daffodils,” says Atkinson.

Lishan Tham, founder of Studio Shan, likes to forage for characterful branches, twigs and holly. “My family and I collect them from the local woodland and display them on our mantel. We also collect huge pine cones on walks and put them in a vintage woven basket near the fireplace, and I dry out orange slices and add those too.” You can buy new oval wicker trugs from retailers such as the Basket Company (£32) if you don’t have time to scour for secondhand ones.

Oval wicker trug

Winter layering isn’t just for outfits; dressing up your bed and sofas will make them look and feel instantly more welcoming. I recently had one of the best night’s sleep of my life at Restaries hotel in Suffolk, which uses Floks’ sustainable, UK-made duvets and pillows (from £52). The wool filling will keep you cool when you’re warm and warm when you’re cool.

If you’re shopping for a new throw, Welsh blankets are a designer favourite for their timeless prints, and they also have a nice weight to them. Melin Tregwynt (from £189) and London Cloth Co are the names to know for new versions and collaborations, though they’re easy to find secondhand, too. Atkinson says: “I have gathered antique ones over the years. I drape them over the back of armchairs, ready to grab if it is especially cold.”

Floks all-season wool duvet, double

Melin Tregwynt Welsh blanket

Many of us know the big light should be permanently extinguished during the cosy season. But how do you get the ambience just right if you’re only using low-level lighting? “I like to make sure every room has at least two sources of light at around eye level when you’re seated, and to use warm white bulbs (2700K and below) to create a soft glow against the increasingly gloomy weather,” explains Carina Harford, the designer behind interiors studio Harford House.

Her favourite piece at the moment is the Loulou portable table lamp by the Swedish artist Yoyo Nasty, in collaboration with Crème Atelier (£233). Featuring a whimsical print on linen, it’s cordless, so you can create a cosy nook wherever you take it. M&S has a vast selection of affordable chargeable lamps. I like the Joshua striped ceramic one (£50).

Joshua striped chargeable ceramic lamp

If the sellout Bayeux tapestry exhibition at the British Museum in London has taught us anything, it’s that the nation loves art that tells a story – especially when it’s handmade. The historic, 70-metre-long embroidered artwork has scale on its side, but introducing woven designs at home, whether on the walls, floor or accessories, will add instant character. Tham loves textural artworks of varying scales in her home projects as they “can hold memory, material and craft in one place, and bring warmth that no mass-produced object can”.

Vinterior stocks a huge range of colourful, large-scale Suzani textiles, hand-embroidered by artisans. Or try adding one of Fine Little Day’s embroidered cushions to your living room (£34.45).

Fine Little Day embroidered cushion

Flagstone or wooden floors may be practical in the warmer months, but in winter putting down rugs not only makes things warmer underfoot, but can also help to zone spaces for relaxation.

Block weave seagrass rugs are trending now for their cosy, country look and feel. In bigger rooms, Atkinson suggests: “I love using sisal rugs to cover a wider space or fill a large part of the room, and then layer an antique rug on top near a fireplace or to create a zone by the sofa or armchair.”

Seagrass Story makes bespoke rugs to fit any room (from £225), while the Natural Rug Company offers made-to-measure sisal rugs and runners, with a choice of weaves and edge bindings to suit your scheme (from £110). Try Emily’s House (from £95) for unique vintage kilims and Berber rugs.

Seagrass Story rug

Open storage has all but disappeared on the feeds of many interior designers, as the trend for cupboard curtains is making a comeback. Cafe-style drapes on poles around open sink units and across wardrobes not only cocoon a room, but can hide a multitude of messes, too.

Kornstein makes her own and is planning to hang them across several doorways this winter. “I like using quilts or vintage blankets as they feel luxurious and warm, and to add a decorative element to the room.”

She uses quilted fabric from Merchant & Mills (from £26 a metre) hung on wrought iron curtain poles, or iron rods (a more frugal choice) to create a lived-in look.

If you’re planning to give one of your rooms a lick of paint, then Alex Glover of Austin James Fine Decorating & Design recommends soft yellows. “Painting rooms that receive the most winter sun in honey tones replicates a sunset glow throughout the day, while combating dullness with natural warmth on greyer days.” His favourite colour for this is Farrow’s Cream by Farrow & Ball (from £34).

For a smaller job that will make a big impact, Glover suggests painting architectural details such as window trims and recesses in earthy tones or shades featuring warm yellow or deep red undertones. “Lick’s Red 07 (from £41), which is a deep bronze-red, has a sophisticated feel for winter. Use a high-sheen eggshell or gloss finish as it adds warmth while projecting light,” he says.

‘You can’t get experience if no one’s employing you’: the vicious circle facing Blackpool’s Neets

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:00:32 GMT

The English seaside town tops the list for 16- to 24-year-olds out of work and education, but not for lack of young jobseekers’ efforts

Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her phone while filming herself in her pyjamas, Amy Butterworth’s relentless search for a job had reached a new level of absurdity.

The 19-year-old from Blackpool was applying for a role at Marks & Spencer, but first had to prove she was not a robot.

After downloading an app, filming her face from different angles, speaking particular words, inputting numbers and sharing a picture of her passport, she eventually received an email offering interview slots.

Yet within two minutes of the message arriving, all the slots were gone. In the small print, the retailer admitted it could not promise an interview to everybody offered one. “I just felt kind of stupid,” Butterworth said.

This is the demoralising reality for many young people in Blackpool, where more than one in five 16- to 24-year-olds are out of work and education, the highest proportion in England.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister, this week urged “full throttle” overhaul of policy across healthcare, education, benefits and employment regulation as Britain reckons with a growing crisis of nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), a far higher rate than many other western European nations.

Eight of the 10 English local authorities with the highest Neet concentrations are in the north or the Midlands. Top of the list is Blackpool, where the town’s reputation as a pleasure resort sits uncomfortably with its deep-rooted issues of poor health, housing and addiction.

On Saturday, dozens of seasiders will put on their glad rags hoping for a ticket to the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing, which is filmed in the Blackpool Tower Ballroom for one week each year. Yet the queues are unlikely to match the town’s annual jobs fair earlier this year, when more than 4,000 jobseekers lined the promenade.

One local official described the enormous turnout in February as a “sad indictment” of the British economy. Of the 2,000 jobs on offer, 1,200 were given out on the spot.

The huge demand for work makes life more difficult for teenagers such as Butterworth, who say they are constantly told by employers they need more experience but find few willing to take a chance on them.

Describing this vicious circle, she said: “You need to get a job, but to have a job you need some experience. And you can’t get experience if no one’s employing you.”

The lucky ones find seasonal work cleaning hotels or serving up chips to day-trippers. But the lack of year-round jobs means competition is extremely high, with some employers receiving 200 applications for every vacancy.

Companies have started using AI to sift through CVs, putting applicants at the mercy of algorithmic bias. Less scrupulous firms use “postcode screening”, effectively blocking applicants from some parts of Blackpool, according to a report by the Social Mobility Commission in September – a practice Chris Webb, the Labour MP for Blackpool South, described as “abhorrent”.

Since finishing her art diploma at Blackpool and the Fylde College, Butterworth has lost count of the amount of job applications she has submitted. Despite volunteering at a local primary school, she has had no end of knockbacks.

“It really knocked my confidence a lot and I felt really disadvantaged, because nearly everyone I knew had got their first job because they knew someone,” she said.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

Butterworth is bright, articulate, hard-working and full of character, with a cuttingly dry sense of humour. But in school she struggled with concentration. Her autism was only diagnosed in February after a years-long wait.

The Covid pandemic, which struck when Butterworth was in her second year of secondary school, left her marginalised. Her mother had just finished cancer treatment and was classed as highly vulnerable, so teachers put Butterworth “behind a wall on a desk on my own”.

“It was very isolating,” she said. “It made me very socially anxious, which definitely didn’t help when I was originally trying to find a job.”

Blackpool has one of England’s highest school exclusion and absence rates, and one of the lowest levels of attainment for GCSEs. Experts say both are a result of the challenging backgrounds of many of the town’s children, as well as mental or neurological conditions that often go unsupported.

Last November, headteachers started adopting less punitive measures to try to keep more children in class. The number of pupils excluded or suspended has since fallen by 33% and 29% respectively, according to Blackpool council.

Local leaders are working to reverse the town’s position as England’s Neet capital. A brightly coloured youth skills hub called the Platform gives 16- to 24-year-olds personalised support with writing CVs, training, doing interviews and securing work or volunteering.

Kath Benson, a Labour councillor who is the council executive’s member for young people, said: “There’s a massive perception about young people that they just want to stay in bed and play on their phones. I know that’s not the case. In Blackpool, they’re queueing up for jobs.”

The Platform was launched in 2022 with £5m of funding from the UK’s shared prosperity fund, which replaced EU money previously given to disadvantaged areas. Since then, it has supported more than 2,350 young people into learning, training or work, according to the council.

Butterworth was one of those it helped, finding her training to work behind a bar while she tries to establish a career as a tattooist. She pulled her first pint last month at Abingdon Street Market, a trendy food-and-booze hall, and is hoping to start an apprenticeship at a tattoo parlour where she showed off her artwork.

Things are now starting to look up, she said: “I just feel very grateful that I was in a situation for once where I actually know someone that can give me an ‘in’ somewhere.”

‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:38:57 GMT

The US, Mexico and Bolivia this week joined the unenviable club of nations that have lost their measles-free status

Deaths caused by measles are not peaceful. In his hospital in Uganda, Dr Eric Wobudeya treats young infants after the virus has attacked their lungs and airways, or triggered pneumonia.

“These are children who are dying, and they are struggling for oxygen,” he said.

Around the world, children are facing the consequences of low or falling measles vaccination rates.

This week, international health officials announced an alarming development: that the US, Mexico and Bolivia had lost their measles-free status. They joined the unenviable club of nations that once had the deadly infection under control, but have seen it return – including earlier this year the UK, Canada, Austria, Armenia, Spain, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Countries lose measles elimination status if the same strain of the disease has spread within their borders uninterrupted for over a year.

It is a trend driven by factors including misinformation, disruption to services during the Covid pandemic, and even the immunisation successes of previous decades that mean people have forgotten how dangerous measles can be. Aid cuts from wealthy countries including the US and UK are likely to exacerbate the situation in poorer countries, experts fear.

The frustration among health advocates is palpable. “We are seeing measles cases in places where the disease was under control, and children are paying the price,” said the Unicef executive director, Catherine Russell. “We have a measles vaccine that protects children and has saved nearly 59 million lives since 2000. We should not be losing ground to this preventable disease.”

Measles infection weakens a child’s immune system, leaving them more vulnerable to other infections for months or years, particularly if they are malnourished. It can cause brain damage, hearing loss or blindness. In 2024, according to World Health Organization figures, an estimated 11 million people caught measles – most of them under five – and 95,000 died.

The virus is extremely contagious, lingering in the air for up to two hours; up to 90% of unprotected people exposed to measles will catch it. There are fears it is the canary in the coalmine for the resurgence of other vaccine-preventable diseases.

Wobudeya, a senior consultant paediatrician at Mulago national referral hospital in Kampala, says measles disappeared from his hospital for a time.

Speaking at the Union World Conference on Lung Health, held in Brazil this week, he said: “Until 2023, we were not seeing measles, for a period of about maybe 10 years. We had a whole [measles] ward – that ward went dry, and actually it was translated into another ward.

“But in the last three or four years, measles came back. What causes measles to come back, is basically failure to vaccinate.”

Global measles vaccination rates have stalled below the 95% threshold needed to create herd immunity and prevent outbreaks of the virus. In 2025, 84% of eligible children received a first dose of vaccine against measles, dropping to 77% for the second dose.

The news from the Americas is not only bad for the countries involved. A measles outbreak anywhere can spread to other countries through travel, experts warned. While the risk is lower in countries with relatively high levels of vaccine uptake, almost everywhere will have vulnerable pockets. In Hackney in east London, for example, only 58% of five-year-olds starting school in 2025 had received two doses of the MMR vaccine.

Some children cannot be vaccinated because their immune system is somehow compromised, for example by blood cancer. Others are too young for routine vaccination. They rely on high vaccination coverage in the wider population to reduce their risk.

Their parents may face difficult decisions, said Dr Boghuma Titanji, an assistant professor of medicine at Emory University in Atlanta, US. “How do you keep these children safe in shared spaces like public transportation, daycares, schools, or just navigating the world at large? Do you keep them indoors, have them wear masks all the time, or live in perpetual fear of an infection that could be life-changing for your child?”

In the US, the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has spread anti-vaccine messages, including questioning whether the MMR vaccine – which protects against measles, mumps and rubella – causes autism. The myth of a link between the jab and autism was first spread by the British doctor Andrew Wakefield in a paper in 1998. He was struck off the medical register over the discredited research.

“The US has historically been a public health leader and pacesetter for health interventions globally. I worry that the prevailing anti-vaccine narratives, which have contributed to declining vaccination rates and the resurgence of measles in the US, risk being exported to other countries as well,” said Titanji – potentially hitting “vaccine confidence, acceptance, and uptake” in those countries.

But the anti-vaccination movement is not the sole driver of declining vaccination levels, said Prof Alex Richter, an immunology expert at the University of Birmingham.

“We also need to consider the lack of positive messaging about the benefits of vaccination and the fact that many people no longer remember how serious diseases such as measles can be,” she said. “When people rarely encounter a disease, it becomes easier to underestimate the risks it poses.”

Practical barriers such as “difficulties booking or attending appointments, language barriers, unstable housing and challenges accessing healthcare” should not be overlooked, she added. “If we want to reverse this trend, we need to address both vaccine confidence and vaccine access.”

Simple systems such as offering out-of-hours appointments or sending reminders have been shown to boost uptake.

Many parts of the world have never been free of measles. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is dealing with the virus at the same time as authorities try to tackle an Ebola outbreak. In Bangladesh, a measles outbreak is raging, with almost 240,000 suspected cases and 1,282 deaths since March.

“I see cases surge when poverty levels are high and food security is low. And these conditions increase the risk for children to develop severe complications,” said Dr Duot Kezekiah, a general surgeon at Kuajok state hospital in South Sudan.

In countries like his, with struggling health systems, a lack of laboratory facilities means the virus may go unidentified for too long, the extensive support needed for a patient be unavailable, and the isolation that is needed to protect other patients is impossible.

Dr Ben Kasstan-Dabush, an assistant professor of global health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said the Covid-19 pandemic had disrupted routine vaccination programmes around the world “and brought a need for intense catch-up and resources to identify and invite children who remained undervaccinated”.

He said efforts to increase vaccination coverage could be hit by “major cuts to funding for global health and development from the US, and particularly the UK”.

But losses in measles elimination status can be reversed. And even in some of the hardest places to reach, new children are getting their jabs. Since 2022, the Reach consortium, led by the International Rescue Committee, has negotiated with governments and de facto authorities to vaccinate more than 1 million children in Chad, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia, living in areas that had been closed off to humanitarian teams.

“We cannot afford to be complacent. We need to make it easier for people to get vaccinated, challenge misinformation wherever it arises, and remind the public why vaccination matters,” said Dr David Hughes, a senior lecturer in the school of biology at the University of St Andrews. “Protecting against measles is a collective responsibility (being vaccinated yourself protects your family, friends and strangers we commute with), and we must act to prevent a disease we know how to control from becoming a serious threat again.”

Friday night will be ‘coldest of the autumn so far’, UK forecasters say

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:18:00 GMT

Lows will be ‘severe’ in the north, down to -9C, with some sub-zero temperatures farther south

Friday night will be the coldest night of the autumn so far, forecasters have said, surpassing the previous chilliest: Thursday.

A low of -8.4C was recorded at Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands overnight, according to the Met Office. Sub-zero temperatures were also recorded in Northern Ireland. More southerly areas stayed substantially warmer overnight on Thursday.

The Met Office said frost and rain, particularly present across northern parts of the UK in the morning, are largely expected to ease through the day on Friday, with some sunshine. But the frost will return fairly quickly as the sun sets, before another cold night.

“It will turn a lot colder as we head through into the weekend,” said meteorologist Clare Nasir.

“Through this evening and overnight, any residual spits and spots of rain will tend to clear as we see starry skies evolve and that frost extends southwards through the night.

“It will be severe in the north, so we could see temperatures as low as around -8C, -9C in one or two glens. And, farther south, we’re expecting some sub-zero temperatures. A cold end tonight, even some freeze and fog patches, particularly across central, southern areas and in Northern Ireland.”

For most, Saturday is forecast to be dry with some sunshine. It follows the first snow warning of the season, with more than an inch recorded in parts of northern England on Tuesday.

A yellow cold health alert is in force for the north-west, the north-east and Yorkshire and the Humber until 9am on Monday. The alerts mean weather conditions could result in an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, according to the UK Health Security Agency. Yellow alerts indicate a moderate likelihood and level of impact.

Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:11:02 GMT

After a humiliating NBA finals defeat, the 22-year-old has returned with a vengeance – and the Spurs look like contenders again

It wouldn’t be exactly right to say Victor Wembanyama didn’t miss a beat after a disastrous NBA finals in June that left him and his San Antonio Spurs defeated, memed and embarrassed. In the Spurs’ first game this season, against an Oklahoma City Thunder team since decimated by injuries, Wemby went an appalling 1-for-13 from the field. Ten of his 12 points came via free throws. After getting blocked by Aday Mara, he leaned over his knees and muttered furiously to himself as if trying to exorcise an intrusive thought. It brought to mind an image from the NBA finals a few months earlier: Wemby on the floor after being fouled by the Knicks’ Mitchell Robinson, crowing, “I’m in your head!” The Spurs went on to blow a 29-point lead, lose the game and the finals. Now Wemby seemed too preoccupied with the issues within his own dome to worry about wreaking havoc in anybody else’s.

Game two saw Wembanyama elect to lay the ball up instead of dunking it in the dying seconds of a close tilt with the Houston Rockets, which the springy Amen Thompson blocked spectacularly. Not a great start, and in a league whose narratives calcify long before sample sizes reach an adequate scale, it allowed for whispers that the Spurs were in trouble. But you could say Wembanyama has not missed a beat since then. After beginning the season 0-2, the Spurs are now 13-3, with 12 of those wins coming in a row before a loss to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday.

San Antonio’s basketball hasn’t been as seamless as those numbers suggest – the starting lineup includes three guards, leaving the offense a bit clunky and wanting for three-point shooting. It also includes Wembanyama, which papers over pretty much every possible problem.

Unofficially crowned the best player in the world during last season’s playoffs, Wembanyama has since distanced his closest challengers for that honor. Somebody has stolen Nikola Jokić’s three-point shot and hidden it in a deep hole, signaling what may prove to be the start of his decline after six consecutive imperious, MVP-caliber seasons. Meanwhile, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander’s efficiency has inevitably suffered as he’s tasked with keeping the injury-ridden Thunder afloat.

Wembanyama, meanwhile, has got better, averaging 28.6 points, 11.9 rebounds and countless plays in which his mere presence causes the opposing offense to spontaneously combust through the first 16 games of the season. The Lakers’ Luka Dončić is playing the best basketball of his career this season, averaging gaudy offensive numbers that, if sustained, would represent the most dominant scoring season in modern NBA history. That Dončić is not the runaway early favorite for MVP is solely because of Wembanyama’s two-way excellence.

Wembanyama’s unprecedented impact on the game of basketball is already well-documented, though the man is only 22. He is at once a void and a force field on defense, vacuuming up plenty of shots with his inflatable-man arms and deterring others simply by standing in the paint. Before the Pistons beat the Spurs on Tuesday, their players warmed up by shooting over teammates who held long foam blocks over their heads, practicing shots with sufficiently steep arcs to escape Wemby’s treacherous fingertips, trying to learn how to play the game on a vertical axis.

Wembanyama racked up plenty of offensive highlights during last year’s playoffs – a half-court buzzer-beater, a logo three-pointer to tie a vital game in the final minute when the rest of the team had gone cold – but his defensive foundation and paint presence are so strong that any three-pointers he can generate are a bonus.

Wembanyama was maligned during the finals for the lack of a “go-to move”, which clogged up the Spurs’ offense as the Knicks erased double-digit deficits late in games as if they were playing a G League team. The Spurs’ game against the Pistons offered a clue to what he’s developing: twice in the first half, Wembanyama threw the ball off the backboard, to himself, so he could collect it and dunk as everybody else watched from the floor. A player this physically anomalous and versatile will eventually have a bag so deep nobody will be able to see the bottom.

Despite Wembanyama’s visually obvious gifts, there are still times when the magnitude of their manifestation on a game is shocking. In a blowout against the Sacramento Kings, he needed only 25 minutes to rack up 40 points, 11 rebounds and eight blocks. In a close game against the Dallas Mavericks, he produced 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks in 34 minutes. On one possession, he blocked three consecutive Mavericks shots, an entire defense unto himself. The Spurs won the game by one point; during Wembanyama’s minutes, they outscored the Mavs by 23. “I haven’t been feeling great lately,” Wembanyama said after the game. “I’m sick. I felt like I got my legs back. So, it should be more like this more often.” Well then.

Even what felt like a fairly quiet Wembanyama performance against the Los Angeles Clippers on Thursday night (he only recorded one block, just before the end of the third quarter) dictated the shape of the game. The numbers are one thing – 32 points, 11 rebounds, no biggie – and watching him is another. He threw down fierce alley-oop dunks. He galloped through the paint, an Ent trampling helpless orcs, for easy floaters. Late in the fourth quarter, he juggled the ball to himself above the basket, reminiscent of a child batting a balloon across a room at a birthday party, before tapping it into the basket.

He found himself with so much space on one play that he rose as if to dunk the ball and dropped it gently through the net instead, flicking his wrist as if he’d just shot a three. On one of those jammed-up Spurs offensive possessions, the Clippers’ Isaiah Jackson was guarding Wembanyama tightly as the shot clock wound down. Wemby took a long two-pointer with Jackson’s hand in his face, a bizarre shot created from thin air, and drained it.

Wembanyama’s highlights won’t get old until 7ft 4in generational talents become commonplace, but equally impressive at this point in his career is his maturity. The finals last season were a nightmare on a few fronts: he enabled a legion of detractors with overly violent fouls and dubious flops, then validated their harshest critiques by underperforming in vital games. It’d be enough to ruin plenty of mortals. Wembanyama has emerged from the adversity intact and evolved, keeping the Spurs firmly on track for a shot at redemption.

Digested week: Pity the touring royals – and the hacks made to schlep around after them

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:47:53 GMT

It’s a hard life for the Prince and Princess of Wales, but spare a thought too for jailed Bankman-Fried and the overlooked 007s

All eyes on China ahead of the trilateral summit this week, but it’s India and the three-day royal tour by the Prince and Princess of Wales that catches my eye. The couple arrive in Mumbai and as a steady stream of photos emanates from their back-to-back schedule, the usual question surfaces: how on earth do they stand it?

In my case, the bafflement comes from direct experience of being on a royal tour many years ago, when, alongside a busload of other hacks, I schlepped to Islamabad in Pakistan after Charles and Camilla. This was my first experience of a royal itinerary and it was like being transported into a comic novel from the 1930s.

Traipsing after the royal couple, we visited a university, a temple, a showcase by local artisans and dancers, 2,000-year-old ruins and – after a long drive into Kashmir on terrible roads – a donkey sanctuary where the hack from the Sun had a panic attack and had to be airlifted out via helicopter.

At every stop, royal snappers yelled over one another – “Oi, fatty! Get out the way!” – while the rest of us assumed various positions of sardonic obeisance and wondered what our lives had come to. In one location, we were made to stand in a ditch so the royals didn’t have to look at us.

It would have been much the same in India this week, where the younger royals faced a gauntlet of bum- and mind-numbing events at which, judging by the photos, they appeared as frozen as salt and pepper shakers. I felt sorry for them, but not as sorry as I felt for the hacks (not shown).

All those years ago in Pakistan, Charles and Camilla met President Musharraf, a meeting at which a single British hack was allowed to be present, before returning with the following morsels for us: type of nuts on the table (cashews); flowers in the vase (gladioli and yellow roses); decor (chintz); and some banging quotes. Camilla, our colleague faithfully reported, said: “We’re quite far north here”, to which Mrs Musharraf replied: “Yes, we’re in the foothills of the Himalayas.” What a world.

I have no strong feelings about Robert Pattinson as James Bond, which feels like a dereliction of duty. Luckily, lots of others have brisk thoughts. Defenders of the decision noted Pattinson’s mould-breaking, alternative vibe and assured us he would be a more interesting Bond than the cookie-cutter alternatives. Critics of the choice made the case that Pattinson is already too famous and that, historically speaking, the whole point of Bond is that the brand is the star, into which only an unknown actor can truly grow.

If Pattinson is, indeed, the “interesting” choice, he is only interesting within narrow limitations. Idris Elba aged out of the Bond race, but one notes that only white actors were mentioned in the shortlist. As an actor, Josh O’Connor is less conventional than Pattinson, but reportedly exempted himself from the race after becoming the favourite.

Meanwhile, the actor I wanted for Bond – and I know this makes no sense because he’s already been in a Bond movie – was Ben Whishaw, whose turn as a hitman in Black Doves, currently winning its second season on Netflix, is the best performance on TV at the moment by far. A gay Bond? Now that would’ve been interesting.

Elon Musk’s mea culpa, delivered at the DealBook summit in New York, is an absolute study in watching an apparently clever man achieve an understanding the rest of the world tends to arrive at soon after exiting childhood – namely that other people are as real as he is.

Asked about his extraordinary, almost $500m investment in the US midterm elections, Musk, affecting a slight stammer, tried to shrug the whole thing off as no biggie, a “foolish” mistake, and to suggest that, far from trying to cement Donald Trump’s supremacy in the White House, he was actually hellbent on preventing a Democratic super majority, owing to his concern for “checks and balances”.

Sinking ships don’t always provide easy escape routes, and for Musk this was a hard one to pull off. “Ideologically I think I’m quite moderate,” he said, struggling to get the words out around his too-large veneers, and “I don’t think I have any extreme political views.” This wasn’t the impression he gave when he was waving around a chainsaw on stage or eviscerating thousands of jobs at Doge.

“American elections are not just about money,” said the guy who thought he could buy them, and one hopes he learns a valuable lesson from this (he won’t). Turns out the little people have interests, concerns and convictions, too.

If that’s not enough schadenfreude for one week, turn your thoughts to Sam Bankman-Fried, the jailed former crypto-king who would have made almost $40bn from the public offering of Anthropic but, sadly, is still in federal prison serving a 25-year sentence for fraud.

Bankman-Fried, who was an early believer in Anthropic when it was just an obscure AI company with no apparent prospects, invested $500m in the company in 2021 via Alameda Research, the investment wing of his crypto company. Cut to five years later and the launch of its IPO this week, where at one point, the company’s value hit $2.1tn on the Nasdaq, before closing at $1.3tn – still the biggest in history.

Bankman-Fried lost all his shares in the company after his bankruptcy ruling, which sold them off for a mere $1.4bn to settle his debts. Talking to the New York Times from jail, he said: “There’s no point in obsessing over regrets. But it’s certainly something that I’ve spent, despite that, a fair bit of time thinking through.” If you’re sad at missing out on the gold rush, at least you don’t have 23 more years in a cell to brood on your lost $40bn.

Let’s end the week with an image to cheer the soul: that of Kim Jong-un (below), the supreme leader of North Korea, parked like a king from a children’s book on a velvet throne dragged on to a ski slope near the North Korean border with China. What an icon: knees apart, cigarette dangling from one hand, aviators locked – all he needed was a gold crown askew on his head to complete the picture of a man in the prime of his rackety reign. But in any case, the little leader who could knew just how to drag eyeballs away from the big boys in Shenzhen. Bravo!

‘I went to bed … then Dad called to say Mum was convulsing’ - This is climate breakdown

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:00:18 GMT

Location: Besançon, France

Disaster: European heatwaves, 2026

This is Anne-Sophie Woronoff’s story

Colette Woronoff was one of at least 50,000 people killed by this year’s ferociously hot summer, a modelling study of 854 European cities found last month. The scientists said two in every three of the heat-related deaths resulted from additional warming due to fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature.

My mother, Colette, was 92 years old, and up until the end I made the most of my time with her. She was a wonderful woman – extremely cheerful, very feminist, very free. She loved art and travel. She adored churches, particularly baroque ones. She always took a small sketchbook with her on trips.

When we went to bury her ashes in her ancestral village in Ardèche last month, it was difficult, but we were surrounded by love, sharing it with family. I maintain that people get what they give. And she got a lot of love that weekend, because she gave a lot too. But it’s the cause of her death that is still difficult to accept.

Since Thursday 25 June 2026, I had been telling myself to bring my parents extra fans to deal with the heat. It was hot everywhere in France, and I was working a lot that week. My sister told me she was going to their place on Saturday, when I would be at a wedding, and I said to myself, perfect. My sister went to see my parents, who seemed well. I came home from the wedding and went to bed.

But at one in the morning my father rang to say my mother had fallen and was convulsing. I immediately called the emergency services. I explained how to get there, told my father to open the door, and left. In 10 minutes, they were in the apartment. I arrived 10 minutes later and the emergency doctor told me my mother had severe hyperthermia, with a temperature of 42.6C. He said: “You know, it’s fatal.” At the time, Mum was calm. She was more or less conscious, and I know she saw me, but it was difficult. There were seven people around her. She opened her eyes but couldn’t talk.

I waited with my father as they took her to hospital. I put myself in her room, in her bed, and realised the heat was just unbearable. Two hours later, the doctors called me and said: “You have to come very quickly.” I arrived with one of my sisters and we thought it was the end. But our mother woke up and smiled at us. There had been a big improvement. They had given her ice baths and the temperature had dropped a lot. Yet the doctor explained that the cells, once they have seen this heat, cannot regenerate. The heart, the liver, the lungs, the brain – everything had been damaged.

My parents met when they were 14, at the Alsatian school in Paris. My mother became an English teacher and my father a teacher of ancient languages. They worked in small towns in France and then had the opportunity to leave for Senegal in 1964, where they stayed until 1979. My older sisters gradually came back to France to do their studies, and Mum didn’t want to stay in Dakar without her daughters, so they moved to Besançon. They had a house in a nice, isolated village, which they liked a lot, but it was not suitable for their mobility, and just under two years ago I found them an apartment to rent. I was about 20 minutes away by car, one of my sisters was about 15 minutes away, and another was about 10 minutes away. With the tram beside her house, my mother could go to her hairdresser in five minutes – something she did every week – and across the street was a market where she liked to buy fresh fruit and vegetables. She walked with a cane but had few other health problems, and was still autonomous for many things.

The image that struck me from that night was when I arrived in the two-person apartment and saw seven people around my mother. I was aware it was going to be serious, but I didn’t realise right away. There were so many people because my parents live on the seventh floor, and although there is an elevator, it was too small for the gurney. They had to carry her down on the stretcher and it took at least four people to do it. When everyone left, my mother’s room was like a construction site. There were things everywhere: items from the first responders, pieces of plastic, bath towels they had wetted to cool her down, everything icy they found in the freezer. My father, who is more fragile than my mother, was completely stupefied. He didn’t understand what was going on. Even today, he still says, “you realise, it’s the heat that took her away”. He spent weeks and weeks asking: “But why did she die like that? It’s not possible.”

Besançon was one of the regions that was particularly affected by the heat, since in eastern France we are not used to having temperatures this high for such a long time. There was no air conditioning in the apartment, but you could open windows on each side to create a cross-breeze. The problem is that for older people the cognitive side is often not completely there, and that night she opened the windows but not the shutters. I repeated to her: “You have to drink, take showers,” and every time she would say yes. I thought she was doing it, but in fact she wasn’t. What’s more, we had no other solutions. In each of our own homes, the rooms where we could have put our parents had stairs they couldn’t go up.

It’s difficult to accept how she died. Even for me, as a research doctor, I hadn’t seen anything coming. We knew elderly people living alone had been found dead in their apartments during heatwaves. But we thought this apartment wasn’t that bad, and there were people passing by every day. Care assistants came every other day for my father, a physiotherapist came twice a week, nurses for my mother twice a week, and my sister went that Saturday to bring them fans. When there is a heatwave, we are told to make vulnerable people drink and put them in the coolest places possible. But when do we say to take their temperature with a thermometer?

After my mother went to hospital on Sunday morning, the luck we had was that we could stay with her until Wednesday. She wasn’t very conscious but she had two or three moments of lucidity. We were in a room where we had the right to come at night, during the day, as many as we wanted, so she was able to see all her family and grandchildren, and that allowed us to say goodbye to her, to be with her when she let go of her last breath. It was less terrible than if she had left on Saturday night, just like that, without us being able to talk to her again.

Afterwards, it was strange. We had to find a funeral home to take care of the body but there were so many dead people that it was hard to find a place. We felt like we were back in Covid. The big companies were really very, very, very full. But we were lucky to find a small family company – the only one to have answered me – with free chambers. After the cremation, we had a few months that still felt like we were in transition, until we buried the ashes in October. Now, we know she won’t move any more. She’s in a place she loves, she’s next to her parents. My father tells us he wants the same thing – that he wants to be next to her.

Sandpaper and silence: Marsh hides away as England’s T20 winners roll into MCG

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:30:31 GMT

Amid an increasingly febrile atmosphere in Australia, the Twenty20 captain is not expected at any press conferences

After a toe-curling, stonewalling press conference before the recent one-day series against England, Australia’s usually happy-go-lucky T20 captain, Mitch Marsh, opted out of a repeat before the Twenty20s that start here on Saturday.

In his place came Victoria’s Sam Harper to talk about his looming debut at the MCG. A nice local angle, for sure, with the 29-year-old wicketkeeper having overcome some troubling concussions in the past. But also a touch optimistic if intended to switch the focus in Australia away from the sandpaper skip fire.

As per reports this week, Marsh nearly pulled out of the third ODI in Hobart in anticipation of Cameron Bancroft, his Western Australia teammate, delivering that incendiary 4,000-word statement. In the end he played, pulling off a dazzling catch but then nicking off early during the series-deciding 97-run defeat.

Marsh gets a couple of mentions in Bancroft’s detailed account of events eight years ago, as one of the four seamers offering him feedback when sandpaper was first being trialled during the second Test in Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha). When it helped produce a burst of four for 28 before stumps on the second day, Marsh claimed two of them. According to Bancroft, he was “joking about how much the ball was swinging and how he never used to swing it like that”.

None of which is damning for Marsh, the only current squad member with links to that ill-fated tour. The 35-year-old did not sign the bowlers’ statement in 2021 that denied knowledge of sandpaper use in Cape Town – a denial that Bancroft says he “struggled to reconcile … with my memories”.

Although as Bancroft carefully noted more broadly in that statement: “There is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used.”

Amid an increasingly febrile atmosphere in the country, Marsh is not expected to attend any press conferences during this five-match T20 series. Any interviews during the live broadcast on Fox Cricket, such as at the toss or the post-match presentations, are likely to stick to the cricket at hand.

England are back here in March for the 150th anniversary Test match, by which time Cricket Australia will pray the storm has passed. Given the scale of the occasion – the first three days already sold out, around 250 past and current players coming, and the hope of a royal attendee – the alternative would be a nightmare.

This was a point made by Greg Chappell in his column for the Nine newspapers on Friday, with the former Australia captain suggesting an independent inquiry be set up. Pat Cummins should not be sacked from his Test role, he added, unless there is compelling evidence he knew sandpaper was being used.

“The mistake of 2018 was punishing people before the facts were known, and I don’t want to see it repeated,” wrote Chappell. “Believing others knew isn’t the same as proving it. No man should lose his job based on a disputed account, no matter which side it comes from.”

For now, at the scene of last year’s solitary win during the Ashes, it is Twenty20 cricket that awaits England. On arrival for training at the MCG on Friday, Sam Curran was apparently quick to remind his teammates that Australia’s mighty coliseum is where Jos Buttler’s class of 2022 lifted the T20 World Cup.

I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:13:21 GMT

Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique

Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way.

I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me.

Since Gisèle Pelicot stepped out of the shadows and waived her right to anonymity, the depraved crime of drug-facilitated sexual abuse has become stamped into the public’s consciousness – rightly provoking outrage and an outpouring of support for survivors.

My experience, some two years before Pelicot’s trial, was different. There was just one single perpetrator, my husband.

I have no idea how many times it happened, nor do I wish to know, but for years he had been crushing sleeping pills into the cup of tea he made for me every night, then waiting for me to lose consciousness before raping me, often taking photographs and filming himself in the act.

There was no outpouring of support when I finally reported the crime. Quite the opposite, in fact. I was ostracised and publicly accused of destroying the reputation of this upstanding pillar of the community. This continued, inexplicably, even after his conviction.

The police were brilliant. The CPS less so. I had to fight to press charges when, after 18 months, it announced it was not going to, even though he had admitted his guilt to medical professionals. I felt as though I was the one on trial rather than him, and the verdict was already in. How could it be true? How could I not have known?

In truth I didn’t, but in hindsight the warning signs had been there: recurrent and unexplained bouts of thrush and urinary tract infections, worsening migraines, and just the nagging feeling that something in my body wasn’t quite right.

The reality was so unimaginable that even when he sat me down and told me what he had been doing, one day after church, it was as though my brain couldn’t process what he was saying. It was months before I told my sister and mum, who gently persuaded me to talk to the police, and it was only then I started to see that what he had been doing – each act – was a crime. A violation of my body, trust and everything I had believed to be true.

It is only recently that I’ve been able to bring myself to call it what it was – rape – and understand (something many survivors struggle with) that just because I can’t remember it, doesn’t mean it didn’t happen. Just because it was my husband doesn’t mean it didn’t count.

I don’t think this type of crime is becoming more common, I think the reporting of it is. The drugs used might be more sophisticated, so, too, the means by which perpetrators communicate with each other and share images and video. The crime, however, has always been there behind closed doors.

Prior to the Pelicot case, this kind of crime was virtually unheard of. What Pelicot did was open the door for people to think that a man could do that to his wife. She created a space in which people could ask questions and could stand up and say, “This has happened to me as well.”

What none of us could have anticipated is the scale. Through #EndEyeCheck, the campaign publicly launched in May this year by fellow survivor-advocate Amanda Stanhope and me, we now know that this has happened and is still happening to hundreds of women around the world – and that doesn’t include those who haven’t yet had that realisation or don’t deem it rape.

The campaign name comes from a term I was blissfully unaware of before all this happened – used to describe the moment an abuser pulls back or lifts the eyelid of their victim to check they are fully unconscious before sexually assaulting them.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Stories such as ours shine a light on this crime, but that is not enough and nor are the sentences handed down. My ex was given 11 years, and I’ll be lucky if he serves the same length of time in prison that his offences span. The government must act now to protect victims.

There needs to be earlier, more effective education around consent, starting in schools, so there can be no confusion and no blurring of boundaries over what is and isn’t allowed. I remember hearing teenage boys on the bus discussing CNC (consensual non-consent) porn and thinking, “Do they even know what it stands for or what it means?”

The platforms, mainstream porn sites among them, that are hosting this almost innocent-sounding “sleep content” must be held to account. It is not innocent – it is perpetuating the idea that consent is not obligatory.

The medical profession and the police also need to be alive to the signs of this type of abuse because the chances are the victims haven’t yet realised what is happening to them and may not, without informed support.

Like many, Pelicot inspired me and played a huge part in the decision to waive my anonymity. It’s not for everyone, but in a strange kind of way it helped me to heal and imagine a future that, at one point, seemed impossible.

It is a complex problem and there is no easy answer, but at least now the conversation has started – and there is a place for women to go for help and to know they are not alone.

Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html
