Men’s tennis boosts prize money for players to more than $350m in major overhaul

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:36:02 GMT

Cash increase via ATP’s creation of ‘One Vision’ company

More rest breaks added to reduce player welfare issues

The Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) has approved major changes to the financial structure of men’s tennis that will make the total prize money available to the players increase to more than $350m (£267m) by 2028, from $270m this year.

The creation of a new company to sell all the tour’s media, commercial and data rights, ATP Ventures, will lead to the investment of an additional $100m in player remuneration including an increased $50m bonus pool, a $25m year-end rankings bonus and $26m player pensions.

The launch of ATP Ventures comes after the breakdown of attempts to set up a joint commercial venture with the Women’s Tennis Association, as revealed by the Guardian in July, but the ATP remains hopeful that those negotiations can be revived.

While the ATP board has opted to defer other major decisions, including finer details of the 2028 ­calendar and a controversial proposal to halve the size of doubles events and cut their share of prize money from 20% to 10%, the changes represent a significant attempt to protect the value of the Masters 1000 events in particular, after Carlos Alcaraz, Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovic all missed this year’s Canadian Open due to injury.

Payments from the $50m player bonus pool, up from $21m this year, will be linked to performances at the Masters 1000 events rather than their end-of-season rankings, with the world No 1 eligible to receive $2m for each of the bigger tournaments they play.

Leon Smith will step down from his role as Great Britain’s Davis Cup captain at the end of this month after 16 years in the position. Great Britain's appearance in the Davis Cup Finals next week will mark his final competition.

Smith has enjoyed one of the longest tenures as a Davis Cup captain in the sport's history and the longest by a British Davis Cup captain. The highlight of his term was Great Britain's historic Davis Cup triumph in 2015, a team also led by his childhood friend Andy Murray.

Smith said: “It has been an enormous privilege to lead the team for so many years, and I feel now is the right time, both for me personally and for the team moving forwards."

Smith had been considering his resignation for some months and the LTA has already started planning for his successor, with the new Davis Cup captain expected to be announced in the coming weeks. Smith will continue his role as the LTA's Head of Men's Tennis, which he took on at the same time that he became Davis Cup captain in 2010. Tumaini Carayol

Alcaraz, in particular, caused alarm by saying in September that he planned to skip more tournaments in future to protect his body, and the ATP has responded by removing the minimum threshold of five tournaments before players receive bonuses.

In another acknowledgment of the importance of player welfare the ATP has also pledged to introduce a clearer season structure, with more opportunity for rest breaks and a longer off-season, although the details have yet to be agreed.

The ATP’s executive chair, Andrea Gaudenzi, told the Guardian that the changes would lead to more of the top players focusing on the elite tournaments. “The new system enables them to focus on quality,” Gaudenzi, an Italian former pro, said. “So they don’t need to play as many tournaments. The rewards are more based on performance. The fact that now they’re going to get paid every Masters they play without any penalties is a big one. The top players are driving the value, and it’s fair to recognise that.”

The creation of ATP Ventures is phase one of Gaudenzi’s One Vision project, a bold attempt to unify a disjointed sport that has seven major stakeholders – the four grand slams, the ATP, the WTA and World Tennis.

Gaudenzi said positive conversations with the slams had taken place about creating one genuine global governing body, with the talks currently focused on creating a single player council after the slams announced plans to set up one of their own at the US Open in August.

“As long as I’m here I will never give up on One Vision,” Gaudenzi said. “I’m not saying I’m going to be able to get it done, and it’s a matter of time, but it’s the right thing to do. I’ve had enough positive feedback from all the stakeholders that they also believe it’s the right thing to do.”

Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:00:29 GMT

The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric

Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black.

“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.”

When it comes to addressing issues outside sport, Hamilton has never been one to hold his tongue. His willingness to keep stating his beliefs plainly, and the principles he has consistently stood up for, set him apart from US sports stars, many of whom have toned down progressive rhetoric considerably during Donald Trump’s second term. The contrast won’t be lost on Hamilton’s legion of American fans as Formula One returns to the US this weekend for the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Hamilton, a seven-time world champion and the only Black driver in Formula One history, occupies a singular position in sport. Unlike, say, Colin Kaepernick – who is nobody’s all-time sporting great, Super Bowl run aside – Hamilton made himself impossible to deny or ignore. And unlike, say, LeBron James – who once set the tone for athlete activism, but has since backpedaled from politics during Trump’s second term – Hamilton still welcomes all the smoke. As Formula One has exploded in popularity in the US over the past decade, Hamilton has remained its most US-facing ambassador. He is the Kardashian boyfriend as likely to turn up at the Met Gala as at a Denver Broncos game, not least because he’s a part-owner of the NFL team. Now he carries the flag as sport’s apex protester.

When US athletes staged silent protests during the national anthem before games, Hamilton was the one making sure Formula One couldn’t look away. During the 2020 and 2021 seasons, drivers gathered for a moment of silence in “End Racism” shirts before each race. Hamilton and four-time champion Sebastian Vettel were the most consistent kneelers. “There was never a second of doubt in my head [about kneeling], first and foremost out of respect for Lewis, and to support him, and the message,” Vettel said. “That’s why I was happy to kneel.”

Hamilton is quick to stick his neck out on US politics, putting the hammer down as readily as he does through Maggotts and Becketts. When Trump took aim at kneeling NFL players in 2017, Hamilton defended free expression. “I think it is open for anyone to have freedom of speech, and I guess we can all play a role in trying to make a difference in the world – particularly if your leader is not helping in that area,” he remarked. In 2020, Hamilton took aim at Trump’s leadership again, saying he “turned off the lights and hid in his bunker” during the unrest that followed the killing of George Floyd.

Hamilton’s influence extends beyond Formula One. Bubba Wallace, Nascar’s most prominent Black driver, has cited Hamilton as an inspiration in his own efforts to push his hidebound sport to confront racial inequality. In a 2025 interview with Time, Hamilton vowed to continue his diversity work even as organizations rolled back support amid Trump administration attacks on DEI. “I’m not going to change what [Trump] does or what the government does,” Hamilton said. “All I can do is try to make sure that in my space, in my environment, I’m trying to elevate people.”

Hamilton has taken a two-pronged approach. In 2020 he became a founding co-chair of the Hamilton Commission, an initiative designed to address Black underrepresentation in UK motorsport and Stem careers. Its 2021 report identified barriers ranging from school culture and university recruitment practices to workplace culture, and estimated that fewer than 1% of people working in Formula One came from Black backgrounds.

Drawing on the commission’s recommendations, Hamilton launched Mission 44 (taking its name from his racing number) to support underrepresented young people in their education and employment pursuits, not just those aspiring to careers in motorsport. He pledged £20m of his own money to get the project rolling. By 2026, seven Mission 44 scholarship recipients were working in motorsport – five of them at Formula One teams.

Behind the wheel, Hamilton has helped change the racial complexion of the grid by inspiring kids from similar backgrounds to dream big. Nineteen years after making history as Formula One’s first Black driver, Hamilton now shares the grid with French-Algerian Isack Hadjar, Thai-British Alex Albon and British-Indian Arvid Lindblad. It may not be much longer before he’s racing alongside Ugo Ugochukwu – the Black American who became Formula 3 champion in September and is reportedly slated to drive practice sessions for Cadillac in 2027. “It’s been amazing to see his rise through the class,” Hamilton said during the Spanish GP weekend. “Really exciting for next year.”

Bringing an Formula One race back to Africa for the first time since the 1990s has been one of Hamilton’s long-running ambitions, and last month’s announcement of the African Grand Prix in Rwanda marked the realization of that dream. Now 41, Hamilton is determined to be on the grid when the race makes its debut in the early 2030s. After the announcement, he expressed his excitement at racing in Rwanda and showing the country off to the world. But he also acknowledged the urgent human-rights concerns surrounding Rwanda, in keeping with his history of calling out Formula One for getting into bed with autocratic regimes.

Hamilton may have the stature to speak freely on matters inside and outside his sport, but that’s easier said than done in motorsport, where teams live and die on sponsorship money and drivers can lose their jobs for failing to bring in enough of it, regardless of how well they perform. Hamilton’s pro-Palestine stance isn’t just the kind of thing that could cost him financial backing; it threatens to make him more vulnerable at Ferrari, the circuit’s flagship franchise, where Hamilton and teammate Charles Leclerc are locked in a power struggle (much as they would have you believe otherwise), with free agency potentially looming for Hamilton again after the 2027 season.

Inevitably, there will be skeptics who dismiss Hamilton’s outspokenness as grandstanding from an athlete nearing the end of his career with not much to lose. But Hamilton has long made clear that his legacy means more to him than his place in the record books. “It’s great having these wins,” he said after a 2020 Eifel Grand Prix victory that drew him level in the all-time wins column with Michael Schumacher, still Hamilton’s best comparison. “But I think the more important things are what you do out of the car. That’s really where I think the impact can be made, in terms of wanting to be remembered.”

Hamilton continues to use his considerable platform to draw attention to the world’s injustices, even when doing so carries risks. In that respect, he offers a model for would-be athlete activists in the US – not just in what he says, but in his willingness to put his feet on the ground and stand 10 toes down.

The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:50:17 GMT

In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

These gestures may be ridiculed as “passports to Pimlico”, but they reflect a deadly and earnest predicament. An emergency Commons debate last month heard the immigration minister, Anna Turley, proclaim Piddington’s fate as “in the national interest”. It would help stop the need for asylum hotels in the middle of towns and cities at a cost rising to billions.

But shouldn’t these villagers have a say? In the planning policy framework introduced by David Cameron’s government in 2012, communities were invited to prepare “neighbourhood development plans”. But from day one, central government treated these as mere wishlists. Delivery targets were progressively introduced that overruled local planning control, none more radical than Labour’s “growth targets” in 2024.

Prime ministers of both parties have drawn up housebuilding targets for every English locality. Councils, it was suggested, should disregard labels such as green belts or areas of outstanding natural beauty when planning where to build. This was despite independent surveys constantly protesting that the national target of 1.5m new homes could already be met within existing built-up areas, with two thirds of sites already with planning permissions. The reality is that private developers make more money building in the country – and the government is in thrall to them. The name of the game is profit.

Hence the imposition from government now witnessed in small towns and villages across England’s south and midlands. Last year, Moreton-in-Marsh in Gloucestershire was ordered to double in size. In a poll, 96% of local people protested, but to no avail. The town is now a gallery of housing horror, encased on all sides by bland private estates. No attempt has been made to build in a village style, let alone fuse estates with the rural landscape. All that matters is the number of houses. Southern England is seeing a repeat of the suburban sprawl over London’s home counties between the wars.

What is stark is the total impotence of local people to play any part in combating this assault. Soon after taking office, Keir Starmer was insulting villagers as “blockers and Nimbys”, as if defending one’s environment was a crime. Andy Burnham then upped the ante by removing powers to block rural development from local planning committees.

This disempowerment is inconceivable in other European countries. In France, Germany, Switzerland or Scandinavia, local communities enjoy sovereignty over their future. They call it democracy. France’s 35,000 communes build plenty of houses, but they grow organically, not by an invasion of “volume builders” whipped on by central government.

The status of small communities is not a quaint archaism. The English village is a valued social construct. Its institutions are the school, the church, the pub and the youth club. Its lifeblood is the high street. Such an informal cohesion of the neighbourhood came to life during the Covid-19 pandemic. It supplied mutual help in time of trouble. It was a salve to loneliness.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Rural parish councils need to be granted powers over their future like those enjoyed by similar communities abroad, notably in planning. But such councils are needed in cities, too. In 2007, Tony Blair’s government boldly attempted to extend parishes from rural to urban areas. Apart from one council created in London’s Queen’s Park, the attempt was snuffed out by Whitehall.

Everywhere should be a parish. The case is overwhelming for the liberation of the village and its inhabitants. Piddington has shown the way.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is published this month

Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 05:00:23 GMT

As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help

“I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”

Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.

As the Cop31 summit nears its close, with a scheduled finish of Friday but which is likely to push into the weekend, Pacific islanders are becoming increasingly frustrated with the UN’s decades-old system of annual climate summits.

The region has its own cash fund – the Pacific Resilience Facility – to pay for damages from climate-driven extremes and to prepare for the future.

The Australian government pledged US$67m (A$101m) three years ago, but the fund has otherwise struggled for support. It is still about US$300m (A$451m) short of a US$500m (A$751m) goal, and a “showcase” event at the summit with the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, garnered only one new offer – US$5m (A$7.5m) from Andrew Forrest, an Australian miner and philanthropist.

It is a far cry from what has been promised.

“Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word,” Ishoda says. “We have money for wars but not to save communities.”

Ishoda’s sleep has been interrupted by a related issue that is receiving more focus in the fortnight-long talks in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya: “overshoot”. In other words, how far and for how long the planet will experience global heating greater than 1.5C, a goal set in the 2015 Paris agreement.

Scientists confirmed months ago the 1.5C goal would be breached and that a temperature rise of 1.8C is the best the planet can hope for in the near term.

Tackling this overshoot and pushing for countries to transition away from fossil fuels are top priorities for the Pacific. But they fear the process in Turkey might fail them again.

The need to deal with fossil fuels was absent from a draft agreement released on Thursday by the Australian and Turkish ministers leading the negotiations after being included in a first draft on Monday. Critics have noted both countries have substantial fossil fuel interests.

Albanese told the summit’s opening last week that he was “proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family”.

But Pacific island nations have had an outsized influence on the UN climate process going back to before the first climate deal was agreed in Kyoto in 1997.

The chief executive of Climate Analytics, Bill Hare, a scientist who has been an adviser to island states at UN summits for decades, says “the planet owes them a lot.”

He says he watched Samoa influence talks that led to the Kyoto protocol, saw Pacific nations help rescue the process after talks nearly collapsed in Copenhagen in 2009, and watched the late Tony de Brum, a minister from the Marshall Islands, become a central player in landing the Paris agreement.

“They have pushed the issue with courage, ambition, and integrity, over this whole period,” Hare says. “They’ve done it in the Pacific way, which has not been to yell and scream, but to make the point quietly, consistently, solidly, and with force.”

A key threat to the Pacific is sea-level rise, caused when warming oceans expand and as melting glaciers and ice sheets discharge more water from the land. A 2024 UN report pointed to Nasa research showing that Pacific islands experienced less than five flooding days a year in the 2010s, which is expected to increase five-fold by 2050. The research found that places including Tuvalu, Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, Micronesia and the Cook Islands could have more than 50 days of flooding every year.

after newsletter promotion

Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, says the scale of the threat means Cop31 must have “red lines”. If the final deal does not articulate the need to transition away from fossil fuels and agree that the 1.5C target has to be kept alive – even if it is temporarily overshot – then “this Cop will be a failure,” she says.

“If that’s the case we will need to find other ways to achieve this.”

Pacific nations are already looking outside the UN process to save themselves.

Next year Tuvalu will host the second conference of the Santa Marta process, which is trying to get countries to agree to a “just transition” away from fossil fuels.

And an idea that sprung from a Fiji classroom at the University of the South Pacific in 2019 continues to reverberate. Vishal Prasad was one of the students who wondered if, given the slow progress at climate summits, international law might be able to do more to help the Pacific.

“There is immense frustration with the process,” Prasad says.

He says the reason for the slow process is clear: the “interests of the fossil fuel industry”. Its lobbyists attend in large numbers and engage in “corporate capture” of the space, he says.

Prasad is backed by Vanuatu’s climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, a champion of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) case who, like other Pacific leaders, has bounced from room to room this week in Antalya. Regenvanu says the region’s nations are engaging in the talks “in good faith” but he finds “great hope” in the potential impact of the ICJ opinion and the dozens of countries who have pledged to work together on getting the world off fossil fuels.

The lead Pacific campaigner at Greenpeace, Shiva Gounden, says there remains a “sickening disconnect” between the negotiating rooms at Cop31 and the devastation facing Pacific communities.

But he says the Pacific will not be “passive victims” of the delays, which he blames on developed countries. “We will secure our survival, our justice, and our financing, whether developed countries find the moral courage to join us at this table, or we have to drag them there through the courts and alternative frameworks.”

As the Antalya talks head into their hectic and likely sleepless final days, there is a push for the ICJ opinion to be referenced in the global agreement at the end of the talks, but its success is far from guaranteed.

Elisa Morgera, a UN special rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights in the context of climate change, says it has been challenged in negotiating rooms. She urges people to listen more to Pacific peoples, describing their leadership as a “gift to humanity”.“All of us will be safer if we learn from what the people who are most impacted by climate change share with us,” she says.

From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 05:00:22 GMT

As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back

Dear British friends,

Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja. Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing.

So this letter could very well be a declaration of love thinly disguised as a reproach. Has it reached your attention that in Germany, we (and by we, I mean most of us) want you back. And, when you consider our history, is that not spectacular? You gave us Brexit, then Bregret; can we please let Breverse lead to Breturn?

Europe is poorer, duller, more humourless and politically weaker without you. In a world dominated by the US, China and Russia, the European Union cannot even pretend to be a strong No 4 without your nuclear arsenal and your UN security council seat, or your financial and cultural strength.

We can turn a blind eye to details: your strange relationship with reality, for instance, your funny king, and your bizarre willingness to let an untalented comedian lead you into a historic dead end – none of these things matter now, in the dark times we are living in.

Back in 2016, when you voted to leave, we said fine, off you go. Without your endless demands and threats, we claimed, the EU would at last function efficiently. Then came the Hungarians.

And now? We have to admit that something fundamental is missing. Yes, British humour. That ability to take yourselves and your own disasters seriously and laugh at them at the same time. This continent, full of Germans and French people, desperately needs someone who can laugh at us both.

And your debating culture. How I love your ability to turn a political conflict into a linguistic spectacle. Yes, your cultural audacity, too. A country that has produced Shakespeare, Fleabag and the BBC should not retreat to an island, even if it happens to be located on one.

And yes, of course, your scepticism. Europe needs grumpy, smart people who will apply a critical eye and dismantle Brussels’ certainties. The EU without Britain is like a dinner party without the one guest we all know: the one who makes everyone uncomfortable, but tells the best stories.

I spent an evening onstage last week in Lübeck, northern Germany, with the German writer Annette Dittert, who lives on a houseboat in London. We talked about you, dearest Britain, and I said I thought the main problem with the idea of reversing Brexit was that stability had deserted international politics.

And even if Andy Burnham manages to complete his mission to take the UK back into the EU, how do we know that Nigel Farage or his successor won’t push through Brexit No 2, a few years from now? “We don’t,” Annette said. “Those days of stability are gone. But every week, every day with Britain is better for everybody involved, than another week or day apart.”

Then I spoke to some German diplomats, and you want to know what I heard again and again? “I hope Burnham succeeds.” Everybody I spoke to said that. But I also heard differing versions of: “A German telling the British what they ought to do is worth a few thousand votes for Nigel Farage.”

And this came straight from a German cabinet member, preparing for Friday’s big EU/UK summit – when Burnham, who has surprised everyone by choosing to spend his honeymoon period pursuing this mission, leads a negotiating delegation to Brussels: “We would rather stay silent in Berlin. But if the Brits were back, I’d be delighted.”

There is a bit of German angst about what may happen next. Will you arrive with a list of opt-outs and exceptions? Will we have to pretend to be surprised by your list? Our old arrangement is long gone, and we have both changed. We’d have to work out what makes sense today, but early talks about food, drinks and youth mobility have gone well.

Germans can forgive a lot – your separate taps, for instance. We can almost forgive Boris Johnson’s lies and Manchester City’s cheating.

Thinking about forgiveness, may I suggest you forgive yourselves for making a mistake? Brexit seemed to happen so rapidly: one referendum, and you were gone. In your position, we would have set up a working group then commissioned a 380-page feasibility study – and after that, made no decision.

Burnham has outlined four future possibilities: the status quo, a customs union, the single market, and full re-entry. “Win-win” is what he wants, he says. Once you crack open a heavy door and some light comes in, you should walk into the sunshine. The difficult part will come when the conversation moves from what Britain has lost, to how much of the European single market you want to share. How do you feel about people being free to move? Ideally, in both directions? Because that’s the idea.

You know you have always been Europeans, right? You still are. Nobody can vote geography away. Nor can you vote history away. Our future will not become any easier just because we try to shape it separately.

And finally, a secret: Europe needs you in order to become less German. My country is large, economically important and erratic, and politically cumbersome. You would make the EU more pluralistic, more pragmatic, more liberal, more Atlanticist, and, hurrah, more rebellious.

We loved you. You left us. We pretended not to care. Now you are suggesting we should get back together.

Our answer? That’s an easy one.

Please come back.

Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany

‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 05:00:22 GMT

From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas

Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles.

I had mentioned the two versions, a routine enough inquiry, but it quickly turns into a discussion about the potential replacement of car stereos with immersive sound systems, which then unexpectedly shifts into an explanation of the work of Michael Levin, an American professor of bioengineering who specialises in morphogenesis. “He’s found some bio-electric instructions that can make an eye grow on the leg of a frog, for example,” says Gabriel, and has apparently “created life forms that never existed before, which really challenges evolution.” Gabriel is interested in “sonifying” some of his data and using it in a subsequent mix of the album.

From there, we move on to software engineer Blaise Agüera y Arcas, whose experiments with an esoteric 90s programming language called Brainfuck have led him to “the radical idea that some constants in maths might actually have some form of life”. This leads us, via the “re-evaluation of what consciousness is and what intelligence is”, to the belief of internet pioneer Vint Cerf that attempting to communicate with other intelligent species might prepare us for the possibility of encountering aliens, and thus to Savage-Rumbaugh and Kanzi the bonobo.

“She used to allow the bonobos to watch videos, and to choose the videos they watched,” Gabriel says, laughing, “and their favourite, perhaps obviously, was Planet of the Apes, then Harry and the Hendersons, which is a film about a sasquatch who came to live with a family. The whole thing blew me away. I think we’re the most arrogant of all apes, and there’s just so much intelligence we’ve chosen to ignore and instead see the world as something that’s entirely available for our exploitation, and I think that’s cost us, as we are now learning.”

Morphogenisis, inter-species communication, the re-evaluation of consciousness: it should go without saying that you don’t usually end up discussing these things when you ask an august rock legend about his latest album. But, as it turns out, that’s what inevitably happens when you ask Gabriel a question. We meet in a pub not far from his home in Notting Hill. He says he’s here “to sell the new album”, but almost every query about it seems to lead him somewhere completely different: science, activism, the nature of consciousness, how language is “a fairly crude tool” for communication, the controversial 1970s self-improvement courses of Werner Erhard.

You can’t fault his diversity of interests, even if that diversity of interests is why it takes so long for him to make albums. o\i is essentially the second part of a project that began with 2023’s i/o, which was his first album of new material in 21 years. Like its predecessor, it contains songs that Gabriel has spent decades tinkering with: he started work on A Hard Lesson in 1989, when he was still a huge mainstream pop star thanks to 1986’s So, an album that shifted more than 5m copies in the US alone.

Yes, he concedes, it is a bit weird to find yourself, at the age of 76, still working on songs you started writing in your 30s: “I recognise that guy, but you’re bound to make different decisions having lived a little longer.” But that’s just the way it is. His friend Laurie Anderson once suggested that Gabriel’s problem was that he was more interested in the process of making something than in finishing it. He thinks the real issue is that he’s easily distracted.

“If you have some measure of success, you end up meeting all sorts of people and having fascinating conversations, which lead to detours, and you think, ‘Well, life is for living,’” he says. “If you get on that conveyor belt of album-tour-album, there’s not time to breathe or have any kind of life, and that always seems somewhat sad to me. I think the diversions feed the music. You know, if you want a better class of shit, you’ve got to eat a more varied diet.”

Hence the digressive nature of our interview. Gabriel seems to have developed a genuinely intriguing theory about virtually everything, from theme parks to funerals: he thinks people should “plant a tree over their dead body, or the dead body of their loved ones, so you’d get woods where there wouldn’t be any signage, but if you go and sit under your dad’s tree, your phone would have the GPS position and you would start seeing his videos, hearing his voice, all the digital data would be locked into that GPS point”.

Moreover, he has an incredibly engaging way of talking about all this stuff, evincing such enthusiasm and curiosity that you’re carried along with him: on the off-chance that you wanted to pitch the idea of growing eyeballs on the legs of frogs, you could do substantially worse than get Gabriel to act as your salesman. It probably helps his cause that Gabriel has a hugely impressive track record of thinking ahead of the curve.

At the height of his fame as the frontman of Genesis, he was sharp enough to realise that the genre of progressive rock they had helped invent was becoming too grandiloquent and remote for its own good – “prancing around in fairyland” as he once put it – and that the band he had formed might be more successful without him. The latter opinion wasn’t very popular with the rest of Genesis, but nevertheless proved to be spot on.

A few years later, he was the first British artist to realise that the future of pop lay in sampling: for some time in the early 80s, if you wanted to use a sampler on your new track you had to borrow Gabriel’s, because he was the first person in the country to own one; he then set up a company to import and distribute the new technology. Twenty years later, he cottoned on very quickly to the idea that music was going to primarily exist online, co-founding a streaming platform that might have become the industry standard had it not launched at exactly the same time as a competitor called Spotify.

If he was right about everything from sampling to streaming to the latter-day career of Genesis, perhaps he’s also right about AI. In a musical world filled with people decrying its malign influence, Gabriel is one of its few high-profile boosters: he recently suggested that ultimately “everything will be done better” by AI than by humans.

He says it again today, albeit with caveats. “The application of AI and robots in warfare is really scary. There’s the sense that we’re creating a species that is way, way more intelligent than we are. If we look around, there are not many good examples of intelligent species looking after less-intelligent species, except as pets.

“You can see the worry on [computer scientist and ‘Godfather of AI’] Geoffrey Hinton’s face,” he continues. “I think we need to slow it down a bit, we need some international agreement, for which there are precedents, like in air safety or the Start treaty for nuclear weapons. We need guard rails, like a seed of wisdom in every algorithm before it’s allowed to be released that could allow for monitoring and a measure of control and an ‘off’ button. But it interests me in the moment as a whole new set of tools that could encourage people to consider themselves film-makers, painters, musicians, to explore themselves in that way.”

With or without AI, Gabriel says he thinks that’s true anyway: “Being those things is just a matter of walking around and saying, ‘This is what I am’, then committing to learning about it. You can get accelerated learning through AI – even though you haven’t learned all the skills to get there, you can quickly access some of the joy of making really nice-sounding things or have the AI eliminate some of your worst moments. So in the long run, as a creative tool: absolutely extraordinary. It’s like you’ve been painting in black and white and someone suddenly throws a colour palette at you, saying: ‘What can you do with this?’”

Contrary to most, Gabriel genuinely seems to believe that AI is capable of creating great art. “It’s just down to better algorithms. So how do we deal with this as a species? I think long-term, if you can’t defeat it, you have to join it. I think we will become cyborgs, because we’ll have these brain-computer interfaces, where you insert something in your brain that allows you then to communicate to the computer … I don’t think there’s any reason why we shouldn’t use our brains to become more AI.”

He’s keen to point out that “any of these things can be used positively or negatively”. He recently had a conversation with American technologist Mary Lou Jepsen, who was concerned about the human rights implications of the whole brain-computer-interface idea and its capacity for being used as a form of torture. But nevertheless, Gabriel seems fascinated by the idea: he has a concept for something so vague, I don’t really understand it, called “the brain show”, that will “allow you to see how the brain affects us and how it might be manipulated” and which would feature some of the songs from o\i as part of its soundtrack. “It could be a virtual thing or a stage thing or both, but how it all works, and the story, I’ve got no idea,” he shrugs. “I’m at that stage where you can feel a sort of lump in the mist and you’re trying to imagine it becoming something, which I think is the way most people approach creativity.”

In the meantime, he has umpteen other ideas floating around. He’s intrigued by the concept of a virtual performance, somewhere between Abba Voyage and U2’s “wonderful and inspiring” shows at the Sphere in Las Vegas. There’s a plan to make a film based on The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, the 1974 concept album that preceded his exit from Genesis: you might have thought it was pretty much unfilmable, given that it features a scene in which the lead character has sex with three snake-like creatures, and another in which his recently amputated penis is snatched away by a passing raven, but Gabriel seems optimistic: he’s been working on the script with Argentinan writer Nicolás Giacobone of Digger fame.

And he wants to “dig into” another of Levin’s ideas, “that you might be able to communicate with cells and get them to behave in a certain way and sound might be a medium for it. I’m fascinated by explorations of consciousness,” he says, then goes on to tell me about experiments in the sentience of plants. “There was a cool guy at MIT who took a plant and put it in a sort of box with a computer on wheels, then moved the plant’s light source around the room and the plant was saying ‘OK’ and moving the box to follow the light around the room. I was wondering if you could do that with an oak tree. Like a sort of Jurassic Park, but with plants instead of dinosaurs. I mean, all these ideas are such great fun to explore.”

o\i is released via Real World on 27 November

No Roasting Pan, No Problem: Easy Sheet-Pan Recipes for Thanksgiving

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Spatchcock turkey, scalloped potatoes, Texas sheet cake and more easy, low cleanup dishes for a laid-back feast.

By Sharon Attia

Published Nov. 6, 2026 Updated Nov. 18, 2026

You don’t need a well-equipped kitchen to produce a well-rounded meal. If you have an oven, a sheet pan and a desire to cook something delicious for you and your pals, you’ve come to the right place. Below are 16 sheet-pan recipes for a low-fuss Friendsgiving. (And if you’re feeling ambitious, or curious, find all our Thanksgiving recipes here.)

Instead of piling potato slices an inch or two deep in a baking dish, Melissa Clark shingles them in a sheet pan. It looks more striking, and you get more browning and crispiness on top thanks to the increased surface area. Flavor wise, this gratin stays pretty classic with lots of Gruyère, as well as sage, garlic and nutmeg for seasoning.

Recipe: Scalloped Potato Gratin

Hey Caesar, meet your new friend, Roasted Brussels Sprouts. Yasmin Fahr’s recipe honors the creamy, crunchy, punchy elements of the beloved salad, but reimagines it as a heartier, wintry side. Instead of anchovies in the dressing, she opts for tahini. The croutons bake on the same sheet pan as the sprouts, which means fewer dishes. (Woo!)

Recipe: Roasted Brussels Sprouts Caesar With Tahini

Repeat after me: I will spatchcock my turkey. Mark Bittman took the technique most commonly used with chickens — cutting out the bird’s backbone and spreading it flat on a sheet pan — and applied it to a Thanksgiving turkey. Brilliant! Roasted at 450 degrees, a 10-pound bird will be done in about 45 minutes.

Recipe: Roast Spatchcock Turkey

This 15-minute side dish from Lidey Heuck is more than the sum of its parts. She roasts green beans and supermarket diced pancetta at a high temperature in olive oil, salt and pepper. Garnish with lemon juice. That’s it!

Recipe: Roasted Green Beans With Pancetta and Lemon Zest

“This ratio of effort (very low) to enjoyment (much higher than expected) has me fantasizing about serving this for Thanksgiving dinner. I’d make with turkey sausage, and a side cranberry. Boom,” one reader wrote about Ali Slagle’s easy sheet-pan recipe. Protein, potato and veg, all cooked on one pan. Boom, indeed.

Recipe: Crispy Gnocchi With Sausage and Broccoli

Our readers can’t get enough of this squash and chickpea recipe from Melissa Clark, which has five stars and nearly 9,000 ratings. The dish takes about an hour from start to finish, but most of that is hands-off roasting, and the actual prep time is relatively short (even shorter if you use pre-cubed squash). Top it all with a drizzle of hot honey and a dollop of yogurt.

Recipe: Roasted Honey Nut Squash and Chickpeas With Hot Honey

If you like the extra-toasty bits of stuffing, this recipe from Yossy Arefi is for you. All the traditional players (celery, onion, apple, herbs, broth) are here, but they’re baked on a sheet pan instead of in a casserole dish.

Recipe: Sheet-Pan Thanksgiving Stuffing

Barely an inch tall (short king!), Genevieve Ko’s version of the famous Texas dessert starts with a cake that’s lighter than devil’s food. Cocoa frosting is poured over the warm cake, soaking into it, making it a rich, chocolate lover’s dream. Toasted pecans are sprinkled on top for crunch in every bite.

Recipe: Texas Sheet Cake

Skipping the turkey? Make Colu Henry’s roasted chicken thighs with apples, fennel and onions. The sheet-pan main, seasoned with toasted fennel seeds and rosemary, feels peak autumn. It’s ready in under an hour and feels special enough for company.

Recipe: Sheet-Pan Chicken With Apple, Fennel and Onion

“One of the easiest, most delicious things I’ve ever made from this site. Omg. I had to stop myself from eating all of it before I even got it into the serving dish,” one reader wrote about Yasmin Fahr’s 20-minute broccoli recipe, which gets tossed in miso butter and lime juice directly on the sheet-pan, straight out of the oven.

Recipe: Miso-Butter Roasted Broccoli

Simple is often best, especially when it comes to a hard-to-mess-up ingredient like the potato. Lidey Heuck’s recipe aims for creamy and tender centers and crispy-golden exteriors. She uses baby yellow or red potatoes, but larger taters work, too; just chop them into 1-inch pieces before roasting.

Recipe: Roasted Potatoes

Perfect for a sweet and intimate gathering, this streamlined Thanksgiving meal from Melissa Clark calls for one sheet pan, one medium pot and one bowl. Seriously, that’s it. It has all the fixings of a traditional holiday menu — turkey, stuffing, brussels sprouts, marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce and gravy — but with far less work and far fewer dishes to wash.

Recipe: One-Pan, One-Pot Thanksgiving Dinner

Cabbage is a criminally underrated vegetable. In this six-ingredient recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon, a head of green cabbage is roasted with a garlicky, lemon-caper oil that your friends will dream about long after the meal has ended. I’m speaking from experience here.

Recipe: Roasted Cabbage With Capers and Garlic

Genevieve Ko bakes this easy carrot cake in a half-sheet pan, then cuts it into three rectangles, achieving thin, even layers without the need for cake rounds. Ultimately, the tender cake is really serving as a vehicle for cream cheese frosting, which Genevieve makes with sour cream instead of butter for extra tang.

Recipe: Easy Carrot Cake With Cream Cheese Frosting

Holiday sweet potatoes don’t have to be cloyingly sweet. Put down the bag of marshmallows and pick up a jar of harissa to make Hetty Lui McKinnon’s roasted sweet potato wedges with red onion. Top with feta, cilantro, mint and a squeeze of lemon for a dish that’s caramelized, smoky, creamy and tangy.

Recipe: Harissa-Roasted Sweet Potatoes and Red Onion

“This is such an awesome amount of flavor for a really easy recipe!” one reader wrote about Zainab Shah’s roasted cauliflower. The true star of the dish is what’s poured atop the subtly sweet veg: Vietnamese nước chấm sauce, which is pungent from fish sauce and garlic, sour from rice vinegar, sweet from sugar and spicy from chile.

Recipe: Roasted Cauliflower With Nước Chấm Sauce

23 Thanksgiving Main Dishes That Are Better Than Turkey

The New York Times September 25, 2026

Maybe you don’t like turkey, or it’s too expensive, or just not worth the work. We’ve got recipes to get excited about.

By The New York Times

Published Nov. 17, 2020 Updated Sept. 25, 2026

Thanksgiving might seem as if it’s defined by turkey, but a big, glossy Norman Rockwell-style bird isn’t required for a festive holiday. Maybe you don’t like turkey, or maybe soaring food prices are making it difficult for you to find one at an affordable price. Whatever the reason, here are 23 Thanksgiving recipes for a turkey-free table.

This herbaceous roast chicken from Octavio Peña is a delicious departure from the one-note poultry of holidays past. Season the bird with pantry spices like cumin, coriander, paprika and oregano. In the last five minutes of roasting, drizzle on mixture of melted butter, garlic, serranos, lime and cilantro — punchy, bright flavors that seep into the carrots and potatoes below.

Alexa Weibel’s show-stopping vegetarian pie is a delight to cut open at the table, and it can be prepped well ahead of time. Cook the caramelized veggies whenever you like, and then, right before serving, assemble and bake, which is easy thanks to the use of store-bought puff pastry.

This autumnal recipe from Ashley Lonsdale is simple but spectacular enough to be the centerpiece of a meatless spread, or the star side: Fluffy, golden basmati rice is jeweled with pumpkin, both grated into the rice and cut into chunks. Add roasted peanuts and thinly sliced celery at the end for a satisfying crunch.

Say you’re having a small get-together, but you still want to serve a gorgeous, burnished bird. Let us introduce you to this sweet and salty roast chicken from Colu Henry. Basting the chicken with a rosemary-infused maple butter throughout cooking helps caramelize the outside and creates pan juices that are delicious served over — you guessed it — mashed potatoes. Brush up your poultry skills with our guide on how to roast chicken.

Recipe: Roast Chicken With Maple Butter and Rosemary

Melissa Clark’s classic beef Wellington is something to truly be thankful for. A tender beef fillet is wrapped in mushrooms and shallots, then enrobed in a golden layer of puff pastry. The key to success is an instant-read thermometer. Bake until a thermometer inserted in the center reads 115 degrees for a lovely pink rare center, 25 to 35 minutes, and not a minute more.

Recipe: Beef Wellington

This gorgeous rainbow gratin from Alexa Weibel showcases layers of beets, butternut squash, sweet potatoes and potatoes with a frilly phyllo topping for a vegetarian centerpiece that’ll make jaws drop.

Recipe: Ombré Gratin

In this 30-minute one-pot recipe from Ali Slagle, brown sugar, apple cider vinegar and white miso are cooked down into a glossy, salty-sweet sauce for the classic combination of pork chops and apples.

Recipe: Skillet Pork Chops and Apples With Miso Caramel

This majestic savory pie from Nadiya Hussain, the British author and television host, is packed with ground lamb, potatoes, peas and spices. The crust is tinted with turmeric so it bakes up a beautiful and vibrant gold.

Recipe: Samosa Pie

In this easy five-ingredient recipe from Genevieve Ko, a combination of maple syrup, mustard and mayonnaise is slathered onto a simple piece of salmon, which is then baked low and slow at 325 degrees for a spectacular main dish.

Recipe: Maple-Baked Salmon

Many Italian American families serve lasagna in addition to their roast turkey, but this lasagna from Regina Schrambling — outrageously rich with layers of pasta, homemade sauce, three cheeses, Italian sausage and meatballs — deserves the spotlight.

Recipe: Lasagna

Don’t let the name intimidate you. It’s just a fancy way of describing the classic French dish of scallops in a lovely cream sauce, nestled under a layer of crunchy bread crumbs and Gruyère cheese. Sam Sifton adapted this easier version from Ina, so you know it has to be good, but the biggest selling point might be that you can make it the night before, then warm it through when you’re ready to eat.

Recipe: Ina Garten’s Make-Ahead Coquilles St.-Jacques

Sam Sifton once called Alexa Weibel’s mushroom Wellington “beautiful and fancy, Idris Elba in black tie, the perfect Thanksgiving guest.” It is no easy feat — there is no shortcut to be taken here, beyond preparing the separate components a day in advance — but set it in front of guests and it can compete with any turkey on any table, unifying vegans, vegetarians and omnivores.

Recipe: Vegetarian Mushroom Wellington

A beloved dish typically served at special occasions in Puerto Rico (especially Thanksgiving and Christmas), pernil is pork shoulder that’s been marinated in garlic, citrus and herbs, then slow-roasted on high heat to achieve a crisp chicharrón, or skin. This version was developed by Von Diaz, who credits the chef Maricel Presilla for teaching her how to achieve crisp skin and tender, fall-apart meat.

Recipe: Pernil

This root-vegetable-and-mushroom potpie from Alexa Weibel offers lots of options: Bake it in a large cast-iron skillet or cook it in individual ramekins. If you’re serving both vegetarians and meat eaters, divide the filling between two pie plates, and add rotisserie chicken, bacon, lardons or even duck confit to one before covering each with a blanket of puff pastry.

Recipe: Mushroom Potpie

This is a cozy, spice-laden dish made of yogurt-marinated chicken bathed in a golden sauce of butter, onions, ginger, tomatoes, garam masala, cumin, turmeric and cinnamon. Sam Sifton adapted this version from Amandeep Sharma, a young kitchen hand at the restaurant Attica, in Melbourne, Australia, who used to make it for staff meal. It’s better than any roast turkey could ever dream of being.

Recipe: Murgh Makhani (Butter Chicken)

Alexa Weibel is a wizard when it comes to making meatless variations of dishes that taste just as delicious — if not more — than their meat-laden counterparts. Take, for instance, this vegetarian lasagna, which begins with a robust vegan Bolognese made with seared mushrooms, toasted walnuts, balsamic vinegar, tomato paste, soy sauce and Marmite. (Skip the Marmite if you can’t find it.) Once you’ve got the sauce made, the rest is just assembly.

Recipe: Vegetarian Lasagna Bolognese

Roasting chicken is a smart option for a small Thanksgiving, but if you want something a bit more interesting, try this recipe from Yasmin Khan. Mussakhan is a beloved Palestinian dish that is brightened with lemon and sumac, but also rich with warming spices like cumin, allspice and cinnamon. It will feel right at home on your Thanksgiving table.

Recipe: Mussakhan (Roast Chicken With Sumac and Red Onions)

This meatless Thanksgiving centerpiece from Samantha Seneviratne has the mashed potatoes baked right in! French green lentils (Puy lentils) are the cornerstone of this hearty pie, and while they can be a little harder to find than traditional brown, they hold up better to long cook times and a creamy potato topping.

Recipe: Vegetarian Shepherd’s Pie

J. Kenji López-Alt takes an affordable piece of beef (any inexpensive, lean meat like top round or tri-tip will do), seasons it generously with salt and pepper and refrigerates it for one to two days, then gives it the reverse-sear treatment: roasting then searing until browned. You’ll end up with moist, succulent meat, but you can whisk together a pan sauce or gravy if you’d like to give it the traditional turkey treatment.

Recipe: Slow-Roasted Beef

Duck is richer, and perhaps even more regal than a Thanksgiving turkey, and this pan-roasted version from David Tanis is easily scalable — one breast easily serves two if your celebration is cozy. This dish is served with a rich pan sauce using fresh and dried mushrooms, red wine and herbs. It’s fancy and festive.

Recipe: Pan-Roasted Duck With Wild Mushrooms

Mrouzia is a Moroccan tagine often enjoyed on holidays or special occasions. Nargisse Benkabbou’s recipe combines lamb shanks with a syrupy sauce of honey and raisins, seasoned with saffron and ras el hanout. It’s a sweet, subtly spiced centerpiece that can be prepared a day in advance.

Recipe: Mrouzia Lamb Shanks

Lasagna has found its way onto holiday tables for generations for many reasons: The dish easily fuels a crowd, feels special and amicably adapts to different cultures and generational variations. In Khushbu Shah’s recipe, the saag base is bolstered by warm spices and earthy dried fenugreek leaves, priming it perfectly for Thanksgiving.

Ali Slagle’s slow-cooked beef nearly cooks itself due its easy, hands-off method. Cola plays double duty here, tenderizing the meat and also reducing into a deeply flavored sauce that lacquers the roast from the inside-out. Even better, it can be prepared ahead of time so that you can spend the big day focusing on dishes requiring your last-minute attention.

Get all of our best Thanksgiving recipes on NYT Cooking.

As a Storm Floods Florida, Heavy Rain Will Creep Up the East Coast

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Hurricane Season

Advertisement

Supported by

A potential tropical storm off the coast of Florida is expected to move up the coast and could snarl Thanksgiving week travel.

Precipitation intensity

Note: Times are Eastern. Source: National Weather Service. William B. Davis, Joel Eastwood and Bea Malsky/The New York Times

By Judson Jones

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and a reporter for The Times.

A sprawling storm system that has been parked off the Florida coast for days will continue to soak the state through Saturday, forecasters warned, before it moves north just in time to complicate travel at the start of Thanksgiving week.

The storm even has a chance of developing into a named system, Tropical Storm Kyle, as it accelerates up the East Coast, eventually bringing rain to the Northeast on Sunday into Monday. It is unusual, but not impossible, for a storm to form this late into the Atlantic hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30.

Conditions are ripe for the system to become subtropical or tropical, a defining characteristic of a named storm, said Andrew Hagen, at the National Hurricane Center.

Whether it is named or not, Mr. Hagen said residents in Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas should continue to monitor the forecast, particularly because heavy rain and flooding have already plagued parts of the Southeast.

On Friday, the storm continued to batter the east coast of Florida with intense rain. Since Tuesday, roads have flooded, rivers have begun to overflow their banks, and parts of Cocoa Beach, Cape Canaveral and Melbourne have received more than a foot of rain.

The area experienced similar flooding at the start of November. Scott Kleebauer, a meteorologist at the Weather Prediction Center, an arm of the National Weather Service, said he would not be surprised if some areas have seen more than 30 inches of rainfall over the past month. “And that’s not an exaggeration,” he added.

Melissa Watson, a Weather Service forecaster in Melbourne, Fla., said the area could record an additional three to six inches of rain, with a chance of local amounts exceeding eight inches. Any additional rainfall will exacerbate the flooding already underway, though Ms. Watson offered some hope that the heaviest rain on Friday might fall farther north.

Since Thursday, the Weather Prediction Center has placed a small portion of Florida under a “high risk” for excessive rainfall. This alert, the highest on the agency’s scale, means meteorologists are highly confident that flash flooding will occur. Over the past decade, some of the deadliest and most destructive floods have occurred in areas under this rare level of risk.

As the storm takes shape and moves parallel to the coast this weekend, it will begin to pick up speed, spreading precipitation into Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia and eventually the Northeast, Mr. Kleebauer said. While forecasters are fairly certain of its path, any change in intensity or subtle shifts left or right could affect how much rain falls in any specific region.

To become a named storm, the system must draw its energy from warm ocean waters rather than just the clash of cold and warm air, and it would need sustained winds stronger than 39 miles per hour.

“It could possibly strengthen into a strong tropical storm,” Mr. Hagen said. While it could produce significant impacts depending on its proximity to the shore, he noted that it is fairly unlikely to become a hurricane.

In the Northeast, forecasters are preparing residents for a wet weekend. “Most of the local tristate is looking at a period of perhaps moderate to heavy rain as we go later into the day on Sunday, then continuing into at least Monday morning before things start to taper,” said Dominic Ramunni, a Weather Service forecaster in New York City.

He expects one to two inches of rain in many places, with some local spots creeping higher. “Of course with that amount of rain, depending on how quickly it falls, we could be talking about perhaps a localized flash flood threat,” Mr. Ramunni said. That’s a familiar scenario for New York City residents who faced multiple strong rain storms this fall.

The pattern aligns with forecasters’ expectations for the season. “Because we are going into a strong El Niño, we have been briefing our emergency manager partners as well as the public,” Ms. Watson said, noting that the climate pattern increases the chances of winter and spring storminess in Florida. A strong El Niño like this one typically develops storm systems that move across the Florida Peninsula and travel up the coast.

This pattern could repeat as early as next week. Forecasters are monitoring another potential coastal system that could affect Thanksgiving travel, though “the jury is still out” as the storm is several days away, Mr. Kleebauer said.

Mr. Ramunni noted that confidence remains “very low” for the New York City forecast, meaning Thanksgiving Day events like the annual parade could be dry, or faced with rain and wind. “It is something to keep an eye on for anyone traveling around the holiday,” he said.

Forecasters are watching the developing system closely, Mr. Kleebauer said. Like many, he said he was hoping it stays away, “Mother Nature’s going to do what she wants to do.”

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times who forecasts and covers extreme weather.

The S&P 500 is close to ending the day in a correction, a drop of 10 percent from its recent high and a symbolic measure of investors’ souring mood.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

The New York Times

By Joe Rennison

Stocks careened toward their worst week in more than a year, deepening a weekslong sell-off driven by concerns about the evolving artificial intelligence industry.

The S&P 500 fell more than 2 percent on Friday and was approaching correction territory, defined as a drop of 10 percent from its recent high and a symbolic measure of investors’ souring mood.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid more than 3.5 percent, a loss that would erase its gains for the year. The index includes the stock moves of many of the technology giants that have powered the A. I. boom.

The past week had been billed by some investors as a referendum on investments in artificial intelligence, with Nvidia, the poster company for A. I. growth, reporting financial results, and Anthropic, another major player, debuting on public markets. But despite Nvidia’s bumper profits and hefty initial demand for Anthropic’s shares, neither could dispel wider held concerns about the A. I. industry.

Investors’ worries have been stacking up for weeks, as concerns grow about whether future profits would justify A. I. companies’ debt-fueled infrastructure spending. The midterm elections increased the likelihood of new hurdles for data center construction; earnings reports highlighted signs of supply chain constraints that could slow the growth of some businesses; and Nvidia, until recently among the market’s highest-flying stocks, faced a leadership crisis.

Even Anthropic, only one day after its blockbuster I. P. O., could not escape the market malaise, with its shares falling 10 percent on Friday.

Investors’ deepening concerns collided this week with profit-taking by many traders that bet big on A. I. at the start of the year now paring back those positions ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Data from JPMorgan showed retail buying remained “lackluster” over the course of the week, as these investors have also backed away from the market.

This is in contrast to previous bouts of volatility, such as the onset of the Iran war earlier this year, when many investors saw the downturn in share prices as an opportunity to buy the dip.

“We are basically staying away,” said Stan Druckenmiller, the billionaire investor and founder of Duquesne Family Office, speaking on Tuesday at a conference in Austin. “We are trying to not lose money as opposed to make money.”

The S&P 500 was on course for its seventh consecutive daily drop on Friday, its worst run since February 2020 and the onset of the pandemic. The index is set to record a drop of over 7 percent this week. It would be its worst week since April 2025, when the market convulsed in response to the announcement of President Trump’s sweeping global tariffs. The index remains less than 2 percent higher for the year, having risen as high as 14.2 percent at its peak in October.

This week, the CBOE Vix Volatility index, a measure known as the market’s fear gauge because it measures investors’ expectations of volatility over the next 30 days, rose above its most recent peak in the aftermath of the midterm elections.

The New York Times

“Unfortunately, there isn’t an obvious catalyst or event to improve sentiment as we head into year-end,” said Stuart Kaiser, an analyst at Citi. He adding that “there are no clear signposts to swing the pendulum.”

The declines have persisted despite generally favorable reactions from analysts and investors to a week of major events.

Nvidia’s earnings report on Tuesday helped to calm fears of a slowdown in growth of the A. I. build-out, with the giant chip maker raising its profit forecast. It was a brief respite for the company, which is reeling after the resignation of its larger-than-life chief executive, Jensen Huang, following revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U. S. intelligence officials determined was feeding information to Beijing.

But the stock has continued to tumble. Nvidia has fallen nearly 40 percent since the S&P 500 peaked in early October, accounting for roughly half of the 8 percent drop in the index over that period, said Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist for LPL Financial. Nvidia has been “the big factor” weighing on the market, he said, emblematic of “the broader fear over an A. I. slowdown.” The chip maker’s stock fell further on Friday.

On Thursday, Anthropic jumped on its first day of trading, achieving a trillion-dollar valuation after setting a record for the largest public offering in history. Robust demand for the shares of the maker of the Claude chatbot suggested that investors were still optimistic about aspects of the A. I. industry.

Analyst recommendations for Anthropic, collated by the market data firm FactSet, showed bullish expectations for the future. Ben Reitzes at Melius Research represents the high-water mark, with an initial price target of $155 per share. At the other end of the spectrum is Patrick Walravens at Citizens, with a target of $125.

Anthropic’s newly listed stock soared as much as 38 percent in early trading on Thursday, but as the day progressed, the air came out of the company’s ballooning price. Its shares ended the day up 17 percent, at $97 a share.

That’s still a healthy rise from its I. P. O. price of $83 per share, but suggested a more restrained optimism for the company’s prospects than the initial flurry of trades.

Anthropic’s 10 percent drop on Friday largely reversed the previous day’s gains.

Britain and Brussels Have Begun a Brexit Rollback. How Far Will It Go?

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

The United Kingdom is removing barriers with the European Union a decade after it voted to leave. Global turmoil, and the disruptive policies of President Trump, helped push them back together.

By Michael D. Shear and Jeanna Smialek

Reporting from Brussels

Ten years ago, when the Brexit vote triggered a major rupture between the United Kingdom and the European Union, Donald Trump hailed the decision as a great victory.

These days, President Trump’s policies, along with an aggressive Russia and an economically dominant China, are helping bring Europe and Britain back together.

Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, has made clear that he wants to pursue a much closer relationship with the 27-nation bloc as Russian aggression in Ukraine underscores the need for European solidarity and Mr. Trump calls into question eight decades of American economic, political and security support.

On Friday, the prime minister took concrete steps toward that goal, knocking down some pieces of the Brexit agreement that walled Britain off from its neighbors.

Under plans he announced in Brussels, many trade barriers on food and agricultural products will be cut. Regulations on emissions will be linked. And 100,000 young people in Britain, along with an equal number in Europe, will again have the freedom to work, live and study for up to three years on either side of the English Channel.

The changes will make trade easier for farmers and retailers, travel easier for students, and regulatory compliance easier for companies. At times in the last decade, they were almost unthinkable amid the rancor of the Britain-Europe political divorce.

Mr. Burnham wants to go even further.

On Friday, he and the European Union’s two top leaders agreed to conduct what he described as a yearlong “brainstorm” about what a deeper relationship with the European Union might look like.

“Incremental steps only take you so far,” Mr. Burnham said.

Brexit damaged the British economy, and its continuing cost to businesses and economic growth helped turn a majority of the public against it. But the geopolitical backdrop has played a vital role in the debate.

The postwar world order has been upended by Mr. Trump’s policies, which have come alongside China’s continued economic rise and Russia’s territorial aggression. In a world that looks increasingly hostile, Britain and Europe have been left looking for close friends. And as the trans-Atlantic relationship ruptures, they have found one another again.

“London has increasingly given up on its post-Brexit great trans-Atlantic hopes that Washington would give us a free trade deal and a new lease of life to the special relationship,” said David Lammy, a member of parliament and former deputy prime minister in Britain.

To many foreign policy veterans in Britain, Mr. Trump has spent the first two years of his second administration making it more and more difficult for Britain to feel special. His trade war dragged its already sluggish economy. His relative indifference toward NATO has upended global security. His friendliness with Vladimir Putin has come as a shock.

The same challenges have rocked Europe, another close U. S. ally, and Mr. Trump’s threat to take over Greenland drove home the deterioration. Europe has been looking for alternatives — striking deals with Canada, Australia, Indonesia and Latin American countries.

And as middle powers unite, Europe and Britain have been creeping closer.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Union’s executive arm, suggested that Europe was willing to discuss a deeper relationship.

“We welcome this brainstorming,” she told Mr. Burnham at the news conference, following his suggestion. “So count on us.”

Britain started on its path toward drawing closer to Brussels last year, under the previous Labour prime minister, Keir Starmer. Friday’s summit delivered detailed decisions on several agenda items that his government had begun.

Mr. Burnham said Friday that his government would introduce a bill into Parliament next week to implement the deal and pledged that “we will not waste any time whatsoever in getting on with implementation, rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago.”

But Mr. Burnham has also been clear that he favors an even more substantial reversal of Brexit after what he called “a decade of drift and division” that has left his country poorer and weaker. He has promised to present options for changes to the long-term relationship to the British public in the months to come, while insisting that any final decision would only take place after the next general election, which must be held by 2029.

The prospect of another fierce debate over Britain’s place in Europe is already roiling politics in the United Kingdom, where Mr. Burnham’s rivals have accused him of going back on a Labour promise not to re-litigate the public’s decision in 2016. And in Europe, it is unclear how high support for a drastically closer relationship will be after a series of elections next year.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative Party leader, said this week that the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is.” Nigel Farage, an architect of Brexit and leader of the populist Reform U. K. Party, said Mr. Burnham wanted “to be part of a globalist governmental structure, as opposed to the nation state democracy.”

Still, Mr. Farage acknowledged Brexit had not gone well. “Yes, of course, we cocked things up, but that wasn’t the fault of Brexit — that was the fault of the government not getting it right,” he said in an interview with The Times of London.

Britain remains far from actually rejoining the 27-nation bloc. It took nearly five years for the nation to exit the union, and reversing that would be a complicated and contested process.

“We have seen an improvement in the relationship,” said Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive of the European Policy Centre, a think tank. “But it has been a slow improvement, because a lot of trust has been lost.”

At the same time, deeper ties seem increasingly urgent.

“Brexit has not been good for the U. K. economy — and meanwhile, the trans-Atlantic situation has gone from bad to worse,” said Rebecca Christie, a senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel.

Mr. Trump hammered that point home when he met this week with Presidents Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and Xi Jinping of China, two autocrats whom he described as his friends. Afterward, Mr. Trump called European and British officials and reiterated that the war in Ukraine was costing lives and money.

Europe views the outcome in Ukraine as vital to its security and has been nervously watching as Mr. Trump takes an often-sympathetic tone toward Mr. Putin and an often-hostile one toward President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

Russia is another factor pushing Europe and Britain closer, with both worrying that Mr. Putin’s ambitions do not end in Ukraine. They are also motivated by an economically ascendant China, which is churning out solar panels, electric cars and cutting-edge artificial intelligence models, threatening European industries.

In remarks on Friday, Mr. Burnham accused Russia of spending the last 15 years trying to break apart “the cohesion of like-minded countries and particularly the E. U.” He said that Russia’s efforts were “designed to weaken our ability to stop them in terms of what they were seeking to do” in Ukraine.

“We are going to have to work in a different way to make the next decade different,” Mr. Burnham said. “That will depend upon closer cooperation.”

António Costa, the president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, prompted a ripple of laughter as he joked about how far Britain, and its prime minister, might be willing to rebuild ties with Europe.

“Dear Andy, welcome to Brussels,” Mr. Costa said. “You are always welcome in the European Union.”

Michael D. Shear is the chief U. K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.
