E-Bikes. Arson. Illegal Homes. Why Deadly N. Y. C. Fires Are on the Rise.

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Fatalities have nearly doubled this year. While a series of factors has driven the increase, the deadliest blazes have occurred in homes built more than 100 years ago.

By Ashley Southall

A family of four was about to sit down for a dinner of curry and rice on Feb. 9 when the smell of smoke wafted into their first-floor apartment in Queens.

Thick black smoke was making its way up from the basement. The home, their refuge since arriving from Myanmar, would soon become the scene of a nightmare.

It took firefighters less than five minutes to arrive at the three-story home on Dongan Avenue, in the Elmhurst neighborhood. But the building had already gone up in flames, killing a 34-year-old Dominican woman and her newborn daughter. It would also take the life of Thet Aung Oo, at 22 the youngest member of his family, on the first floor.

Mr. Thet Aung Oo, also known as Alex, was the 18th person to die in a fire in New York City this year, a number that had grown to 90 by Nov. 20. That’s substantially more than the 51 fire deaths recorded by this time in 2025, and the highest toll since 2023. Fire marshals have yet to determine the cause of the blaze that killed Mr. Thet Aung Oo.

But it was typical of deadly fires this year in the city, which have largely swept through older homes, and have killed some of the city’s most vulnerable people.

Fire marshals have not been able to point to an individual reason for this year’s increase. Instead, officials say a range of familiar dangers, from the lack of fire protection in older buildings to illegal living conditions, have contributed to this year’s toll. Deaths blamed on arson, sometimes just the reckless flick of a lit cigarette, and lithium-ion batteries, usually being used by delivery vehicles, have also ticked up.

The increase in fire deaths this year has shined another spotlight on the city’s affordable housing crisis, and represents a reversal of years of progress in fire safety.

City officials, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, are worried about the start of the winter, when most deadly fires occur as people celebrate the holidays and try to stay warm.

“As the weather starts to get cold, we have concerns,” Chief John Esposito of the Fire Department said. “What we don’t want to see is the carelessness dealing with fire safety, dealing with electrical safety. The causes, unfortunately, are repeated year after year.”

There are more than one million buildings in New York City. Many of those are residential — townhouses, brownstones and walk-ups as tall as six stories — and were built roughly 100 years ago or more, using flammable materials, like wood, and without fire safeguards, like sprinklers and fireproof stairs.

Six of the deadliest fires to unfold this year occurred in such buildings, according to an analysis of fire and buildings data by The New York Times. And most of the victims have been poor people of color, older citizens, children and immigrants.

The City Council held a hearing on Friday to address the rise in fire deaths. The hearing focused on lithium-ion batteries, which have been linked to nine deaths this year, an alarming spike after the death toll associated with them had dropped in recent years. In 2023, the City Council pushed for measures that helped reduce the number of fires tied to the batteries, which are often used to power delivery bikes.

The fire deaths linked to lithium-ion batteries include those of a woman and her three sons last month in the Bronx. Officials have theorized that the fires may be on the rise because the many batteries purchased for delivery vehicles during the coronavirus pandemic are now reaching the end of their lives.

Julie Menin, the City Council speaker, grew frustrated with fire officials during the hearing over why a trade-in program to get unsafe batteries off the street had ended in 2025.

“If we have effective strategies, we need to be proactive and keep using them,” Ms. Menin told reporters after the hearing.

The Council is considering several bills to regulate batteries. But Lillian Bonsignore, the city’s fire commissioner, said at the hearing that she had concerns about most of them. She said the city was focused on limiting the sale of unsafe devices and on a new public education campaign to warn about the dangers of batteries.

Fire officials also said they were “optimistic” that President Trump would sign a federal bill, approved by the Senate this week, to set standards for lithium-ion batteries, and that it would help limit the proliferation of unsafe batteries.

The Council also examined the issue of enforcement of fire safety laws. At least two fires have raised concerns about the city’s application of rules addressing illegal living conditions, including one this month in Sunset Park in Brooklyn that killed six people. It was the deadliest blaze this year.

Sam Raskin, a spokesman for Mr. Mamdani, said the administration “is taking a coordinated approach to reducing fires and fire fatalities through stronger enforcement of housing safety requirements, public education, building inspections and long-term investments in safer housing.”

Another area of concern has been a spike in deadly arsons. This year, 19 people have died in fires that were deliberately set, compared to two in 2025, according to the Fire Department.

Seven of the deadliest fires this year have highlighted the city’s aging infrastructure. Those fires occurred in homes that were built before the city adjusted its rules in 1938, requiring most new buildings to have sprinklers and either fireproof stairwells or exterior fire escapes.

In older homes, the contemporary demand for electricity to power our gadgets and appliances is taxing outdated electrical wiring systems. Fires sparked by electrical wiring have killed 13 people so far this year, according to Fire Department statistics.

Many tenants use extension cords and surge protectors to power multiple devices, which can cause old wiring to overheat and spark a fire, Chief Esposito said.

“People need to have discipline about that,” he said. “The fact that you can plug those things into a power strip and it works doesn’t mean that it is safe.”

Some of the buildings that were the scenes of deadly fires had been converted into illegal dwellings that were difficult to escape. The city contains thousands of illegal basement and cellar apartments that are often the only housing some people can afford.

The city received multiple complaints that the building in Sunset Park, and the house in Flushing had been illegally subdivided. The city fined the owners in Flushing after inspectors found illegal apartments and hazardous extension cords.

In the Sunset Park case, the complaints were closed after inspectors were not granted access. Marshals have not determined the cause of the fire.

In the house on Dongan Avenue, several fire risks seemed to overlap.

The two-story, wood-framed building was built in 1920. The basement was crowded with people living in one or more illegal apartments, which were reported to the city in 2009 and 2022. The complaints had been closed after inspectors were not allowed into the building.

Tin Aung Oo, Mr. Thet Aung Oo’s brother, said the apartment that he and his family moved into two years ago had many electrical issues. Using the microwave and rice cooker simultaneously tripped the circuit breaker. There were no fire alarms or sprinklers, Mr. Tin Aung Oo said. When they complained to the landlord, he came over and tinkered with things but never fixed the problem, he said.

A man listed in public records as the owner of the house did not return phone calls seeking comment.

About 10 people lived in the basement, according to Mr. Tin Aung Oo. Among them was Miguelina A. Alcantara Garcia, an immigrant from the Dominican Republic who had given birth just 17 days before the fire.

Ms. Alcantara Garcia, a hospital housekeeper, and her daughter, Emma, never made it out alive. Emma’s tiny body was pulled from the rubble the next day.

Mr. Tin Aung Oo said he believed the outcome of the fire and others like it would have been different if the city inspected buildings more aggressively and forced landlords to remedy safety issues.

“If we had all the fire protection,” he said, “my brother and the lady who died with her baby would not have lost their lives.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Ashley Southall writes about cannabis legalization in New York.

Democrats Strengthen the Legal Line With Attorneys General Triumphs

The New York Times November 20, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Once considered vulnerable to local issues, Democratic candidates for attorneys general romped on Tuesday, with the final contests called against Republican attorneys general in Kansas and Ohio.

By David W. Chen

With The Associated Press’s late declaration on Friday that a Democrat has won the attorney general’s race in Ohio, the party wrapped up a midterm election surge that will fortify the Democrats’ legal bulwark against President Trump.

Democrats ousted two incumbents and won three additional attorney general posts that had previously been held by Republicans.

Among the incumbents defeated was Kansas’ Kris Kobach, known for writing and pushing divisive state level legislation on immigration, voting and abortion restrictions. Beyond Kansas, Democratic attorneys general have taken open posts in Iowa, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all of which are currently Republican.

Additionally, vulnerable Democratic incumbents such as Keith Ellison in Minnesota and Kris Mayes in Arizona cruised to re-election, despite Republican hopes that local concerns would overcome the national environment. Democratic newcomers easily prevailed in open contests in Michigan and Nevada as well.

With Democrats now poised to be the top law enforcement official in 29 states, they will have even more collective muscle to spearhead their party’s efforts over the last two years of the Trump administration. In the first two, Democratic attorneys general filed more than 150 cases against the administration on issues ranging from the withholding of federal funds to tariffs and the deployment of National Guard troops.

“At a time when people are worried about the rising cost of living and their rights and freedoms being put at risk, voters see that it’s Democratic A. G. s who rise to the challenge and will fight to protect them,” Sean Rankin, president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said in a statement.

During the campaign, Republican candidates tried to sidestep questions regarding their views on state lawsuits against the Trump administration — or on Mr. Trump, whose approval ratings have sagged in Republican and Democratic states alike. Instead, they stressed local issues, such as a social services fraud scandal in Minnesota.

But Mr. Ellison won by more than 8 percentage points over Ron Schutz, a longtime trial lawyer and Republican activist. Other triumphant Democratic incumbents in battleground states included Josh Kaul in Wisconsin and Ms. Mayes in Arizona, who won by 280 votes in 2022 but more than 10 percentage points on Tuesday.

Republicans had been bullish about Michigan, where a high-profile U. S. Senate race and control of the State Legislature were also on the line. But Eli Savit, a progressive Democratic prosecutor, defeated Doug Lloyd, a Republican prosecutor, by almost 8 percentage points — the same winning margin for Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat.

In Georgia, State Representative Tanya Miller, a Democrat and former prosecutor, won by double digits. In Texas, State Senator Nathan Johnson won comfortably as well, though by a smaller winning margin than Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. Mr. Johnson will succeed Ken Paxton, the scandal-scarred attorney general of Texas who tried and failed to leap to the U. S. Senate.

“After years of A. G. s who mired the office in corruption and petty politics, today Texans said enough is enough,” Lottie Ash, political director of the Democrats’ attorney general group, said on election night.

In Kansas, Mr. Kobach, a longtime Republican lightning rod, lost to Chris Mann, a former police officer and prosecutor, by one percentage point, part of an unlikely Democratic surge in the state that saw State Senator Cindy Holscher win her race to succeed a Democratic governor and Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister in Kansas, handily beat Senator Roger Marshall.

In Iowa, Attorney General Brenna Bird lost by about two percentage points to Nate Willems, a former state representative. She outperformed Representative Ashley Hinson, who lost to State Representative Josh Turek in the U. S. Senate race, and Zach Lahn, a businessman, who was trounced by Rob Sand, the state auditor, in the governor’s race.

Republicans had better news in Florida, up and down the ticket. Attorney General James Uthmeier edged Jose Javier Rodriguez, a former state legislator, overcoming a late $5 million investment by the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

And in South Carolina, where Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, stunned Senator Darline Graham, David Stumbo, a conservative prosecutor, won an open race to run the office which will handle the retrial of Alex Murdaugh.

Still, Adam Piper, the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, wrote in a memo that Tuesday’s results constituted “a category-five political hurricane” up and down the ballot.

Democrats won every statewide office in Texas and Georgia, and nearly did the same in Ohio. Moreover, Democrats scored new trifectas — controlling both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — en route to netting at least 460 legislative seats.

“With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican A. G. s are both America’s front line and its last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list — such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE,” Mr. Piper wrote.

David W. Chen is a Times reporter focused on state legislatures, state level policymaking and the political forces behind them.

Jonathan Yardley, Who Reviewed 3,000 Books and Pulled Zero Punches, Has Died

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As a Pulitzer Prize-winning critic for The Washington Post, he believed praise could be boring. He was 87.

By Sam Roberts

Jonathan Yardley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning bibliophile who wrote often scabrous book reviews for The Washington Post that challenged celebrated authors whose works he felt had been cursorily acclaimed, and who ran a popular column reacquainting his readers with neglected gems, died on Friday in Washington. He was 87.

His death, at an assisted-living residence, was confirmed by his son Jim.

Reviewing some 3,000 books for The Post for more than 33 years — and “never missing a day’s work,” as he put it — Mr. Yardley delivered blunt appraisals of established, best-selling writers, eschewing euphemisms in fulfilling what he considered his mission to spare readers a wasted investment of their precious time and money.

The writer Joe McGinniss, for instance, had risen to critical acclaim with his first book, in 1969, about the marketing of Richard Nixon during his 1968 presidential campaign. But Mr. Yardley had these words for Mr. McGinniss’s salacious 1993 biography of Ted Kennedy, “The Last Brother: The Rise and Fall of Teddy Kennedy”: “a textbook example of shoddy journalistic and publishing ethics.”

“It is also a genuinely, unrelievedly rotten book,” he added, “one without a single redeeming virtue, an embarrassment that should bring nothing except shame to everyone associated with it.”

In the same vein, Kathryn Harrison’s widely praised 1997 memoir, “The Kiss,” a brutal recounting of her sexual relationship with her estranged father, was dismissed by Mr. Yardley as “slimy, repellent, meretricious.”

“The temptation to go on and on about this book,” he wrote, “piling one abusive paragraph upon another, is extreme, but must be resisted. Space is short in this newspaper.”

Neither was the canon spared from his scrutiny.

John Steinbeck, in his view, was a “plodding, graceless prose stylist” who was not “a great, or even near-great, writer,” he wrote in 1994. Mr. Yardley remembered cherishing J. D. Salinger’s 1951 novel “The Catcher in the Rye” as a teenager, but he reread it decades later and described it as “almost literally a painful experience: The combination of Salinger’s execrable prose and Caulfield’s jejune narcissism produced effects comparable to mainlining castor oil.” Neither did he hold much regard for Ernest Hemingway’s 1952 novella “The Old Man and the Sea.”

Those works by Mr. Salinger and Mr. Hemingway, while “durable and beloved,” he concluded, were also “by any reasonable critical standard, two of the worst.”

He admitted, as a reviewer, to relishing the attack more than heaping praise. “The very vocabulary of attack is more varied and interesting,” he told Washingtonian magazine in 2007. “‘Wonderful,’ ‘extraordinary,’ ‘exceptional,’ ‘accomplished’ — blah, blah, blah. You get bored fast.”

For him, good literature was unpretentious and not of the navel-gazing variety, and instead cast a reflective eye out onto the world. Of those that undoubtedly qualified for him were the works of C. S. Forester, William Faulkner, Flannery O’Connor, Peter Taylor and Ralph Ellison, whose “Invisible Man” he said he had read multiple times.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

When praise did come, Mr. Yardley could greatly lift the profile of new authors, and he had a hand in propelling the careers of John Kennedy Toole, John Berendt, William Boyd, Michael Chabon, Olga Grushin, Edward P. Jones and Anne Tyler.

Mr. Toole’s “A Confederacy of Dunces” first appeared in print in 1980 after a yearslong crusade by the mother of the young novelist, who had died by suicide following the unanimous rejection of his manuscript.

Writing in The Washington Star, the paper where Mr. Yardley worked before joining The Post in 1981, he noted: “There’s a temptation, in the circumstances, to regard the book as a freak — a novel more notable for its history than for its merits. Nearly a dozen New York publishers can’t be wrong, can they? Yes, they can; even the best of them make mistakes.”

“‘A Confederacy of Dunces’ is a marvelous book,” Mr. Yardley continued. “It may be a trifle shapeless and discursive, but that simply doesn’t matter. This is rich, outrageous, hilarious, moving stuff, alive with vivid characters and true-to-life settings.”

Mr. Toole’s novel won the Pulitzer in fiction in 1981. Mr. Yardley was also the chairman of the Pulitzer fiction jury that year, and his review of the book was one of the citations for his own Pulitzer win, for criticism, that same year.

Mr. Chabon, too, was a beneficiary of Mr. Yardley’s positive appraisal. “There’s no getting around it,” Mr. Yardley wrote in The Post in 1995 of Mr. Chabon’s third book, “Wonder Boys.” “Chabon leaves no doubt that he is the young star of American letters.”

Mr. Chabon later recounted that Mr. Yardley’s gentle prodding, in the review, to “explore larger worlds,” pushed him to pursue what would become his Pulitzer-winning novel, “The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay.”

For seven years beginning in 2003, Mr. Yardley wrote a column every month or so called “Second Reading,” which reconsidered some of the notable but forgotten or neglected books — about 100 in all — that he retrieved from his bookshelves.

Among them was Edwin O’Connor’s 1964 novel of a vaudevillian, “I Was Dancing” (“I’d be hard-pressed to say that any book discussed therein is more undeservedly neglected than this one,” Mr. Yardley wrote), and Thornton Wilder’s “The Bridge of San Luis Rey.” “It is no exaggeration to say that on second reading,” he noted of Mr. Wilder Pulitzer-winning 1927 novel, “I was completely blown away, not so much by Wilder’s sensitive treatment of his central theme as by the richness and power of his prose.”

“I came to this task as a journalist, not a literateur, and I have remained one to this day,” he told readers of The Post in 2014 as he was retiring. “I have high literary standards and delight in the expression of strong opinion, literary and otherwise, but I also read a book as if I were a reporter: looking for what it is ‘about’ in the deepest sense of the word, determining what matters about it and what doesn’t, trying to give the reader a feel for what it is like as well as passing judgment on it.”

Sam Tanenhaus, a former editor of The New York Times Book Review, wrote in an email in 2024 that Mr. Yardley was “the rare reviewer who earned the designation ‘critic’ — which is to say he did not just tell you what he thought of a book, thumbs up or down, but what authors were trying to do.”

“He assumed readers looked for the same things he did, high literary ambition and developed artistry,” Mr. Tanenhaus added.

Jonathan Yardley was born in Pittsburgh on Oct. 27, 1939, and grew up in Chatham, a town in southern Virginia. His father, William Woolsey Yardley, was an educator who taught English and the classics and was the headmaster of Chatham Hall, a girls’ boarding school. His mother was Helen (Gregory) Yardley.

After graduating in 1957 from the Groton School in Massachusetts and in 1961 from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, he was an intern for James Reston, a columnist and the Washington bureau chief of The Times.

While working as an editorial writer and book reviewer for The Greensboro Daily News in North Carolina from 1964 to 1974, he was a Nieman fellow at Harvard University, where he studied American literature and literary biography, and also contributed reviews to The Times.

Mr. Yardley served as book editor of The Miami Herald from 1974 to 1978, then moved to The Star, where he won the Pulitzer for criticism in 1981. After The Star folded in 1981, he joined The Post and announced his retirement at the end of 2014.

Mr. Yardley, a jazz enthusiast, also edited anthologies and wrote several books, including a biography of the sports columnist Ring Lardner and another of the fictional memoirist Frederick Exley.

His own chronicle of the white, Anglo-Saxon Protestant world of his parents, “Our Kind of People: The Story of an American Family” (1989), was praised by Elizabeth Janeway in The Times Book Review as reading “like a first-rate novel.”

In 1991, H. L. Mencken’s unfinished memoir was released from archives where it had been held for 35 years since his death, per the author’s instructions. Mr. Mencken’s publisher, Knopf, then commissioned Mr. Yardley to edit the sprawling 300,000 to 400,000 pages into what became “My Life as Author and Editor” (1993).

Terry Teachout, in a review in The Times, praised Mr. Yardley for transforming “a massive document of interest mainly to scholars into a rich, absorbing memoir.”

His marriages to Rosemary Roberts and Susan L. Hartt ended in divorce. In 1999, he married Marie Arana, an author and journalist who edited The Post’s Book World section.

In addition to his wife, he is survived by two sons from his first marriage, Jim and William Yardley; two stepchildren, Lalo Walsh and Adam Ward; two sisters, Jane and Sarah; a brother, Benjamin; and 11 grandchildren.

(Jonathan and Jim, who is currently an assistant managing editor at The Times, are among the few father-son Pulitzer recipients.)

When Mr. Yardley retired, he wrote in The Post that he looked forward to reading books simply for pleasure: “lots of P. G. Wodehouse and Peter Taylor first and foremost, of course, and Flannery O’Connor, and Ward Just, and Ellen Glasgow, and Raymond Chandler, and Anne Tyler, and John D. MacDonald, and doubtless ‘The Count of Monte Cristo’ for the umpteenth time.”

“I promise to make one last attempt to read ‘Ulysses,’” Mr. Yardley also wrote, “the gargantuan novel by James Joyce that was admitted to this country by my great-great uncle, federal Judge John Woolsey, whose famous opinion authorizing its admission” — after its ban for obscenity — “I regard as considerably more engaging, witty and intelligible than the novel itself.”

Mr. Yardley expressed optimism for the future of books to “survive and perhaps even thrive.”

“I am an old-fashioned man in a new-fashioned world,” he wrote, “which is reason enough to step aside, though, while doing so, to argue for the continuing value and pertinence of much that is old-fashioned, above all the carefully, scrupulously written word.”

Sam Roberts is an obituaries reporter for The Times, writing mini-biographies about the lives of remarkable people.

John Grisham: The Meaning of Scott Colom’s Victory

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By John Grisham

Mr. Grisham is an author.

In January of 1984, I took my newly won seat in the Mississippi House of Representatives as one of 122 members. Only about 15 percent were Black. Down the hall in the Senate, things were even whiter. In a state that is 37 percent Black, the disproportion was obvious. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 had empowered Black people to register and vote, but all manner of nefarious schemes by white lawmakers guaranteed Black strength remained diluted. The idea of a serious Black candidate seeking statewide office was too far-fetched to even discuss.

Today, with Republicans in control of all three branches of the state, many of those schemes are still effective. However, on Nov. 3, they backfired.

When Scott Colom began his quixotic campaign for the Senate a year ago, he faced considerable obstacles. First, he’s Black, and white people in Mississippi rarely vote for Black candidates in statewide elections. Black politicians have made remarkable gains in local elections, and Mississippi has more elected Black officials than other states. But they have succeeded locally, not statewide.

Second, and almost as daunting, was the fact that Mr. Colom is a Democrat. No Democrat has been elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982. The math became frustratingly simple: The vast majority of the state’s Black population votes Democratic while white voters overwhelmingly support Republicans. The conventional wisdom was that Democrats would always lose.

The third obstacle was a lack of money coupled with a lack of national interest. Early in the campaign, the serious blue money went to other states where Democrats had much better chances. The general feeling among Democratic donors was that spending money in Mississippi was a waste. Mr. Colom had no chance.

If Mr. Colom heard those warnings, he wasn’t fazed. The only optimism came from the fact that the Republicans weren’t spending money either. Why bother? Mississippi was a deep red state, and it was impossible for the incumbent to lose.

The fourth obstacle was history. No Black candidate had been elected to the Senate since Reconstruction.

How did Mr. Colom win?

Look at the candidate. He is a genuinely likable young man from a prominent family with a long tradition of public service and a passion for civil rights. He’s bright, sharp, well-educated, a quick study who speaks eloquently, though a bit fast at times because he has a lot to say. He’s a lawyer known for his ability. A judge known for his evenhandedness. A prosecutor known for his fairness. He’s a devout Christian serious about his faith. A husband and father devoted to his family.

In Mississippi, all of the above usually translates to about 45 percent of the vote for a Democrat running statewide. In 2020, Mike Espy, a popular Black former congressman, ran a well-financed campaign for Senate and received 44 percent of the vote against the incumbent Mr. Colom just defeated.

Next, look at the turnout. Republican Party officials have been relentless in their efforts to (1) suppress voting; (2) water down blue districts; and (3) protect incumbents. Sixty years ago, Black people barely voted in Mississippi. Under Jim Crow, they had been denied basic rights for roughly a hundred years. Their struggle for suffrage was historic, protracted and often violent. A lot of blood was shed on the way to the polls. People don’t like their voting rights tampered with. Black voters may have been predisposed to Mr. Colom, but there was also widespread anger at schemes to rig the maps and suppress the vote. On Nov. 3, that anger helped drive more voters in some majority-Black neighborhoods to the polls than in 2024.

Next was the Trump factor. As was proved across the country, voters are fed up with inflation and blame the war and tariffs.

They are also frustrated with President Trump’s incompetence, corruption, frivolous fixations, coziness with Putin, lack of support for Ukraine and so on. It’s a long list. And Mr. Colom managed to win 25 percent of the white vote, which is more than anyone expected.

Mr. Colom had a message, a little upfront money and a lot of hope. He became a ferocious campaigner and did not shy away from the state’s tortured history on race relations; rather, he embraced it. He often invoked memories of his idols from the civil rights struggles. Medgar Evers is a favorite. In one of his most effective ads, he stands in front of the home where Evers was murdered by a white supremacist in 1963.

Mr. Colom narrates: “There’s a home in Jackson every Mississippian ought to walk through once. It looks like every other house on the street, except for it isn’t. It has no front door. You come in through the carport, where the walls give you some cover. The children slept on the floor, below the windows. Their father taught them that if they ever heard gunfire, they should crawl to the bathroom. He made it a game.”

He continues: “I’ve been a prosecutor for 10 years. Unfortunately, I’ve stood in a lot of houses where something terrible happened. This isn’t any house. This isn’t any tragedy. This is where Medgar Evers died. He fought for this country at Normandy. He came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote.”

His ads resonated with the younger crowd. During a rare interview, his opponent was quizzed about inflation and the rising cost of beef. She flippantly replied that people were free to choose other, cheaper types of protein. “You have so many proteins to choose from,” she said. Words that would haunt her.

“Pick another protein” became a viral sensation when Ryan Sayles, a 27-year-old content creator, produced a 30-second ad that parodied the choice of picking another protein or picking a different senator. The video roared through social media and entertained millions.

In the campaign’s final weeks, the breaks began to fall Mr. Colom’s way. His crowds were larger, his message clearer. The polls tightened and more money came in. The Republicans were so rattled that Mr. Trump made a last-minute stop in the state to inspire his people.

Late on the night of Nov. 3, as the blue wave kept gaining momentum and producing upsets across the country, we watched in amazement as Mr. Colom clung to a narrow lead. As county after county reported, and even the reddest ones were trending blue, we asked ourselves the great question: “Could this finally be happening in Mississippi?”

Mr. Colom’s victory does not mean that most people in my home state are suddenly more tolerant. What it does mean is that a new, clear voice has arrived. And that voice will not be silent in the struggle to alleviate childhood hunger, or to reform criminal injustice, or to properly fund schools and hospitals, or to oppose unnecessary wars, conflicts and corruption. The blue wave brings a chorus of new progressive voices to politics, and Mr. Colom’s will be heard.

Pride in his win runs deep. And statewide! A lot of white folks are saying: “Hey, that wasn’t so difficult. And we won!”

When he won, he thanked his crowd and graciously deflected credit for the miracle. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he said. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we could show the country that Mississippi matters.”

As a kid, I once watched the Ku Klux Klan burn a cross in my hometown in Mississippi. Sixty years later, I look forward to shaking Mr. Colom’s hand and telling him I’m proud he’s my senator.

Thank you for capturing in eloquent words what many of us in Mississippi experienced over the years, and felt the night Scott was elected. He brings a new brand of political leadership: Who else would have stood in the Trump line in Corinth to understand the mind of the voters? Now, he is holding his first town hall in the reddest county, Itawamba, because he is committed to serving all Mississippians. We are so proud of him, and we are proud of Mississippi. Mississippi matters deeply.

As an Alabamian, raised in a family of civil rights and political activists, I love this piece. Thank you, Mr. Grisham and Senator Colom for charting this amazing story of what American democracy can and should be! This centuries long struggle for Black freedom and full citizenship is it the heart of how multiracial democracy was constructed in this country, despite supremacists determination to suppress it. This is the line of patriotism I live in and how I can, despite difficult history, authentically love this country.

John Grisham served from 1984 to 1990 in the Mississippi House of Representatives. Now an author, he still dabbles in Mississippi politics when he’s not writing.

Spying Suspect’s Chip Network Has Ties to Chinese Military Suppliers

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

Companies linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, are part of a network of Chinese tech firms and defense contractors that need advanced computing power.

By Julian E. BarnesPaul Mozur and Ana Swanson

The journalists have been reporting on Alice Huang’s connections to the Chinese government and her efforts to help China gain access to advanced A. I. chips.

Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, has extensive ties through her family and associates to China’s defense industry, according to an independent research firm and corporate filings reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings show a web of relationships, most of them indirect, linking Ms. Huang’s family and companies that acquired Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The nature of those relationships, including the vital question of whether Nvidia chips ended up being used to support Chinese military projects, remains murky. But the revelations, along with an investigation by The Times published on Wednesday, underscore how the Chinese effort to acquire access to the computing power of Nvidia’s chips is intertwined with Beijing’s desire to harness artificial intelligence to bolster its military capabilities.

That outcome has long been feared by U. S. national security officials, given that the technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A. I. into the battlefield.

A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm that employs former intelligence officers and experts on China and specializes in corporate intelligence, shows that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Ms. Huang’s family or associates. The government money funded technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia chips.

The New York Times reviewed the Strider findings. Many of the corporate ties revealed by Strider were independently confirmed by The Times.

The Times reported last month that U. S. officials believe Ms. Huang, a Chinese citizen also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to the Ministry of State Security. The Strider Technologies analysis and the review of corporate filings by The Times show that she; her sister, Huang Yu; and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Alice Huang’s business partner and often introduced as her husband, are tied to a web of companies that connect official Nvidia partners, which can buy advanced Nvidia A. I. chips, to state- and military-linked projects.

Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as the company’s chief executive after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, who is no relation.

Companies in the Huang family’s network co-own a cybersecurity venture with an arm of China’s main military-electronics conglomerate, lease Nvidia-powered servers financed by an affiliate of its largest military aircraft maker and in one case share a parent company with a maker of radar and missile components.

Two companies that have partnerships with Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong, are connected to Ms. Huang. Ms. Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm that is under investigation by the Justice Department for smuggling advanced chips into China. Megaspeed has said Ms. Huang, whose involvement with Mr. Huang corresponded with a period when it was acquiring large numbers of Nvidia chips, no longer works for the company.

Ms. Huang’s family members had prominent roles and significant investments in the data center firm that founded Century Litong, which is based in Shanghai and rents out computing power to major Chinese companies and military contractors. The family members include Ms. Huang’s sister and Mr. Kang.

U. S. officials are also working to learn more about Ms. Huang and her efforts to help supply chips to data centers. The nature and extent of her ties to the P. L. A. and the companies it controls are a focus of that work, according to people briefed on the American efforts.

The ties are complex and often indirect. The research does not show whether the P. L. A. used computing power in the data centers that the family’s companies helped build. But it shows how deeply Ms. Huang and her family are intertwined with the Chinese state, and the inextricable connections between China’s tech industry and its military.

“Beijing has spent years building these networks that reach deep into Western economies,” said Greg Levesque, the chief executive of Strider. “Follow the money and, too often, you find the P. L. A. at the end of it.”

Mr. Levesque said China was exploiting more Western technology, capital and talent than ever before to build its defense industrial base. “This is happening on a scale we simply weren’t seeing a few years ago,” he said.

Nvidia declined to comment. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Huang could not be reached for comment.

From late last year into early this year, Century Litong appears to have been one of only a few sources able to supply Nvidia chips to China at the vast scale needed for its A. I. build-out, according to Strider.

Those chips were key to building the data centers that drive China’s A. I. development. Investigators are trying to determine how many of the chips that were used in those data centers were banned under U. S. export controls and, in essence, smuggled into the country. Companies controlled by Ms. Huang and her relatives were instrumental in supplying the chips, Strider found.

“Essentially, those entities worked around the controls to continue to meet the chip demands of the customers they already had, including at new data centers,” Mr. Levesque said.

On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information on Nvidia’s license applications to legally sell H200 chips to Chinese firms. The list showed that Nvidia had sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to the Hong Kong subsidiary of Century Litong.

An Nvidia spokesman said that, despite receiving some licenses, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and Nvidia had not and would not ship to that firm.

Century Litong has said it has no business dealings with Ms. Huang. But the company was founded in 2023 by Century Longteng, a data center operator that was then 27 percent owned by an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister. Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s presumed husband, had been Century Longteng’s executive director since February 2022, according to Strider.

In 2023, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, a Shanghai-listed maker of metal parts for flat-screen TVs, bought 90 percent of Century Litong, and owned all of it by 2024. Lettall also owns 80 percent of Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a maker of components that Lettall has said are used in Chinese radar and missile systems. Strider said Jinning’s parts go into the P. L. A.’s DF-series missiles, including intercontinental ballistic missiles and anti-ship “carrier killers,” as well as the J-20 stealth fighter plane.

China’s defense industry wants advanced A. I. chips to design better missiles and build other military software, experts have said.

Lettall did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Asked about Ms. Huang’s network of companies and their efforts to acquire chips, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said he was not familiar with the situation. “We have made clear more than once our principled position on U. S. chip exports to China,” said the spokesman, Liu Chang.

Century Litong delivered servers containing Nvidia’s H800 chips to a supercomputing center in Shanghai in October 2023, according to Strider. It is unclear where Century Litong obtained those chips, but they may have been obtained legally, since U. S. restrictions on the sale of the H800 to China did not go into effect until that same month.

Century Litong now runs servers at the Shanghai supercomputing center under a lease of about $54 million from a leasing arm of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, China’s state aerospace and defense conglomerate.

Century Litong’s reach extends far beyond the Chinese A. I. giant Tencent. When Lettall bought into the company in 2023, it said all of Century Litong’s computing business would be housed in two places: the Tencent center in Shanghai and a data center in Shenzhen.

The Shenzhen center was built for the cloud unit of Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant that has long been under sanctions by the United States over national security concerns. Huawei awarded the project in 2022 to a company controlled by Century Longteng, according to corporate filings.

Century Litong’s customers have also included a unit of China Electronics Technology Group, or C. E. T. C., a state-owned military electronics maker. The United States has included C. E. T. C. on its list of companies that it publicly identifies as doing work with the Chinese military, banning the firm from doing work with Pentagon suppliers.

Another Century Litong partner is Hangjin Technology, a listed company whose subsidiaries make chips for China’s military.

Until last December, Hangjin controlled Chaoqing, an Nvidia partner whose website once listed High-Flyer, the hedge fund behind the Chinese A. I. start-up DeepSeek, as a partner. Others on the list included the military-linked Zhejiang Lab and its co-founder, Alibaba.

DeepSeek has attracted attention for its cutting-edge A. I. models. But lawmakers in the United States have also accused it of presenting national security risks, and the federal government has banned employees from using it. The Information earlier reported ties between Ms. Huang’s network and DeepSeek.

Hangjin did not respond to an emailed request for comment. It has said it does no business with DeepSeek.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

A Supermodel Will Finally Get Her Day in Court

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Carré Otis spent years trying to serve her former agent in a lawsuit accusing him of sexual abuse. It took an international operation to make it happen.

By Vanessa Friedman

In mid-October, Gérald Marie, a former modeling agent who was at the heart of the French fashion world in the 1990s, lounged poolside at his home, high in the lush hills of Ibiza. Around him, his garden bloomed with greenery; below him, the deep blue waters of the Balearic Sea glittered.

And though he probably didn’t know it, high above him a drone hovered, tracking his moves, monitoring when he would be leaving his compound that balmy day.

The drone was a part of a marathon effort on behalf of the former supermodel Carré Otis to get Marie to answer accusations of sexual abuse and trafficking of a minor.

Otis, famous for modeling in Calvin Klein and Guess ads in the 1990s, first made the accusations in her 2011 memoir, “Beauty, Disrupted,” describing how, at age 17, she had been sent to Paris by her modeling agency to live in his apartment, where, she said, he repeatedly raped her when his girlfriend at the time, the model Linda Evangelista, was away.

Otis also wrote that she and other young models were brought to parties by Marie, where they were trafficked to other men. Eventually, 11 other models also made claims against Marie; Evangelista also accused him of physical abuse. He has denied all allegations.

Ten years after her memoir, Otis said she finally worked up the courage to legally pursue Marie. The Child Victims Act, which allowed claims that fell outside the original statute of limitations, was about to end in New York. Fearful that it might be her last chance to have her case heard, she had her lawyer, John Clune, a former prosecutor who now works with survivors of sexual assault, file a lawsuit on Aug. 12, 2021, in Federal District Court in Manhattan.

Otis thought she’d made it to the other side of a tough, emotional decision. The next step was to serve Marie the papers. What she didn’t realize was that it would take another five years, plus the efforts of a YouTube activist and a French tutor, to do it. “It was actually really, really crazy,” Otis said.

Otis and Clune believed Marie was living in a villa atop a hill overlooking the town of Es Cubells on the Spanish island of Ibiza. The house was named Casa Linda, presumably a nod to Evangelista (they were married from 1987 to 1993).

According to an international agreement, Clune needed to go through the Spanish Central Authority to get the lawsuit to Marie. But it took nearly a year for Clune to learn that their repeated attempts to serve Marie had been thwarted — a misspelled name, door knocks that went unanswered.

In New York, meanwhile, Otis’s case had been dismissed, appealed and — yet another year later — reinstated. At which point Clune tried to go through the Spanish Central Authority again. But by April of this year, with Marie still not served, Clune realized that they would need a new approach.

He contacted a private investigator named Juan V. Cruz, who attempted to serve Marie three times at his home. Twice a woman answered the door and said Marie was not home; once no one answered at all.

Frustrated, Clune tried to have the papers delivered through the mail, using the Postal Service, FedEx and DHL. In one case, Marie never showed up to sign for his mail at the post office; in the others, Clune was told that the address he provided was not usable.

Finally, Clune decided, “we just needed somebody out there.”

Carly P. Reilly, 32, is no one’s idea of a clandestine agent. She grew up in Vermont, has long, brownish-blond hair and talks at 1.5 speed. She had worked as the finance director for Andrew Yang’s 2020 presidential campaign and had a podcast on cryptocurrency before moving to Paris in 2024. Her namesake YouTube channel and Substack focuses on dissecting the story of Jeffrey Epstein and similar power networks. Reilly became interested in Otis’s case after they were introduced through an Epstein victim and fellow model.

In one of their texts, Otis told Reilly about her challenges getting to Marie. Otis and Clune had become wary of working with Ibiza locals, fearing they might be connected to Marie in some way. Though she had never done anything like this before, Reilly volunteered to step in.

“I was like, ‘Look, I’d love to help you, and I’d love to document this process,’” Reilly said.

At that point, however, they weren’t even sure he was in Ibiza. Then, in late August, the French radio station RTL published the first interview with Marie, 76, in six years. In it, he was described as speaking from his home in Ibiza. He denied raping anyone and called his sexual relations with Otis “consensual.”

Reilly had discovered that home listed on a luxury vacation rental website. To pin down Marie’s movements, she posed as a rich woman looking for a lavish holiday retreat, despite not knowing the first thing about what such a person might demand — Reilly lives in a studio apartment with a mini-fridge and a two-burner stove. So she turned to the chatbot Claude.

“It told me to ask if any of the master suites felt more like junior suites and how many of the bedrooms had true sea-facing views,” she said.

She called up the rental company, feigning interest in several homes, then flagged Casa Linda, with a pretend question: “It seems the most private. Is that really true?”

The listing agent started talking dates. Casa Linda wasn’t available in October, he said, because the owner was coming back.

Now Reilly had a time frame, but she needed backup. She enlisted her French tutor, Jean Mouzet, 36, who also speaks fluent Spanish, to help with translation and logistics. She has a “complete inability to do any map stuff,” she said.

Then she got in touch with Donal MacIntyre, a former BBC investigative reporter, who had confronted Marie for “60 Minutes Australia” at a cafe in Ibiza.

MacIntyre introduced her to a group of people who had helped him, including Jon Clarke, a onetime Daily Mail journalist who had relocated to start a local newspaper.

Clarke had identified the cafe where MacIntyre ultimately confronted Marie by driving around the ritziest areas of Ibiza and asking people if they recognized him. “One of them said: ‘Oh yeah, that’s Gérald. Comes a lot with his wife. Russian girl.’”

MacIntyre, Clarke and the team prepped Reilly. “You basically have to park yourself somewhere, hide out and wait,’” she remembers them telling her. “You’re going to be paranoid, and you’re going to constantly think that you’ve been discovered, but you probably haven’t, and that’s just, like, how this work goes.”

She and Mouzet kept Otis in the loop via Signal.

For Otis, the entire experience was surreal. “We’d been talking for months about this, and it was like, ‘This is going to happen,’” Otis said. “It would be the craziest thing if it actually worked.”

On Oct. 13, Reilly and Mouzet arrived in Ibiza. They booked a cheap hotel, then took an Uber to the base of the winding road that leads to Marie’s house and hiked up to check out his villa. “There’s not a sound except for the birds,” Reilly recalled. They angled an iPhone over the vegetation to capture Marie’s gray Mini Countryman.

The next day, they went over the plan. They met with a local cameraman and a sound guy, rented a moped, and chose the intersection at the bottom of Marie’s road as their stakeout spot. Reilly thought they could masquerade as a crew making “a little documentary about the stunning beauty of Ibiza.”

On Oct. 15, they were ready. When they arrived at noon, Reilly was wearing white jeans and a camisole. “I felt like there was sort of a statement to be made about feeling feminine and being the person to do this,” she said.

At 12:30 p. m. the drone captured Marie by the swimming pool, “chilling,” Mouzet said. Half an hour later, he was no longer there. Then, Mouzet said, “I see a car in the intersection, and I’m like: ‘That’s him. He’s here.’”

The cameraman’s car began following Marie; Reilly and Mouzet hopped on their motorbike, a GoPro camera on the handlebars.

“I’m recording a selfie video at this point, trying to pretend to be some influencer,” Reilly said. Marie’s car accelerated, and she realized, “He’s right in front of us. He just passed us! We’re right behind him.”

They were so focused they didn’t notice a white car pulling out of a driveway until it smacked into the motorbike.

“We go down,” Reilly said.

The car struck her leg, and Mouzet hit his head on the ground. Dazed, they gathered their cameras. The motorbike was totaled.

Mouzet called the cameraman and the sound guy. “I’m like: ‘Listen, we just had a car accident, but focus on the target. Don’t lose him.’”

Marie had arrived at a beachfront restaurant and was eating on the patio. The video crew picked up Reilly and Mouzet and drove them to the restaurant, then set up as if they were filming the water.

Reilly, who had a bleeding knee, grabbed the court papers out of a backpack and limped into the eatery. As she reached Marie, she said, “Gérald Marie, you’re being served on accusations of rape of Carré Otis when she was a minor.”

Moments later, Reilly called Otis from the car. “It wasn’t a moment of rejoicing,” Otis said. “I sat down at my little meditation station and just started crying. It was like, ‘Wow, this has been a lonely road.’ Fifteen years of being blacklisted, having people recoil. It is so sad that we had to go to these lengths because the system has failed us again and again and again.”

Reilly and Mouzet went straight to the hospital, where she got two stitches and Mouzet was evaluated for a concussion. Soon after, they sent an affidavit of service to Clune as well as photographs of the event.

Clune filed a notice with the court that the papers had been handed to Marie, leaving him 21 days to respond to the lawsuit. As of Friday, Marie still has not acknowledged the receipt.

Céline Bekerman, who represents Marie in France, said in an email on Nov. 10 that she did not “consider it appropriate to comment on procedural matters before the New York courts, or to anticipate any position Mr. Marie may take in that context.”

Now, Clune said, he will be seeking entry of a default judgment and a determination of damages. He hopes there will be a public hearing, at which Otis and other models who have accused Marie of assaulting them can testify before a judge.

(Some of those women and Otis are part of another lawsuit underway in France, also accusing Marie of rape and trafficking.)

“To have a judge hear it in some sort of official capacity and then make a decision based on her testimony would be very meaningful,” Clune said.

Given his lack of response thus far, it is unclear whether Marie would be there. But “so much of what we do at this point is symbolic,” Otis acknowledged. “What Gérald Marie represents is a mind-set. For me, it’s about seeing change within the systems that enable all of this.”

Since 2018, I have reported extensively on the sexual abuse of models by powerful figures in the fashion industry. I've become familiar with very emotional stories and stories about the system being broken, but I had never come across a story like Carré Otis’s. It took her five years — with help from a YouTube activist, a French tutor and a chatbot — to get the lawsuit against her former agent served. This story added a whole new dimension to my understanding of why it can be so hard for these lawsuits to even get to court.

Vanessa Friedman has been the fashion director and chief fashion critic for The Times since 2014.

What Are King Tides, and Why Is Everyone Talking About Them?

The New York Times November 20, 2026

West Coast Weather

Advertisement

Supported by

Because of El Niño, the Pacific Ocean is already higher than normal. This year, that could lead to some especially high tides.

By Amy Graff

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

Every fall and winter along the West Coast of the United States, the ocean swallows beaches. The Pacific lifts up and over the shore, and salt water spills onto roads and pathways. Hours later, it pulls back, exposing broad expanses of beach, seafloor, rocks and marine life that are usually covered by water.

This dramatic display comes from the highest and lowest tides of the year, commonly called “king tides” by the people who experience them. Usually, they bring only minor flooding and inconvenience. But the damage can become more serious when the high tides coincide with rain, winds and waves.

This winter, forecasters have warned that with sea levels along the West Coast higher than normal because of the strong El Niño climate pattern, these tides could reach their highest levels on record.

“King tide” is an informal, nonscientific term for the highest high tides of the year. It has no entry in the National Weather Service glossary of meteorological terms.

It was mentioned as early as the 1800s, in Australian newspapers; one, in 1868, described the tides as ebbing and flowing “with great violence.” In the early 21st century, an environmental effort in Australia thrust the term into the modern public eye, when the King Tides Project there sought to document dramatically high tides as a way to help communities conceptualize what sea level rise would look like in a changing climate.

Other countries and communities with vulnerable coastlines adopted similar programs, from New Zealand and Tuvalu to the Western United States.

Government agencies in the United States didn’t start using the term until recently. “It was not a thing when I left the N. W. S. at the end of 1997,” said Jan Null, a veteran meteorologist and former forecaster for the Weather Service.

“Somewhere in the last 20 years, the term has become more commonly used,” he said, citing its increasing popularity on social media.

Tides are vast waves rolling around the ocean that are generated by the gravitational attraction between the moon and the sun on Earth. The moon and the sun both tug at the Earth and its oceans as it spins around on its axis. The laws of physics take over, resulting in the high and low tides each day.

What people call the king tides occur when the gravitational pull between the sun, moon and Earth is at its maximum strength.

“A couple of times a year, the moon is closer to the Earth, which is a little more gravitational pull, and the moon and the Earth together are closer to the sun, and that adds to that gravitational pull,” said Gary Griggs, a professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

They happen on coastlines around the world during certain seasons. On the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States, that’s mainly during late summer and fall; on the West Coast, it’s during the winter.

Tides have already set records this fall in California, when October’s sent water over shorelines up and down the coast.

Many expect some of those records to be broken again.

The exact dates and times for the highest tides vary by location (look up those closest to you here). The California Coastal Commission, which runs the state’s King Tides Project, lists these dates for the state:

Nov. 24-26

Dec. 23-25

Jan. 21-22

Officials in Oregon and Washington list similar dates, but it is mostly in California where emergency officials and meteorologists are anticipating the kind of flooding that can affect daily life.

“Our coast is more sparsely populated than the coast of California,” said Noah Alviz, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Portland, Ore.

This will vary up and down the coast, but the short answer for some places is probably higher than ever before, experts warned.

King tides on the West Coast can be up to two feet higher than typical high tides.

But this year, the tides are hitting when the water levels along the coast are even higher because of El Niño. The climate pattern is defined by warm water in the Pacific Ocean, and as water warms, it expands, giving sea levels a little lift.

On top of that, the pulses of water known as Kelvin waves are arriving on the shores of the West Coast, sending sea levels even higher. (Go here for more on the science of a Kelvin wave.)

A few more of these waves of water will move across the ocean this winter, but they’re tricky to track in real time, Mr. Griggs said.

A worst-case scenario for residents and emergency officials would be a storm slamming the coast at the same time as the king tides. That would layer the tides, heavy rains and lashing waves on top of the already high sea levels.

“There are agencies that are trying to plan for a situation where all of these things happen at once,” said Karen Kavanaugh, an oceanographer at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

October’s record tides weren’t technically king tides, the Weather Service office in San Francisco noted, though many called them that anyway.

The city’s mayor, too, has embraced a more liberal definition.

Daniel Lurie, the mayor, said in a video last month that San Francisco was expecting 30 king tides between November and January. Even NOAA defines it just as “a nonscientific term people often use to describe exceptionally high tides.”

Some experts worry the term is being overused and, because of that, risks losing its power to raise awareness about the potential for flooding at the coast.

“It brings in warning fatigue,” said Todd Hall, a meteorologist with the Weather Service in Los Angeles. “If you call everything big, it brings in a different factor of, ‘Oh my goodness, this is going to be the worst ever.’”

There is no official scientific definition of king tides and it can be used loosely. Some meteorologists consider only the December tides, which will be the absolute highest, to be king tides. Others embrace the term because it helps them communicate when tides are going to be so much higher than normal. Regardless of what you call them, the experts agree the Thanksgiving week tides are going to be extremely high. They could bring significant flooding if they're layered on top of sea levels that are also elevated from the effects of El Niño and a storm, wind and waves. If you live on the coast what are you doing to prepare for the exceptionally high tides this year?

Amy Graff is a Times reporter covering weather, wildfires and earthquakes.

As He Leaves Office, Ken Paxton Drops Suits Against Political Opponents

The New York Times November 20, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The Texas attorney general has abandoned suits against Muslim and immigrant rights groups — and the N. C. A. A.

By J. David Goodman

Reporting from Houston

Attorney General Ken Paxton, long seen as the tip of the spear for the conservative legal movement in Texas, is no longer in a fighting mood.

Since losing his bid for the U. S. Senate and watching his fellow Republicans lose every statewide race on Election Day, Mr. Paxton has dropped a number of high-profile lawsuits that antagonized his political opponents and appealed to his base.

In recent days, he has abandoned a yearslong lawsuit seeking to shut down a migrant shelter in El Paso and a separate suit aimed at closing a Houston-based immigrant rights group. He dropped a case against the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, which Gov. Greg Abbott had labeled a terrorist organization.

Mr. Paxton also decided to dismiss a suit against the N. C. A. A. after accusing the sports association of deceptive advertising for labeling competitions as “women’s sports” when they could include transgender athletes.

The cases helped Mr. Paxton burnish his standing among conservatives and fuel his reputation as a no-holds-barred litigator. The decisions to drop them were welcomed by the defendants in each case, and the legal filings lacked any explanation from Mr. Paxton or lawyers from his office.

Mr. Paxton’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

One case, a five-year-old lawsuit accusing Planned Parenthood of committing Medicaid fraud, has not been dropped by Mr. Paxton’s office, but the U. S. Justice Department signaled its intention to intervene. The move suggested there was concern among conservatives that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general, Nathan Johnson, would not continue the case.

In a statement, Mr. Johnson said that “irrespective of the likely political motivation behind it, I applaud the termination of these lawsuits,” adding that it was “the first tangible and important result of the election.”

But Mr. Paxton has not thrown in the towel in every instance. His office revived a lawsuit against the city of Houston this week after John Whitmire, its mayor, said the city’s police officers would no longer notify federal immigration agents about unauthorized migrants encountered during routine street stops. The ultimate resolution of that case will most likely not occur until after Mr. Paxton leaves office.

Since the election, lawyers from Mr. Paxton’s office have repeatedly gone to court to ask judges to withdraw lawsuits they had brought.

The timing suggested to many, including the defendants in the cases, that the election of Mr. Johnson, a Democratic governor and enough Democrats to control the Texas House was a central motivation to drop the lawsuits.

“If it goes away in an instant, then what was this about to begin with? If there’s nothing there, then why was this initiated?” said Ruben Garcia, the executive director of the El Paso shelter Annunciation House. “Then this whole thing is political? That’s not the way justice is supposed to work.”

Mr. Garcia was supposed to be deposed by Mr. Paxton’s lawyers last week in the case against Annunciation House, which was first filed in state court in 2024. But rather than move forward with the deposition, the attorney general’s office simply withdrew the lawsuit.

Still, Mr. Garcia said the legal process had done damage to his nonprofit. “They have almost endless resources to go after people,” he said. The suit confused people into thinking the nonprofit had already been closed down, he said, and prospective volunteers worried that getting involved could land them in trouble.

“When someone calls you a smuggler, a trafficker, that your houses of hospitality are stash houses, that’s really severe,” Mr. Garcia said.

Mr. Paxton’s suit accusing the immigrant rights group FIEL Houston was similarly costly, said its executive director, Cesar Espinosa. The attorney general argued that the organization had violated its nonprofit charter by posting about elections and criticizing the Trump administration. The suit had dragged on since 2024, sapping the group’s resources, Mr. Espinosa said.

“We had to move money from other programs to staff time and resources to be able to be all things on deck with this lawsuit,” he said. “It was a very tough last few years.”

The group had not been given advance warning that the suit would be dropped, he said, and no one explained why.

For Edward Ahmed Mitchell, a deputy director at CAIR, Mr. Paxton’s decision to sue his group was made at a time when many Republican elected officials in Texas, including Mr. Abbott, were embracing anti-Muslim rhetoric and actions.

The lawsuit against CAIR was filed in February, in the middle of the Republican Senate primary, which Mr. Paxton won. He dropped the case this week.

Mr. Mitchell said Republicans had used “American Muslims as a political boogeyman” and it failed with voters. “That is a huge turning point,” he said. “Even in Texas, anti-Muslim hate was not enough.”

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.
