Connections Coach

A rising technology based on “neutral atoms” has accelerated the competition — prompting many experts to believe that a usable machine could arrive this decade.

Optical tools in a quantum computer at Harvard University. Credit... Lucy Lu for The New York Times

Supported by

By Cade Metz

For almost a decade, a Google lab in Santa Barbara, Calif., has led the global race to build a computer that harnesses the power of quantum mechanics: the unseen physical properties that allow light, subatomic particles and other exotic matter to behave in ways that defy common sense.

But this year, a brand-new lab in Colorado — developing a totally different path to a quantum machine — has changed the narrative and accelerated the competition.

The most surprising part of all is the new lab’s funder: Google itself.

Forty-five years after scientists first floated the idea of a quantum computer, the race to build one has turned into a sprint, with many experts now believing that the first viable machine could arrive before the end of the decade or soon after. This new excitement has unlocked enormous investment, with tech giants like Amazon, IBM and Microsoft racing alongside Google. In May, after China vowed to pump more than $15.2 billion into quantum research, the Trump administration fed $2 billion into a long line of American start-ups and chip makers.

But not all companies are approaching this big idea in the same way, and it is increasingly unclear which method will prevail — which is why Google has decided to hedge its bets.

To understand this twist, it’s necessary to go back to 2014, when Hartmut Neven, a German American physicist, founded the Google lab in Santa Barbara, hiring more than 20 scientists from the physics department at the University of California campus a few miles down the road.

Like several other tech giants, the Google scientists chose to build their quantum computer with a technology called a superconducting qubit, which relies on cooling metals to extremely low temperatures. And over the next five years, Google appeared to edge ahead of its rivals. In 2019, the company announced that its machine had achieved “quantum supremacy,” defined by the completion of a task that traditional computing couldn’t solve. In under four minutes, Google’s machine performed a calculation that would have taken an existing supercomputer 10,000 years.

Even as the field has progressed, one major hurdle to the creation of a usable quantum computer has remained: the problem of “error correction.” Error correction is an essential part of any computer, ensuring that calculations aren’t skewed by heat, electrical inference or other physical forces. The silicon microchips we use every day rely on robust electrical devices and sophisticated algorithms that eliminate such errors before they crash programs or corrupt data.

But the same methods of error correction used in conventional computing and communication don’t work with quantum computing. In recent years, even as Dr. Neven’s lab made progress on the problem, he began to see research from competitors using a totally different kind of quantum computing — the “neutral atoms” method, which involves trapping individual atoms with beams of light — that seemed to make error correction easier.

Faced with that research, Dr. Neven and Google took a bold step. In April, after a decade of investment in the Santa Barbara lab, the company opened a second, competing lab in Boulder, Colo., to explore neutral atom technology.

“Superconducting will get us there, but I wanted to avoid that last moment when some other technology might pass us by, even if it is only temporary, ” Dr. Neven said. “Neutral atoms have that chance.”

Dr. Neven is among the luminaries in the field who now think that powerful quantum computers are imminent. When they do emerge, they won’t replace the computers we rely on every day. But their facility with certain types of calculations could transform the world we live in — helping researchers discover new medicines, create new materials and accelerate the progress of artificial intelligence, among other things.

A quantum computer “can allow you to look at corners of the universe where you have never been,” said Mikhail Lukin, a physics professor at Harvard.

In the basement of the Harvard Physics Laboratory — a 100-year-old building in the North Yard of university’s campus in Cambridge, Mass. — a door opens into a small room filled with computer screens, oscilloscopes, keyboards, surge protectors and a rat’s nest of electrical cables.

The floor is barely visible, mostly because the room is dominated by a rectangular enclosure surrounded on all four sides by a black curtain. As Dr. Lukin pulls back the curtain, he reveals a maze of lasers, lenses and mirrors designed to bounce beams of light into a tiny vacuum chamber in the middle of the enclosure. This is a quantum computer built from neutral atoms.

“See that little glow?” Dr. Lukin said, pointing to a nearby computer screen on which an optical microscope provided a live image from inside the tiny vacuum chamber. “That is a cloud of atoms.”

Traditional computers perform calculations by processing “bits” of information, with each bit holding either a 1 or a 0. Even the largest supercomputers, which span several buildings the size of football fields, operate in this simple way. But a quantum computer does not. It uses a new building block called a quantum bit, or qubit.

A qubit relies on superposition, a quantum-mechanical phenomenon that allows a single object to exist in multiple states — or even in multiple places — at the same time. By harnessing this strange behavior, a qubit can store a combination of 1 and 0 — two values held in the same place, at the same moment.

This means that two qubits can hold four values at once. Three qubits can hold eight values. And as the number of qubits grows, a quantum computer becomes exponentially more powerful than a traditional machine.

If this feels nonsensical, that is only natural. Famously, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman once said, “Nobody understands quantum mechanics.” The point is: Quantum systems do not behave like objects encountered in everyday life.

Out in Santa Barbara, Google’s researchers have built qubits by cooling metals to temperatures near absolute zero. They wire these metals into microchips that look a lot like the ones sitting at the heart of conventional computers.

But here in the Harvard Physics Laboratory, Dr. Lukin and his colleagues lean on a very different process. Four floors below the Harvard Yard, they drop atoms of rubidium into a vacuum chamber, where lasers can slow the movement of these tiny objects and separate them from one another. These lasers can grab hold of each atom — like a pair of tweezers pinching a house fly — and carefully isolate it from the rest of the world.

As they do, each atom becomes a qubit. Dr. Lukin and his colleagues can perform calculations by manipulating these qubits, reading and writing information through subtle changes to their physical behavior. Much as a classical machine writes data into a bit by changing its charge, a quantum computer writes data into a qubit by shifting its quantum state.

The neutral atom technique is particularly effective because it gives researchers fine-grained control over each qubit. Because these atoms are neutral — because they are separated from the rest of the world — researchers can readily move them and manipulate them. Then, exploiting a phenomenon called the Rydberg blockade, individual atoms can be excited to high-energy states that let them trade information over long distances, without interacting with other atoms close by. This allows researchers to build the equivalent of circuits, capable of running complex calculations.

But arranging clouds of atoms into viable machines involves years of work. Dr. Lukin started working on the problem in the early 2000s, and the technology is only now reaching the point where it can start to realize its promise.

Dr. Lukin is also one of the founders and the chief scientist of the Cambridge start-up Quera, which aims to commercialize the technology. Increasingly, others are following his lead. In October, he attended the Nobel Symposium on Quantum Computing in Cape Town, where Jian-Wei Pan, widely known as China’s “father of quantum,” told him that no fewer than 20 Chinese companies were building machines using neutral atoms in the city of Shanghai alone.

“We have finally demonstrated all the elements that we need to get there,” Dr. Lukin said. “For the first time, the ideas that people had three or four decades ago are now within our line of sight.”

In Santa Barbara, Google’s quantum computer looks more like a Byzantine chandelier than a maze of lasers. This silver-and-gold lattice holds computer chips made from exotic metals that Dr. Neven and his team drop into massive refrigerators, cooling them to temperatures nearly 460 degrees below zero.

For years, these superconducting qubits looked like the surest path to a viable quantum computer. Like Amazon, IBM and others, Google strung together hundreds of qubits, showing that these quantum contraptions could perform increasingly complex calculations.

Google’s research indicates that a quantum computer is capable of the feats that scientists have promised for decades. But first, like all researchers in the field, they must solve the error correction problem.

Why is error correction so much harder in quantum computing than in traditional computing? Quantum systems are plagued by the famous “Heisenberg uncertainty principle,” which explains that with superposition — the state that quantum computers use to achieve their advantage over traditional machines — measuring one of the many properties of a particle will cause others to become unmeasurable. This means that merely looking at the information in an individual qubit causes it, in the terminology of quantum mechanics, to “collapse”: It slips back in the world of classical physics and transforms into an ordinary bit.

To deal with this problem, researchers design quantum computers that span far more qubits than they need for each calculation. That way, they can then read some qubits while leaving others undisturbed.

This is effective because quantum systems exhibit another strange property called “entanglement.” Through entanglement, one quantum system can influence the behavior of another, even when very far away — a phenomenon that Albert Einstein described as “spooky action at a distance.” Thanks to entanglement, researchers can glean information from a qubit by reading other qubits inside the same machine.

Part physical and part mathematical, this elaborate process is how researchers aim to crack error correction.

“It is intricate and complicated,” said Chris Langer, a fellow at Quantinuum, a company that is using a third quantum technique called “trapped ion” computing. “The basic idea is that you don’t measure the individual bits themselves. You measure information about the collection state.”

As far back as December 2024, Google said its machine had surpassed the “error correction threshold,” meaning that as its researchers increased the number of qubits, they could exponentially reduce the number of errors. Quantinuum recently showed similar progress with trapped ions — charged particles that researchers trap and isolate in much the same way they isolate neutral atoms. But other researchers argue that error correction could be most efficient with the neutral-atoms method, because it offers more freedom to rearrange the qubits, tinker with their behavior and make the process more efficient.

When you build a quantum computer from neutral atoms, you have more room to manipulate them, to move them from place to place, to reconfigure them into new logical circuits, said Adam Kaufman, a professor of physics at the University of Colorado, Boulder. That means you have more freedom to do error correction.

“You have a way of turning their interactions on and off,” Dr. Kaufman, who leads Google’s new team in Colorado, added. “This gives you the flexibility to realize a quantum circuit that you can rewire as you evolve your quantum computer over time.”

Dr. Neven still isn’t sure which method will reach the finish line first. Even if neutral atoms win the day, he believes, superconducting qubits will be more effective in the long run. Regardless, he has faith that Google is on track to solve the error correction problem in the coming years.

The result would be a machine that is nothing like today’s supercomputers. One long-feared consequence will be the breaking of today’s encryption technologies, which rely on huge factoring problems that quantum computers will, in theory, be able to solve; earlier this year, Google vowed to overhaul its encryption techniques before 2030.

“In 2022 or 2023, I would have a told you that the encryption scare was far out,” Dr. Neven said. “The timelines have come down.”

But such a machine will also provide a way of examining the world through the lens of quantum mechanics — helping to better understand biology and disease, the world around us and the ways we navigate that world. All are dependent on the strange behavior of the quantum realm.

If you want to build a computer that simulates the natural world and helps unlock its deepest mysteries, it must operate at a level that today’s computers do not, Dr. Feynman, the physicist, explained during an 1981 lecture. “Nature isn’t classical, dammit,” he said. “If you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.”

A quantum computer is practically impossible to wrap your head around, because these machines defy common sense. They exploit quantum mechanics — the strange properties of subatomic particles and other exotic matter. For scientists like Hartmut Neven and Mikhail Lukin, who appear in this story, that super-weird behavior could let computers do things they’ve never done before.

The hope is that these counterintuitive machines will help us discover new drugs, build new materials, and even accelerate artificial intelligence. Above all, they believe these machines will help us better understand the world — since, as hard as it is for us to grasp, everything around us is ultimately driven by the strange physics of subatomic particles.

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

Watchdog Officials Considered Investigating Trump’s Memecoin, Then Punted

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Lawyers at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission looked into possible fraud soon after the digital token’s launch, then decided they would not get the commission’s support.

By Sharon LaFraniere

Sharon LaFraniere has been covering how regulators are handling Trump family businesses.

On Sunday, President Trump will for the third time be hosting a gala to promote the digital token he launched just before he returned to office.

As with the two previous events, it will allow the top buyers of his token, called a memecoin, to have face time with a president who has showered the crypto industry with favors.

But there was a moment when the fate of his memecoin could have turned out very differently.

Soon after the coin’s debut in early 2025, career officials at a federal watchdog agency opened an investigation into possible fraud. Then they quickly backed off, convinced that the agency would never approve the subpoenas or other investigative steps needed to dig into the allegations. The inquiry by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which has not been previously reported, was described by three former agency officials with direct knowledge of it who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions.

The investigation did not get far enough along to determine whether any wrongdoing had transpired. But the decision not to pursue the inquiry helped clear the way for Mr. Trump to enrich himself through token sales.

He collected at least $636 million last year in transaction and licensing fees, according to his financial disclosures. Nearly a million buyers of his memecoins lost a total of $3.81 billion through the end of June, according to Nansen, a cryptocurrency analytics firm.

The gala at the Trump National Golf Club in Northern Virginia — billed as “the most exclusive dinner in the world” — follows closely on an election that polls indicate turned in part on the issue of government corruption.

Democratic members of Congress have said the event is another attempt by Mr. Trump to monetize the presidency. The gathering explicitly allows supporters to purchase access and funnel money to a sitting president. At the first memecoin dinner, held in May 2025 at the same club, protesters chanted “shame, shame” along the road as the attendees arrived.

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said, “The president’s attendance at a privately organized event does not make it a White House event or government function.”

The promotional efforts have brought diminishing returns for Mr. Trump. The coin’s price spiked temporarily to $16.25 from $9.30 after the first event. It jumped to $4.37 from $2.87 after the second event, a luncheon at Mar-a-Lago, was announced.

Not so this time. The coin is now trading at about a dollar, lower than before the midterm election and down from a peak of $75 in January 2025. Overall, it appears to have become progressively cheaper for coin owners to win invitations to the events and to the more intimate receptions with the president.

For every coin they have purchased, buyers receive a point on a public leaderboard. The longer they hold the tokens, the more points they accrue. The top 185 are invited to the event and the top 29 to a “V. I. P. reception” with Mr. Trump.

The short-lived C. F. T. C. inquiry is the first known federal investigation that targeted a business that directly benefited Mr. Trump since his return to office. The C. F. T. C. is charged with overseeing cryptocurrency and prediction markets, two business sectors in which the Trump family is deeply invested.

A spokeswoman declined to comment on how the agency handled the investigation into the Trump coin.

Agency officials opened the inquiry amid a spate of media reports that some early buyers had profited hugely in the memecoin’s first 48 hours of trading, during which its value peaked. For example, five traders who made huge buys in the first five minutes cleared more than $44 million in profits, according to an analysis by Nansen for The New York Times. The agency also received at least one outside complaint, former officials said.

Only 20 percent of the coins were initially for sale; the Trump Organization and its partner, the entrepreneur Bill Zanker, owned the other 80 percent. Those coins were locked up according to a staggered three-year schedule to reassure buyers that the backers of the coin would not suddenly cash out and rob it of its value — a practice sometimes called a “rug pull.”

Even if Mr. Trump and other backers were barred from selling his coins, though, C. F. T. C. officials were concerned about possible insider trading or other abuses.

The inquiry was assigned to Dan Ullman, an enforcement division lawyer and 16-year veteran of the agency who specialized in cryptocurrency cases. Mr. Ullman, who left the C. F. T. C. in late 2025, declined to comment on the inquiry.

Agency lawyers have the authority to open investigations, but they need the commission’s approval to issue subpoenas, which would have been necessary for identifying suspicious traders. While the memecoin trades are recorded on a public blockchain, many of the buyers are anonymous.

At that time, the board had four commissioners, including two Democrats. But three of them were on their way out, either by choice or because their terms were expiring.

That left Caroline D. Pham, a Republican commissioner whom Mr. Trump had elevated as the agency’s new temporary chairman.

In early April 2025, Ms. Pham directed the agency not to seek to charge crypto players with regulatory violations, The Times has previously reported. She pressured enforcement staff to drop existing crypto investigations, The Times reported.

Given all that, agency officials decided that she would never approve subpoenas involving the president’s cryptocurrency, the people with knowledge of the situation said.

Ms. Pham, who left the agency last year to join a crypto firm, did not respond to requests for comment.

The C. F. T. C. had previously brought at least one case charging illegal manipulation of the price of a memecoin during the Biden administration. In 2021, it charged a businessman and an adviser with a “pump and dump” scheme that involved, in part, the popular “Doge” memecoin. (Elon Musk, who promoted but did not create that coin, borrowed the name for his federal cost-cutting initiative.)

The agency said the two men secretly accumulated the coins and artificially drove up their prices by hyping them on social media — all the while lying to the public about their financial interest in them. They then dumped their holdings and cleared more than $2 million in profits.

Both men also faced criminal charges for commodities fraud and money laundering related to the scheme. The businessman died shortly after he was charged. His adviser paid a civil penalty of $145,000.

Sharon LaFraniere is an investigative reporter focusing on the Trump administration.

Threats, Insults, Settlements: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

The Nvidia co-founder’s belittling behavior toward employees goes back decades. It once led to a confidential settlement agreement with an executive who said Mr. Huang “terrorized” staff.

By Emily SteelKalley HuangRyan Mac and Tripp Mickle

The reporters interviewed more than a dozen current and former employees and reviewed court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. You can send them tips at nytimes. com/tips.

As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.

“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.

Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.

Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Mr. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Mr. Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.

Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Mr. Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U. S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Mr. Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)

Mr. Huang denied Mr. Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Mr. Fisher said. Mr. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Mr. Huang’s behavior.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Mr. Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Mr. Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C. E. O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Mr. Huang.

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.

Mr. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A. I. boom.

Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Mr. Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Mr. Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.

But in the eyes of some, Mr. Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.

In September 2004, Mr. Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Mr. Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H. R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Mr. Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.

In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.

That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.

“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Mr. Huang said at one point.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”

Mr. Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”

Mr. Winston said he then confronted Mr. Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.

Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

That November, Mr. Winston was called into a meeting with Mr. Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Mr. Huang told Mr. Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Mr. Winston sued Nvidia, Mr. Huang said he would make sure Mr. Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.

“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Mr. Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”

In the months that followed, Mr. Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Mr. Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Mr. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.

Mr. Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.

In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Mr. Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Mr. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”

Mr. Pettigrew discussed Mr. Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Mr. Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Mr. Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.

Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Mr. Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.

After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Mr. Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A. I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A. I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A. I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A. I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.

Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U. S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.

“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”

Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A. I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A. I. start-up Mistral.

During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.

“You’re not even speaking human,” Mr. Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.

Daniel Gutierrez, an A. I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

Emily Steel is an investigative reporter covering business for The Times. She has uncovered sexual misconduct at major companies and recently has focused on the ride-hailing industry.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Ryan Mac is a Times reporter who covers corporate accountability across the global technology industry.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Quantum Computing Is Even Weirder Than You Think

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a new study, Google researchers demonstrated a strange phenomenon called quantum contextuality, in which a quantum machine’s data can change as the context does.

By Cade Metz

Cade Metz loves thinking about quantum computers. But like the rest of the world, he is still waiting for them to fulfill their promise.

Every time you open an email on your laptop or smartphone, it looks the same. The same words appear in the same order. Now, imagine if the email changed each time you read it, shifting in response to everything else you were reading on your computer.

In a paper published on Thursday in the journal Science, a team of Google researchers showed that the company’s experimental quantum computer exhibited behavior along these lines — though the particulars were much weirder and even harder to wrap one’s head around. This mind-bending phenomenon, called quantum contextuality, is a strong sign that quantum computers will one day do powerful things that no traditional machine could ever do.

“All of that weirdness can fit on a chip,” said Rodrigo Cortiñas, a Google researcher who was part of the study. “That is what we are building.”

A quantum computer is a machine that leverages the power of quantum mechanics, the strange physical properties of subatomic particles and other exotic matter. Google is among the many companies that, together with academic labs and government institutions, have spent decades working to realize this idea, which could help discover new medicines, create new materials, accelerate the progress of artificial intelligence and more.

But as the Google researchers show in the new paper, the calculations performed by a quantum computer are nothing like those made by a classical machine. When you read a piece of information from a quantum computer, what you read is not fixed in advance but instead depends on all sorts of other information you are reading from the machine.

In their paper, the Google researchers demonstrate this phenomenon using the company’s quantum computer in Santa Barbara, Calif., which relies on what are called “superconducting qubits” — metals cooled to nearly 460 degrees below zero. Thanks to quantum contextuality, the paper shows, Google’s machine outperforms the best possible classical strategy on “the magic square game,” an elaborate mathematical contest.

This game is a bit like Sudoku: Two teammates work to fill a three-by-three grid with numbers that meet certain mathematical criteria. But the two teammates are not allowed to communicate.

By exploiting the weird way that information is created only when they read individual qubits — the “quantum bits” that these nascent machines are built on — teammates can settle on a common strategy more often than they do in the classical realm. And that means they win the game more often.

Google’s magic square game is a “toy problem” — a puzzle that demonstrates the power of a technology but provides no practical benefit. Researchers at Google and inside many other labs are still working to refine their quantum computers, so that they can tackle big, practical tasks. But if a quantum computer can crack problems like the magic square game, Google’s researchers believe, it could open the door to calculations that really mean something.

“You can describe quantum contextuality as the superpower of quantum mechanics,” said Michel Devoret, a Google researcher who won a Nobel Prize for his work on quantum mechanics.

To explain quantum contextuality, one of the paper’s authors, the Google researcher Shashwat Kumar, uses the example of a coin flip.

When you flip a nickel or a quarter into the air and cover it with your palm before actually looking at it, the result of the flip has been determined. Under your palm, the coin is either heads or tails. And that won’t change when you lift your palm.

But with quantum contextuality, he says, this familiar dynamic changes. If you also measure the size of the coin as you are checking for heads or tails, the result of the coin flip will change.

“The outcomes of quantum measurements are not predetermined,” Dr. Kumar said. “They are not ready to be read from a list. They come into existence while you are making the measurements, and they are shaped by other measurements around them.”

If that seems hard to understand, don’t worry. Like so much of quantum physics, it does not make sense to human beings accustomed to thinking about the world through the lens of classical physics.

For Mark Howard, a physicist at the University of Galway in Ireland who was not involved in the study, the point is that quantum computers behave in a way that classical computers do not. If scientists can harness this power, they can run calculations that would never be possible on a traditional supercomputer.

“The dream is that contextuality is the fuel that makes a quantum computer superpowered,” he said.

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

Dudes Online Are So Mad That GTA VI Makes Them Respect Women

Wired November 19, 2026

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)

More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

And Andrew Tate himself denounced the game in a Thursday email blast to his newsletter subscribers. “The establishment does not understand the male spirit,” he wrote from jail in Miami, where he and his brother Tristan Tate are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape, human trafficking, and assault. “No man wants to be a slave who breaks his back and gets nothing back.” Promoting a link to classes for building “AI systems,” he exhorted his readers: “Put down the game controller.”

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.)

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.

It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

Phone accessories are aplenty on Amazon, but few look as good as Moft’s. You can pick up this ingenious wallet-kickstand hybrid that attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe, or peruse the rest of Moft's Black Friday deals.

Amazon

Amazon

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our short list, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s you, it’s NBD. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $40, but it’s 50 percent off right now.

Soundcore by Anker

Amazon

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boom box in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

Ecoflow

Amazon

Amazon (20,000 mAh)

This EcoFlow portable battery is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s pick as the best power bank for laptops. It has a large 27,650-mAh capacity, which is plenty for charging smaller devices too. It’s great for travel since it’s allowed on a plane, and it has a retractable USB-C cable, so you can leave extras at home.

Bose

Amazon

Bose

At $359, the second-gen Bose QuietComfort over-ear headphones seem overpriced considering the competition. But when they’re on sale at $199 to $219 (depending on the color), they suddenly become a great buy. As expected from Bose, the noise cancellation and sound quality are excellent. They are also comfortable, making them great travel companions. Note that the first-gen version is also on sale for $169 (it’s frequently at this price), but it’s outdated, and we think you should spend $30 to $50 more on the latest version instead.

Nespresso

Amazon

Love them or hate them, but pod-based coffee makers are popular for their convenience. The Nespresso Vertuo Pop+ is our recommended espresso pod maker, and the Deluxe model is under $100. It has a larger water tank than the standard version, and the Vertuo pods are recyclable. For more savings on coffee-related products, check out our Early Black Friday Espresso Machine Deals.

Eufy

Eufy

De'Longhi

Amazon

Best Buy

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.

What’s With All These Outages?

Wired November 19, 2026

Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and the administration’s new rule to stop Chinese companies from renting AI chips just before Trump meets Xi.

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Sophie Kleeman on X/Twitter at @sophiekleeman, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired. com.

Wake Up, the Hatch Sleep Clock Is the Latest Big Black Friday Deal

Wired November 19, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

If you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking into one bedside gadget. And for the first time, it’s going on sale (early) as a Black Friday deal.

From November 19 through November 20, the Sleep Clock is 25 percent off at Hatch and Amazon. Normally $250, it’s down to $188, which is just $18 more than the Hatch Restore 3’s $170 retail price. And unlike its predecessor, the newer Hatch adds passive sleep monitoring, which is pretty compelling for anyone who hates wearing wearables to bed. Or maybe you’re like me and occasionally forget to wear your Oura Ring to bed, in which case, you wouldn’t have to worry because the Hatch is already quietly tracking your sleep in the background.

Hatch

Hatch

I’ve been testing the Hatch Sleep Clock for over two months, and it’s earned a permanent spot on my nightstand. As someone who already wears a smart ring and smartwatch to bed, I’m not exactly short on sleep-tracking data. But I’ve never owned a sunrise alarm clock, and I instantly became a convert. Unlike my iPhone or Amazon Echo Dot, it doesn’t wake me up by blaring an obnoxious alarm in my pitch-black bedroom. Instead, it gradually illuminates the room within my scheduled wake-up time. You can customize the sunrise's duration and brightness, and pair it with a soundscape of your choosing. It truly makes getting out of bed feel less jarring, especially as the mornings get darker.

Most notably, the Sleep Clock also doubles as a contactless sleep tracker, using a built-in motion sensor to detect your movements and breathing throughout the night. I compared its readings against my Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12, and while sleep duration estimates were generally aligned, the sleep-stage readings were less consistent. The device doesn’t measure physiological metrics like heart rate, and it can’t detect snoring or other audio-based sleep disruptions. I also found that placement significantly matters. My nightstand tends to collect clutter, so I had to rearrange my trinkets to make room for the clock.

Each morning, the Hatch app gives you a breakdown of when you went to bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and how much time you spent in different sleep stages. The color-coded reports are easy to understand without burying me in random metrics. Plus, unlike most sleep trackers, Hatch doesn't require a subscription to access your sleep data. (You will need that Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) if you want to access the full audio library, however.)

Overall, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the best all-in-one bedside device. I wouldn’t recommend replacing your dedicated wearable with it if detailed health tracking is your priority. But if you’ve been wanting a sunrise alarm clock that can also offer a little insight into your sleep, do not sleep on this Black Friday deal.

If you don’t care for sleep tracking, Hatch is also offering discounts on several other products across its lineup.

The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants

Wired November 19, 2026

Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”

Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023.

Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.

“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.

“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”

Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.

Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop.

In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars.

The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.

But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business.

The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.

Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”

Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”

Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents

Wired November 19, 2026

As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness,” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed, so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see; the exploration space that we have to address is huge, and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgment when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that, in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode-type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step; there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated, we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself

Wired November 19, 2026

After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”

Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.)

Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.)

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

“Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz says. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”

Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the company offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest company in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.
